blind_text:
statement: The system accumulates a scalar '[X] debt' D that integrates the deviation between observed avalanche-size exponent and a reference exponent over time; D then additively shifts the location of the [X]'s control parameter, producing hysteresis: the critical point visited depends on the avalanche history rather than being fixed by the bare Hamiltonian.
what exists: [X] heights h_i; running estimate of avalanche exponent τ_hat; scalar debt variable D; control parameter p_eff = p0 + κ·D that sets the [X] location
what changes: τ_hat is updated after each avalanche from a sliding window; D += (τ_hat - τ_ref); the order parameter's transition point shifts to p_eff, which in turn changes toppling thresholds.
what persists: D persists indefinitely (bounded by a slow leak term) forming a long-term memory trace of past deviations.
what is selected: no discrete selection; but trajectories that stabilize D near zero are dynamically favored (self-correcting).
what can reproduce: not applicable.
what can learn: D functions as a single learned scalar summarizing the system's history and biasing future [X] location — a minimal memory.
what can transfer: D can be copied into a freshly initialized lattice to test whether it reproduces the hysteretic critical point without needing to relive the avalanche history.
distinguishing observable: forward and reverse sweeps of a slow external drive show a hysteresis loop in the order parameter whose width is set by accumulated D; null twin recomputes p_eff from the current avalanche [X] only (no integration/memory), producing a reversible, loop-free transition.
minimal world: [X]-order-parameter system with D as described; intervene by replacing D's integral (memory) with an instantaneous function of current τ_hat only (null, memoryless); drive p0 up and down slowly and compare hysteresis loop area between the two.

nearest_priors.name: Leaky integral feedback (homeostatic) control of a near-critical system: self-tuned criticality via adaptive thresholds or couplings, e.g. Levina–Herrmann–Geisel dynamical synapses and homeostatic tuning of branching ratio
nearest_priors.field: Statistical physics / computational neuroscience / control theory
nearest_priors.explains: A slow scalar integrates the error between an observed avalanche statistic and a target and shifts the control parameter and toppling thresholds. The leak bounds the memory. Trajectories that drive the error to zero are favored, as with an integral controller's set point. Hysteresis and loops appear under a swept drive because the integrator lags. A memoryless proportional version (the null twin) gives no loop.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Using the avalanche-size exponent τ_hat estimated over a sliding window, rather than branching ratio or activity, as the error signal is a specific choice. Transplanting D into a fresh lattice is an extra experimental protocol, not part of the prior.

nearest_priors.name: Self-organized criticality sandpile (Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld / Manna) with slow drive and dissipation
nearest_priors.explains: Lattice heights h_i, toppling thresholds, avalanches with a power-law size exponent, and slow external drive.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The explicit memory variable D, the shift of the critical point, and hysteresis dependent on history. Standard SOC has no integral controller.

nearest_priors.name: Rate-dependent hysteresis from a slow internal variable (dynamic hysteresis / Preisach-like memory / slow-fast systems with a leaky integrator)
nearest_priors.explains: The loop area under forward and reverse sweeps is set by accumulated internal state. The loop vanishes when that state is made instantaneous. The loop width depends on sweep rate relative to the leak rate.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The avalanche-exponent sensing and the lattice toppling dynamics.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. The loop is essentially the lag of a leaky integral controller acting on an SOC lattice. It should shrink to zero under quasistatic sweeps slower than the leak time, so it is dynamic hysteresis rather than true multistability. Using a noisy sliding-window estimate of τ as the error signal is a design choice, not a new mechanism. The 'transfer D' test simply restores the controller's integrator state.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Sweep p0 at several rates and with several leak constants. If the loop area goes to zero as sweep period greatly exceeds the leak time, and scales with κ times the integrated error, this is plain leaky integral-control lag, which is the prior. A loop that persists in the quasistatic limit, or that depends on the ordering of avalanche history beyond what the integral captures, would indicate genuine multistable memory beyond the prior. Also swap the τ error signal for a branching-ratio error signal. If the behavior is unchanged, the exponent-specific framing adds nothing.

blind_text:
statement: Memory is a recursive partition tree caching sound bounds and local sensitivity at each node; updates propagate upward only when change exceeds a threshold that shrinks by a fixed ratio per level, producing scale-free (power-law) cache-invalidation cascades rather than characteristic-scale ones.
what exists: partition tree nodes with (bound_lo, bound_hi, sensitivity_est); per-level threshold tau_l = tau_0*beta^l
what changes: leaf updates propagate to ancestors only while |change| > tau_l at each level; surviving ancestors recompute bounds as sound hull of children
what persists: the invalidation-event size distribution remains a stable power law as long as beta and the input's own fractal [X] are stationary
what is selected: nodes with high true local sensitivity are effectively selected for more frequent refresh, allocating memory bandwidth self-similarly
what can reproduce: the same update rule instantiates identically at every tree depth
what can learn: beta and tau_0 can be tuned to match observed real invalidation [X], implicitly learning the process's fractal dimension
what can transfer: a fit beta transfers to predict cache-update costs on a but statistically similar stream without re-tuning
distinguishing observable: invalidation cascade sizes follow a power-law tail under the scaled threshold rule versus an exponential/thin tail under a constant-threshold rule at matched average update rate
minimal world: World: streaming signal with known fractional Brownian [X] (Hurst H) feeding a fixed-depth binary tree maintaining sound running min/max at every scale. Intervention: set tau_l=tau_0*beta^l with beta matched to H, record cascade sizes. Null twin: identical tree/signal/average update rate but constant threshold across levels; predicted to lack the power-law tail despite matched average bound tightness.

nearest_priors.name: Hierarchical aggregation trees with per-level error budgets and filter-based suppression (Olston–Widom adaptive filters, TAG/approximate in-network aggregation, sensor-network dead-band/send-on-delta reporting over segment-tree-style min/max caches)
nearest_priors.field: databases / distributed stream monitoring / data structures
nearest_priors.explains: Recursive partition tree caching sound interval bounds (min/max hulls) per node; leaf updates propagating to ancestors only when the change exceeds a node-specific tolerance; parents recomputing bounds as the hull of their children; per-level threshold allocation; tuning thresholds to match observed update costs.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Does not predict or target a power-law distribution of cascade sizes. It gives no link between a geometric per-level threshold ratio and the Hurst exponent of the input.

nearest_priors.name: Scale-dependent (level-wise geometric) thresholding of multiresolution coefficients for fractional Brownian motion (wavelet/Haar thresholding, Flandrin/Wornell fBm wavelet analysis)
nearest_priors.explains: fBm increments at dyadic scale 2^l have spread ~2^{lH}. A threshold tau_0*beta^l with beta tied to H makes the exceedance probability scale-invariant across levels, which gives the self-similar refresh allocation and the implicit estimation of fractal dimension from fitted beta.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Does not account for the cache/sound-bound maintenance framing or for propagation of invalidation cascades up a tree as an event-size distribution.

nearest_priors.name: Critical branching process / self-organized criticality (sandpile-style avalanches) versus subcritical threshold cascades
nearest_priors.explains: Each level passes the event upward with some conditional probability. When that probability is scale-invariant (critical tuning via beta), cascade sizes are power-law distributed. A constant threshold makes the pass-through probability decay with level (subcritical), giving an exponential/thin tail. This explains the distinguishing observable and the transfer of a fitted beta to statistically similar streams.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The criticality here is externally tuned, not self-organized. The branching picture also ignores the soundness of hull bounds and the specific tree data structure.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. The novel part is only the combination: using the geometric per-level dead-band ratio, matched to the Hurst exponent, as a criticality knob so that invalidation cascades in a sound-bound aggregation tree become power-law distributed. The description also leaves some details open. It is unclear whether 'change' means the change in a child's hull or the raw leaf delta, and since hull changes can only shrink going upward, the direction of the scaling needed for criticality needs care. The claim that bound tightness is matched under the null is asserted but not derived.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Feed fBm streams with several Hurst values H into the same binary min/max tree. Sweep beta and record the cascade-size distribution. If the mechanism is simply a critical branching process tuned by beta relative to 2^{-H}, the power-law tail should appear only near beta ≈ 2^{-H}, with an exponential cutoff on either side. The tail exponent should follow mean-field branching (≈3/2 for size), independent of the soundness constraint. A plain per-level dead-band aggregation tree without the H-matching would show no such sharp transition. Replacing the sound hull with an unsound averaged summary while keeping the thresholds fixed tests whether the hull semantics matter beyond the scaling of the threshold.

blind_text:
statement: The agent's belief is a finite-state hypothesis automaton H_t that explains an observed trace under a temporal-[X] goal spec φ. At each tick, a model checker searches exhaustively for a counterexample to 'H_t is consistent with all observations and satisfies φ'; any counterexample becomes a explanandum fed back into the [X] generator, which emits H_{t+1}. Neither abduction alone (no falsifier) nor [X] alone (no generator, fixed hypothesis set) produces this closed refinement loop.

what changes: H_t is replaced by H_{t+1} = Abduce(H_t, counterexample); the counterexample buffer accumulates falsifying witnesses.
what persists: all previously found counterexamples (a monotonically growing falsification set) and φ itself.
what is selected: hypotheses that satisfy φ against the entire accumulated counterexample set, not merely the newest observation.
what can reproduce: surviving H_t can spawn structural variants (added/merged states) as candidate H_{t+1} offspring.
what can learn: the abduction generator learns which counterexample shapes call for which repair (state-split vs transition-add).
what can transfer: learned repair heuristics transfer to φ over the same observation alphabet.
distinguishing observable: counterexample-recurrence rate strictly decreases over time only in the combined condition; abduction-only control shows drifting hypotheses with recurring failures, [X]-only control shows a static hypothesis set that never grows to accommodate counterexamples.
minimal world: A 6-state hidden Markov-like environment emits symbol sequences; the agent must produce an automaton satisfying φ='eventually always safe'. Intervention: inject a rare trap sequence at episode 50. Null twin: an agent that re-runs abduction on raw observations every step but discards model-checker output (verdict is computed but not fed back), matching compute cost and observation [X] but lacking the counterexample-conditioned update; the twin fails to stabilize on the trap sequence while the true mechanism converges.

This is essentially meta-learned CEGIS or learned refinement heuristics, which is known but not intrinsic to the base loop. The 'reproduce' clause (spawning structural variants) is a thin evolutionary gloss rather than a central mechanism.

If counterexample-recurrence and iterations-to-convergence match plain CEGIS or L* with a fixed refinement rule, the mechanism is just CEGIS. If the learned-heuristic agent converges in measurably fewer refinement rounds on phi' and on a trap sequence at episode 50, the learned repair component adds something beyond the prior. distinguishing observable: final performance on a shifted input [X] depends sharply on when exposure occurs relative to tau (steep drop if delayed past closure), whereas a null twin with constant plasticity (matched total weight-change budget) shows timing-independent, graceful learning regardless of when exposure occurs
minimal world: A classifier is exposed to an altered input [X] (e.g., rotated feature distribution) either early or late during a fixed-length training run with eta(t) annealed. statement: A role vector and a filler vector are bound into a joint representation via their outer product (tensor product binding); a bound representation can be unbound by contracting it with a role vector to recover an approximation of the associated filler, and multiple bindings can be superimposed by summation before unbinding.
what exists: a set of role vectors; a set of filler vectors; a superimposed binding tensor (sum of outer products)
what changes: bindings are added by outer-producting a role and filler and adding the result to the binding tensor; unbinding contracts the binding tensor with a probe role vector.
what persists: the summed binding tensor persists as the memory trace of all bindings made so far.
what is selected: role/filler vector sets that are sufficiently orthogonal/incoherent are effectively retained (low crosstalk on unbinding); highly correlated role sets degrade and are effectively 'forgotten' by interference.
what can reproduce: the same binding/unbinding operation can be applied recursively to bind bindings (structured/nested roles), reproducing the mechanism at a higher level.
what can learn: which role vectors to assign to which relational slots so that unbinding recovers fillers with minimal interference.
what can transfer: a fixed role vocabulary (e.g. 'subject', 'object') can be reused across arbitrary fillers without retraining the binding/unbinding operation itself.
distinguishing observable: unbinding accuracy degrades gracefully and predictably as a function of role-vector correlation and number of superimposed bindings (interference), a signature curve absent in a lookup-table memory that stores each binding as a separate labeled slot (which shows no correlation-dependent interference).
minimal world: Define a small set of near-orthogonal role vectors and filler vectors; bind k (role,filler) pairs by summing outer products into one tensor, then probe with each role to retrieve fillers and measure retrieval error as k increases and as role-orthogonality is degraded. The null twin stores each (role,filler) pair in a separate indexed memory slot with a dedicated lookup key (matched total storage size), so retrieval error stays flat regardless of k and role-correlation, isolating the interference signature specific to superposition-via-outer-product.

nearest_priors.name: Tensor Product Representations (Smolensky, 1990)
nearest_priors.explains: Nearly all of it. Role-filler binding is the outer product, and superposition is a sum of bindings. Unbinding contracts with a role, or with its dual or inverse vector. Recursive binding of bindings gives nested structure. A fixed role vocabulary is reused across arbitrary fillers. Crosstalk depends on role non-orthogonality.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard TPR unbinding is exact when roles are linearly independent and the unbinding vectors are chosen correctly (orthonormal roles or the dual basis). The 'graceful degradation with k' holds only when roles are near-orthogonal but not independent, or when k exceeds the role dimensionality. The 'learning role assignment' is an add-on, as in later learned-TPR work (e.g., TP-Transformer, TPR-RNN), not core TPR.

nearest_priors.name: Correlation-matrix / linear associative memory (Kohonen 1972; Anderson 1972; Hebbian outer-product storage)
nearest_priors.explains: Stores pairs as a summed outer-product matrix and retrieves by matrix-vector product with the key. Crosstalk grows with key correlation and number of stored pairs. It shows the capacity and interference curve, contrasted with addressable slot memory.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not frame keys as reusable symbolic roles. It has no recursive binding of bindings into higher-order tensors to represent nested structure.

nearest_priors.name: Holographic Reduced Representations / Vector Symbolic Architectures (Plate 1995; Kanerva; Gayler)
nearest_priors.explains: Role-filler binding, superposition by summation, and approximate unbinding with noisy recovery. Graceful degradation with the number of bindings and with role similarity. Recursive composition and reusable role vectors.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: HRR uses circular convolution, which compresses to fixed dimension, rather than the full outer product. Its dimensionality therefore does not grow with nesting depth, unlike the described tensor-rank growth.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially nothing. The only novelty is the framing of 'selection/forgetting' of correlated role sets as interference, which is standard crosstalk analysis. Learned role assignment corresponds to existing learned-TPR models.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Use exactly linearly independent roles with k ≤ role dimension and unbind with dual-basis vectors. TPR predicts zero retrieval error, whereas the described claim of unavoidable graceful degradation with k would predict nonzero error. Separately, nest bindings to depth 3. TPR predicts representation dimension growing as d^depth. HRR-style compression would keep the dimension fixed, with noise accumulating.

statement: A transition operator's action is projected onto the subspace spanned by its top-k eigenvectors (by eigenvalue magnitude) before being applied, so dynamics are forced through a low-dimensional invariant channel that preserves slow, persistent modes and discards fast-decaying ones. what is selected: eigenvectors are kept in proportion to eigenvalue magnitude (persistence over time), not variance of the raw signal
what can reproduce: different high-dimensional trajectories sharing the same dominant modes reproduce the same k-dim summary
what can learn: k or the projector can be tuned to trade off reconstruction error against long-horizon predictive accuracy
what can transfer: the compressed k-dim code, once learned from one task, can be reused to predict a different observable generated by the same underlying T
distinguishing observable: long-horizon prediction accuracy from the k eigenvector code versus a same-dimension random projection baseline (matched dimensionality/variance but not aligned to T's slow modes) — the eigenvector code degrades much more slowly with horizon

statement: Removing or adding a single node changes not just fixed-point locations but the volume and boundary geometry of the basins of attraction in a multistable community; a species' 'keystone-ness' is defined as the derivative of basin-volume partition with respect to its removal, independent of its biomass or degree.
what exists: state vector x in R^N; signed weighted interaction matrix A; multiple coexisting attractors; basin partition of initial-condition space
what changes: removing row/column i of A changes the vector field f(x;A); Monte Carlo sampling of initial conditions recomputes the fraction converging to each attractor before vs after removal.
what persists: the identity of surviving attractors, even as their basin volumes shift.
what is selected: none directly; this is a structural rule, not a selection process.
what can reproduce: species reproduce logistically within f(x;A).
what can learn: not applicable to this mechanism alone.
what can transfer: keystone rank should be invariant to uniform rescaling of all edge weights, testable directly.
distinguishing observable: a low-biomass, low-degree species can produce disproportionate basin reorganization (large total-variation distance in basin partition), which a biomass/degree-based ranking cannot predict.
minimal world: A 4-species Lotka-Volterra system engineered with two coexisting stable attractors; intervention removes each species and resamples 10,000 initial conditions to measure basin-fraction shifts. Null twin: replace the removed species with a passive constant biomass offset added to other species' growth terms (matching total redistributed biomass) but without its nonlinear coupling terms; basin volumes should not shift in the null.

Scores node importance by how much basin fractions change when that node is removed. nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Does not by itself supply the ecological framing: the keystone label and the explicit contrast with biomass-weighted importance.

Removes row and column i and assesses the consequences for the community. Also covers alternative stable states in multistable communities (May 1977; Scheffer's regime shifts).
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Classical deletion studies score secondary extinctions or local stability, not the reallocation of basin volume among surviving attractors.

nearest_priors.explains: Treats a node knockout as a structural perturbation of the vector field that preserves attractor identity while shifting basin sizes and boundaries. Matches the observation that nonlinear coupling, rather than the mean-field offset, drives basin reorganization.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is left unexplained. The claimed invariance of keystone rank under uniform rescaling of A holds only if the initial-condition sampling domain is rescaled consistently. In gLV, scaling A by c scales equilibria by 1/c, so fixed sampling bounds would break the invariance. The 'derivative with respect to removal' is really a finite difference. The null twin, a constant growth-rate offset, also moves fixed points, so the claim that basins will not shift in the null is not guaranteed. These are specification weaknesses, not novel mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare the proposed keystone ranking with a pure deletion-basin-stability ranking (Menck-style) on the same 4-species gLV system. Then rescale A by c while holding the sampling box fixed, and separately with the box scaled by 1/c. If the rankings are identical to basin-stability deletion scores and the invariance holds only under the scaled box, the mechanism reduces entirely to node-deletion basin stability. Any residual difference would have to come from an added ingredient, such as boundary geometry beyond volume fractions.

nearest_priors.name: Partial-update / selective-update adaptive filtering (M-max NLMS/RLS, selective partial update) applied to the Kalman filter, i.e. top-m masking of the gain or update vector
nearest_priors.explains: Thresholding the gain or update vector to its m largest entries each step. Correction applied only along the retained coordinates. Support that changes step to step according to a magnitude ranking. Mask size m tuned against the tradeoff between tracking error and compute.

nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The literal top-m thresholding of gain entries, as opposed to selecting whole sensors before the update. The sparse-dictionary state code.

nearest_priors.name: Sparse/compressive Kalman filtering (Kalman filter with sparse state in a dictionary, e.g. KF-CS, l1-regularized or dynamic sparse coding filters)
nearest_priors.explains: A state that is a sparse code over dictionary atoms and is updated recursively by gain-weighted innovations. It serves as the null twin in which sparsity is imposed on the state only.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. The divergence itself follows directly from applying two independent sparsity masks, to the gain and to the state. The description leaves the ranking criterion only loosely specified (a mix of innovation magnitude and uncertainty reduction). It also treats K_t as a vector, which holds only for scalar observations or after flattening.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Hold the dictionary and the state support fixed and switch sensor noise variances across channels quickly. If the mechanism reduces to these priors, the supports will match the baselines step by step, and the divergence between gain support and state support will appear equally in all of them. If the mechanism is genuinely distinct, its combined innovation-and-uncertainty ranking should yield supports and tracking error that measurably differ from both baselines.

blind_text:
statement: Within a basin of attraction, the local flow has negative Lyapunov exponents that contract nearby trajectories back toward the attractor. When an external perturbation displaces the state within the basin (but not across its boundary), this contraction automatically restores the state toward its pre-perturbation trajectory without any explicit error signal, comparison, or corrective computation—the correction is a direct consequence of the deterministic flow's local stability.
what exists: state x on or near an attractor A; local flow f with negative local Lyapunov exponent near A; perturbation vector delta applied at time t*
what changes: x_{t*} = x_{t*} + delta (perturbation); thereafter x_{t+1}=f(x_t) evolves normally, contracting back toward A
what persists: the attractor A and its basin boundary persist unchanged by the perturbation, provided delta doesn't cross the boundary
what is selected: no selection; this is an automatic consequence of local stability
what can reproduce: not applicable directly
what can learn: the basin's contraction rate (correction speed) can be shaped by slowly modifying f
what can transfer: the same correction property transfers to any perturbation of the same magnitude class, as long as it stays within the basin
distinguishing observable: measure recovery time to baseline trajectory as a function of perturbation magnitude: within-basin perturbations show fast exponential recovery (rate = |local Lyapunov exponent|) while perturbations exceeding basin boundary show no recovery (system settles at a different attractor)—this threshold behavior distinguishes true attractor-based correction from a system with globally uniform (linear, boundary-free) restoring force
minimal world: A single-well potential representing one basin with a known boundary at x=+/-B; apply perturbations of increasing magnitude at a fixed time and measure return time to the attractor. Intervention: push perturbation magnitude past B and observe failure to return. Null twin: a linear restoring force (harmonic oscillator with damping, no boundary) matched in small-perturbation recovery rate, which continues to 'recover' (converge to origin) even for arbitrarily large perturbations, lacking the true system's boundary-dependent failure mode.

nearest_priors.name: Asymptotic (Lyapunov) stability of an attractor with a finite basin of attraction; linearization and local contraction (Lyapunov 1892, Poincaré; Hartman–Grobman; contraction analysis of Lohmiller–Slotine)
nearest_priors.explains: Negative local Lyapunov exponents or eigenvalues give exponential return at rate |λ|. Perturbations inside the basin decay and those crossing the separatrix go to another attractor. No error signal is needed because stability is a property of the flow itself. The threshold contrast with a globally stable linear system is the textbook local-versus-global asymptotic stability distinction.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Slow learning that reshapes f to tune the contraction rate is not part of the stability theory itself.

nearest_priors.name: Attractor-network error correction / content-addressable memory (Hopfield 1982; continuous attractor and multistable neural networks)
nearest_priors.explains: Corrupted states within a basin relax back to the stored pattern with no explicit comparison. Corruption beyond the basin retrieves a different memory. Learning (Hebbian weight changes) reshapes the basins and their depth.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It usually concerns fixed-point memories rather than restoring a moving trajectory, and it rarely stresses recovery rate equal to the Lyapunov exponent.

nearest_priors.name: Homeorhesis / canalization in the epigenetic landscape (Waddington); ecological resilience and tipping points in multistable potentials (Holling; Scheffer)
nearest_priors.explains: Trajectories (chreodes) return after perturbation without any regulator. Basin width sets resilience, and perturbations past a threshold flip the system to an alternative stable state. Evolution or slow change of the landscape tunes the buffering.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It is a qualitative framework without the quantitative Lyapunov-exponent recovery-rate prediction.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially nothing. One quibble: a strictly single-well potential has no basin boundary at ±B, so the minimal world implicitly needs barriers or a multi-well landscape, such as a quartic double or triple well. Standard theory also predicts critical slowing down near the boundary, where return time diverges, rather than a clean step from 'fast recovery' to 'no recovery'.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: No intervention separates the description from asymptotic stability of an attractor with a finite basin, because they are the same mechanism. To check fidelity: sweep perturbation magnitude in a double-well system x' = x - x^3 (attractors at ±1, separatrix at 0). Recovery rate for small delta should equal |f'(x*)|. Recovery time should diverge logarithmically as delta approaches the separatrix. Past the separatrix the state should converge to the other well. The damped linear oscillator should show a magnitude-independent rate and no failure.

blind_text:
statement: Instead of computing credit via analytic backpropagation through a fixed forward graph, each unit's parameters are updated using the covariance between independently injected exogenous perturbations to that unit and the resulting change in global loss, holding other units' perturbations statistically independent (node perturbation). This produces an unbiased estimate of each unit's causal effect on the loss even when units are confounded by shared upstream input.
what exists: network units u_i with independent injected perturbations δ_i per trial; global loss L; running covariance estimate between δ_i and ΔL per unit; a confound: two units sharing a common upstream driver, only one of which is causally read out downstream
what changes: Δparameters_i ∝ Cov(δ_i, ΔL) estimated over trials via random independent perturbation and loss comparison, updated incrementally
what persists: causal effect estimates accumulate and stabilize distinguishing truly load-bearing units from merely correlated ones
what is selected: units whose independent perturbation reliably changes the loss are reinforced; units correlated with the outcome only through a confound are not
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: correct attribution of credit under confounding, i.e., not reinforcing a unit that merely correlates with, but does not cause, downstream loss changes
what can transfer: the causal attribution remains valid and predictive under distribution shifts that break the original confounding correlation
distinguishing observable: after training under conditions where unit A mirrors causally-relevant unit B via a shared upstream input (A itself has no causal path to the loss), a test intervention that decorrelates A from B (breaks the mirroring) leaves the node-perturbation-trained network's performance intact, because A was correctly assigned near-zero credit; a correlation-based learning rule (e.g., plain [X] update on raw activity-loss correlation, matched update magnitude) degrades in performance because it had assigned spurious credit to A
minimal world: A small network where a hidden shared driver feeds both unit A (causally inert, no downstream connection) and unit B (causally connected to the loss), inducing training-time correlation between A and B. Intervention: at test time, decorrelate A from the shared driver while leaving B's causal path intact. Null twin: identical network structure and training data, but weight updates use correlation between raw unit activity and loss (rather than independent-perturbation covariance), matched total number of updates and learning rate.

nearest_priors.name: Node perturbation / REINFORCE-style stochastic gradient estimation (Williams 1992; Fiete & Seung 2006 'gradient learning by stochastic node perturbation')
nearest_priors.explains: Independent noise δ_i injected into each unit per trial; parameter update proportional to Cov(δ_i, ΔL), usually against a running loss baseline; incremental accumulation giving an unbiased estimate of ∂L/∂u_i; a unit with no causal path to the loss gets zero expected update because its injected noise is independent of ΔL.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The explicit framing as causal attribution under confounding, and the robustness test under distribution shift, are interpretive additions, not new machinery.

nearest_priors.name: Randomized controlled intervention / interventional causal-effect estimation (Fisher randomization; Pearl do-calculus; instrumental variables)
nearest_priors.explains: Why randomized exogenous perturbation removes confounding by a shared upstream driver. Why the covariance with the randomized variable identifies the causal effect rather than the observational correlation. Why the estimate stays valid when the confounding correlation is broken.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not by itself supply the incremental parameter-update learning rule inside a network.

nearest_priors.name: Weight perturbation / SPSA / finite-difference gradient estimation, contrasted with Hebbian or reward-modulated Hebbian (three-factor) correlational learning
nearest_priors.explains: Perturb-and-measure gradient estimation as an alternative to backpropagation. The null twin, a correlational rule on raw activity × loss (likely [X] = Hebbian or reward-modulated Hebbian), which assigns spurious credit to a confounded unit.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Weight perturbation perturbs weights rather than node outputs, and SPSA perturbs all parameters simultaneously rather than giving per-unit covariances. Both differ only in parameterisation.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The claimed advantage over correlational rules is the standard reason for using randomized intervention; the distribution-shift robustness follows directly from unbiased causal-gradient estimation. One minor point: the description says unit A has no downstream connection, so its credit is trivially zero under any gradient method. The contrast is meaningful only against correlational rules.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare against exact node perturbation (Fiete & Seung) with a baseline-subtracted loss. Train both on the confounded A/B network, then check two things. First, test whether the learned per-unit updates match E[δ_i ΔL]/σ² ≈ ∂L/∂u_i, including the 1/σ² scaling and the variance that grows with network size. Second, check whether any behaviour departs from this, such as bias under correlated perturbations or credit to A that is nonzero in expectation. If the updates match node perturbation in both mean and variance scaling, the mechanism is node perturbation itself.

High-information zones secrete [X] that diffuses and elevates plasticity in a surrounding neighborhood, producing a spatially structured learning-rate field rather than a uniform one.

what changes: dM/dt = D∇²M - λM + σ·I_local(r,t); dw_ij/dt = η·M(r_ij)·(pre·post - decay)
what persists: the steady-state [X] field pattern and the resulting weight matrix

what can transfer: the [X] spatial template can be transplanted to a sensory task and bias early learning trajectory there

blind_text:
statement: A family of maps between representations at different domains is constrained to commute with a fixed set of structural operations (a naturality square: F(g(x)) = g'(F(x))). This [X] constraint forces learned maps to respect compositional structure rather than fit arbitrary pointwise correlations, guaranteeing generalization to any element reachable by composing the structural maps.
what exists: domains X, Y each with structural operations g in X, g' in Y; candidate map F: X->Y; training pairs (x, F_target(x))
what changes: F's parameters are updated to jointly minimize pointwise prediction error and naturality-violation ||F(g(x)) - g'(F(x))|| averaged over sampled g, x
what persists: once naturality-violation reaches zero it persists under further training as an algebraic identity, not a statistical regularity
what is selected: among F's fitting training data equally, those with lowest naturality-violation
what can reproduce: F can be composed with itself or other natural maps to construct natural transformations by construction
what can learn: the correspondence g<->g' itself can be searched for if not given
what can transfer: F trained on a small orbit of X generalizes exactly to the entire orbit reachable by composing g's, even unseen compositions
distinguishing observable: test error on elements reachable only by unseen compositions of g stays near zero for the naturality-constrained F, while a null twin with identical data/architecture/pointwise loss but no naturality penalty shows error growing with the number of compositional steps away from training examples
minimal world: X = symbol sequences with shift operation g; Y = their numeric encodings with corresponding shift g'. Train F on unshifted and once-shifted examples; test on 2,3,4-times-shifted sequences. The constrained learner adds a naturality loss enforcing F(shift(x))=shift'(F(x)); the null twin uses identical architecture, data, and optimizer with only the pointwise reconstruction loss.

nearest_priors.name: Soft equivariance regularization (equivariance/consistency loss penalizing ||F(g·x) − ρ'(g)F(x)||)
nearest_priors.field: Machine learning (geometric deep learning, symmetry-regularized training)
nearest_priors.explains: The whole setup, renamed. A 'naturality square' is equivariance of F between group or monoid actions on X and Y. The update rule is the standard joint loss of pointwise task error plus an equivariance-violation penalty averaged over sampled g and x. Among F that fit the data equally, it selects the one with least equivariance violation. The predicted observable matches known results: equivariant models extrapolate along the orbit, while unconstrained models degrade with distance from the training orbit. The shift-equivariance toy is the canonical example.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The claimed exactness. A soft penalty only reaches zero on the sampled points. Exact generalization to 2-, 3- and 4-fold shifts needs the identity to hold at those unseen points, which a penalty does not guarantee. Hard-wired architectural equivariance does. The claim that zero violation 'persists as an algebraic identity' under SGD is also not guaranteed for a penalty.

nearest_priors.name: Group-equivariant architectures / weight tying (CNN translation equivariance, G-CNNs, Cohen & Welling; categorical deep learning viewing layers as natural transformations)
nearest_priors.explains: Exact generalization to the entire orbit reachable by composing the g's, proved by induction: F(g^n x) = g'^n F(x). This architectural route is what actually delivers the 'guaranteed' orbit generalization. It also covers closure of natural maps under composition, which is standard vertical composition of natural transformations.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The described mechanism enforces the constraint through a loss rather than through the architecture. It also does not search for the correspondence g↔g'.

nearest_priors.name: Symmetry discovery / learning homomorphisms (Augerino, LieGAN, homomorphism autoencoders, disentangled representations per Higgins et al.)
nearest_priors.explains: The 'what can learn' clause, i.e. searching for the representation g' corresponding to g when it is not given. It also covers learning F as a structure-preserving (equivariant) map from observed transitions.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing additional beyond the first two priors. It is simply the search-over-actions extension.

parsed.unexplained_residual: No new mechanism is left over. The only residual is an overclaim: exact orbit-wide generalization and 'algebraic persistence' are guaranteed only when equivariance is imposed architecturally, or when the penalty is enforced on the whole orbit. A soft penalty on sampled training points does not give that guarantee.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare three models: (a) the soft-penalty learner, with the naturality loss evaluated only on training-orbit points, (b) an architecturally shift-equivariant model (convolutional or weight-tied), and (c) the null twin. Measure naturality violation and test error at n = 2…10 shifts. If (a) matches (b) exactly, with zero error at all n, the claimed guarantee holds. If (a)'s violation and error grow with n, though more slowly than (c), then (a) is ordinary soft equivariance regularization, as expected.

blind_text:
statement: Repeated correlated activity locally up-regulates a slow-decaying [X] trace, distinct from the fast synaptic weights, so the trace's spatial profile becomes a durable record of past correlated-activity sites. If weights are subsequently erased (lesion, reset), [X] synapse growth is biased toward high-trace locations, regenerating the original connectivity pattern from the trace alone.
what exists: fast weight field w(x,t); slow [X] trace T(x,t); regrowth bias rule after a reset event
what changes: dT/dt = gamma*(correlated activity at x) - delta*T (delta << decay rate of w); after w->baseline, synapse growth probability proportional to T(x)
what persists: T persists on a slower timescale than w and survives a w-reset event
what is selected: high-T locations are favored during regrowth (soft selection on synapse placement)
what can reproduce: the original weight pattern can be regenerated from T after a wipe, i.e., the pattern reproduces itself via the trace
what can learn: T is continuously learned from ongoing correlated activity, serving as implicit long-term memory beneath w
what can transfer: T-encoded structure can guide regrowth even under a subsequently different (uninformative) activity regime, still recreating the old [X]
distinguishing observable: after full synaptic ablation, regrowth under /random input that reconverges to the pre-lesion pattern indicates a T-based memory; a null twin with weight reset but no separate slow field (regrowth driven only by current input [X]) shows no correlation between post-regrowth and pre-lesion connectivity
minimal world: A small sheet of neurons develops a specific connectivity pattern under structured correlated input over a long period, building up T. Then all weights are reset to noise and a [X], statistically matched but uncorrelated-in-identity input is given during regrowth. Intervention: regrowth biased by T. Measure correlation between pre-lesion and post-regrowth weight maps. Null twin: identical reset and identical regrowth input, but T is held at zero / uniform (no accumulated trace, matched total [X] budget spent instead as a flat non-informative field) — post-regrowth map should then correlate only with the input, not the original.

statement: Factor entries (core tensor or component vectors) are perturbed by Gaussian noise whose variance is itself set by an entropy-regularization temperature λ, so the mutation rate is a maxent-selected free parameter rather than a fixed hyperparameter, and mutated libraries are then culled by control-cost fitness. This differs from the residual-driven error-correction mechanism by being undirected: mutations are blind to the current residual structure.

what changes: each generation, every component vector receives i.i.d. Gaussian perturbation N(0, σ²(λ)); λ itself is adapted by a slower outer loop maximizing population-average fitness
what persists: the component library's shape (rank, mode structure) persists; only entries mutate
what is selected: post-mutation libraries with lower expected cost survive to the next generation
what can reproduce: surviving libraries are copied (with fresh mutation) into offspring
what can learn: λ (and thus mutation variance) is learned via an outer bandit-style search over a grid, tracking which λ produces the fastest fitness improvement
what can transfer: a learned λ schedule transfers to environments of similar noise/cost scale
distinguishing observable: optimal λ should scale with the curvature of the true cost tensor (steeper cost landscapes select smaller λ); a fixed-σ mutation baseline (no λ adaptation) should show slower convergence specifically in high-curvature environments, without the compensating variance reduction
minimal world: Two environments with matched mean cost but different cost-tensor curvature (one 'sharp' rank-2 basin, one 'broad' rank-2 basin). Run the λ-adaptive mutation-selection loop on both, tracking converged λ and generations-to-fitness-threshold. Null twin: fixed-σ mutation operator with σ chosen as the average of the two adapted λ-implied variances; compare convergence speed on both environments — the null should underperform on the sharp environment and overshoot (excess variance) on the broad one.

blind_text:
statement: An encoder can be tuned along a rate-distortion tradeoff to compress an input into a representation that retains only the information relevant to predicting a target, discarding irrelevant input variation. Sweeping the tradeoff parameter traces a frontier of achievable (compression, relevance) pairs that dominates representations chosen blind to the target.
what exists: input X composed of relevant signal and irrelevant noise; target Y = f(signal); stochastic encoder p(z|x); mutual informations I(X;Z) and I(Z;Y)
what changes: encoder parameters are updated to minimize I(X;Z) - beta*I(Z;Y) for a chosen beta; sweeping beta yields a family of encoders
what persists: at each beta, an optimal (rate, relevant-information) point on the achievable frontier
what is selected: encoders that maximize retained predictive information per bit of compression are favored (Pareto-optimal along the frontier)
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: the encoder learns to discard X-variation that does not predict Y while retaining predictive structure
what can transfer: the compressed representation Z transfers to auxiliary tasks that share the same relevant structure as Y, outperforming Y-blind compressions on those tasks
distinguishing observable: as beta varies, the achieved (I(X;Z), I(Z;Y)) pairs trace the theoretical rate-distortion frontier, dominating a target-blind compression (e.g., [X] on X alone) which achieves strictly lower I(Z;Y) at matched bit-rate
minimal world: synthetic X formed by concatenating a relevant signal s and irrelevant noise n, with Y = f(s); intervention: sweep beta and measure the resulting (I(X;Z), I(Z;Y)) curve; null twin: a [X]-based compression of X to the same bit-rate that ignores Y entirely.

nearest_priors.name: Information Bottleneck method (Tishby, Pereira & Bialek 1999), including its parametric Variational Information Bottleneck form (Alemi et al. 2016)
nearest_priors.explains: Every central element. It covers the stochastic encoder p(z|x) and the Lagrangian min I(X;Z) - beta*I(Z;Y). Sweeping beta traces the information curve, the relevance-compression frontier, which is rate-distortion with KL-to-p(y|x) distortion. The encoder learns to discard Y-irrelevant variation of X. The Pareto-optimal points form the frontier, and parameter updates of an encoder are VIB/deep IB.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Transfer to auxiliary tasks is not guaranteed by IB itself. It holds only when those tasks are functions of the same sufficient statistic of s. Strict dominance over a Y-blind baseline depends on the noise structure of the synthetic world.

nearest_priors.name: Rate-distortion theory (Shannon 1959) and Blahut-Arimoto computation of the R(D) curve
nearest_priors.explains: It gives the frontier traced by a Lagrange multiplier sweep, the tradeoff parameter, and the iterative self-consistent encoder optimization. IB is the special case where distortion is the relevance loss.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard R(D) uses a fixed, target-blind distortion on X. It does not involve a target Y or relevance selection, so on its own it corresponds to the null twin.

nearest_priors.name: Supervised dimensionality reduction versus PCA: sufficient dimension reduction, Gaussian IB / CCA, LDA, supervised PCA
nearest_priors.explains: It explains why a Y-aware projection beats a variance-based, target-blind projection (PCA, the likely [X]) at matched dimension or bit-rate. Gaussian IB (Chechik et al. 2005) reduces to CCA-like eigenvectors along the beta sweep.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not use explicit mutual-information rate accounting or a stochastic encoder, and it only gives a continuous frontier in the Gaussian case.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially nothing. The only addition is the transfer claim, which is a known empirical and theoretical observation about minimal sufficient statistics and IB representations, not a new mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: No mechanistic difference from IB is expected. As a check, compute the exact IB curve with iterative Blahut-Arimoto-style IB on the discrete synthetic (s, n) world and compare it with the trained encoders' (I(X;Z), I(Z;Y)) pairs. Coincidence confirms IB. Also add a variant where the noise n has higher variance than s, to confirm that PCA at matched rate loses I(Z;Y). If transfer holds for tasks depending on s and fails for tasks depending on n, the behaviour is IB sufficiency, not something new.

blind_text:
statement: The hidden code between encoder and decoder is passed through a channel with a fixed hard capacity (e.g., stochastic quantization tuned so mutual information with the input cannot exceed B bits per timestep, regardless of training). The encoder/decoder are trained to maximize task-relevant mutual information subject to this hard cap, forcing nuisance variation out of the code.
what exists: input X; encoder producing hidden code Z; fixed-capacity noisy/quantized channel enforcing I(Z;X) <= B; decoder producing Y_hat from Z; label Y
what changes: encoder/decoder weights are trained to maximize I(Z;Y) given the hard channel cap B, which is an experimentally varied dial (implemented via calibrated quantization levels or injected noise).
what persists: only task-relevant, capacity-surviving features of X remain encoded in Z throughout training; irrelevant variation is structurally excluded because it cannot fit through the fixed channel.
what is selected: among all possible codes Z, training selects the encoding that best preserves I(Z;Y) given the fixed cap on I(Z;X)-supporting capacity.
what can reproduce: None.
what can learn: to discard nuisance variation (background, pose, color) increasingly aggressively as B is lowered, retaining only the minimal sufficient [X] for the task.
what can transfer: the compressed code generalizes better to out-of-distribution nuisance conditions never seen in training, compared to an uncompressed code with equal training-distribution accuracy.
distinguishing observable: as capacity B is swept down, out-of-distribution accuracy under nuisance shifts improves or stays flat even as in-distribution training accuracy may slightly drop — a dissociation not seen in a capacity-unconstrained model tuned via generic regularization to match the same in-distribution accuracy curve.
minimal world: Synthetic images with a task-relevant shape feature and a nuisance feature (color/background) uncorrelated in training but shifted at test. Train (A) an encoder-decoder with an explicit hard-capped stochastic channel at several values of B, and (B) an identical architecture with the same in-distribution accuracy achieved via generic dropout/[X] regularization instead of a hard mutual-information cap (null twin). Compare out-of-distribution nuisance-shift accuracy between A and B at matched in-distribution accuracy.

blind_text:
statement: A candidate mechanism is only accepted as 'causal' if the conditional distribution of effect given cause remains statistically invariant when the environment is resampled with different nuisance/confounder settings; mechanisms whose apparent cause-effect relationship depends on the confounder distribution are rejected regardless of their in-sample predictive accuracy.
what exists: cause variable C; effect variable E; confounder Z varying across environments; set of candidate structural equations E=f(C,Z,noise)
what changes: for each candidate f, compute P(E|C) in multiple environments with different Z-distributions; retain f only if this conditional distribution's parameters vary less than a tolerance threshold across environments
what persists: the true structural mechanism f*(C, noise) (independent of Z) persists and is the only one satisfying the invariance test across all environments
what is selected: among a hypothesis space of candidate f's fit to pooled data, only those passing the cross-environment invariance test are retained as causal explanations
what can reproduce: validated invariant mechanisms can be reused/composed as building blocks in larger causal graphs constructed later
what can learn: a search procedure learns to propose candidate structural forms and prune non-invariant ones via repeated environment resampling
what can transfer: an invariant mechanism validated in training environments correctly predicts E|C in a genuinely environment with unseen Z-distribution, while a spurious (Z-dependent) mechanism does not
distinguishing observable: measure prediction error on a held-out environment with a confounder distribution for invariance-selected mechanisms versus mechanisms selected purely by pooled-data fit; the invariance-selected one should show markedly smaller error increase
minimal world: A synthetic dataset where E = 2*C + 3*Z + noise in training environments but Z's correlation with C is spuriously strong, making a naive regression pick up Z's effect as if it depended on C; intervention creates a test environment where the C-Z correlation is reversed. Null twin: a model selected by minimizing pooled training error across all environments without ever checking cross-environment parameter stability, using the identical pooled dataset size, so total data is matched but the invariance-checking constraint is absent.

blind_text:
statement: A control parameter is continuously adjusted by local feedback that estimates the system's own finite-time Lyapunov exponent, pushing the parameter toward the value where the exponent is near zero (the edge of chaos). No global objective or teacher signal is used; only a local measurement of trajectory divergence drives the parameter update, and this maximizes the range over which distinct inputs remain distinguishable over time.
what exists: state x; tunable parameter r; estimated local Lyapunov exponent lambda_hat
what changes: lambda_hat estimated from two nearby trajectories; r_{t+1} = r_t - alpha * lambda_hat (push toward lambda_hat=0)
what persists: the target value lambda=0 as the fixed point of the parameter's own dynamics
what is selected: parameter values are selected for proximity to [X], not for any external task fitness
what can reproduce: the self-tuning rule itself can be copied to instances with different starting r
what can learn: downstream readouts can learn to exploit the resulting near-critical dynamics for input separation
what can transfer: the tuning rule transfers across any parametrized chaotic map without retuning alpha
distinguishing observable: measure the distribution of r over time: a true self-tuning system converges and stays near the critical r regardless of starting r, while a system with a fixed r (no feedback) shows no such convergence; also compare input-discrimination performance near vs away from the settled r
minimal world: A logistic map x_{t+1}=r*x_t(1-x_t) where r is updated by the local-Lyapunov feedback rule above, starting from several different r0 values (some in periodic regime, some in chaos). Intervention: perturb r away from its settled value and observe whether feedback restores it. Null twin: r updated by a random walk with matched step-size variance but no dependence on lambda_hat, so it does not preferentially settle near the critical boundary.

blind_text:
statement: Two or more oscillatory subsystems each have an autonomous phase that advances at its own natural frequency, but each phase is also nudged by a coupling term proportional to the sine of the phase difference with its neighbor(s). When coupling strength exceeds a critical value (a bifurcation), the oscillators lock into a shared frequency (synchronization); below it, they drift independently. This provides a mechanism for information/timing transfer between otherwise independent dynamical units.
what exists: phase variables theta_1, theta_2 (...theta_n); natural frequencies omega_1, omega_2; coupling strength K
what changes: theta_i,t+1 = theta_i,t + omega_i + (K/n) * sum_j sin(theta_j,t - theta_i,t)
what persists: each oscillator's natural frequency identity persists as a bias even after synchronization (locked but not identical without further coupling)
what is selected: no explicit selection; the coupling strength determines which regime (synchronized vs drifting) the pair occupies
what can reproduce: the coupling rule can be instantiated between any pair of oscillators
what can learn: K can be adapted based on a downstream task's need for synchronized vs independent timing
what can transfer: phase information (and anything encoded in phase, e.g., timing of events) transfers from one oscillator to the coupled other once locked
distinguishing observable: measure the order parameter (phase coherence) as K is swept: true coupling shows a sharp bifurcation from low coherence to near-1 coherence at a critical K_c (Kuramoto-like transition), whereas independent oscillators with only shared noise (no phase-difference-dependent coupling) show coherence increasing only gradually and never reaching a sharp transition
minimal world: Two Kuramoto-style phase oscillators with slightly different omega_1, omega_2, coupling term K*sin(theta_2-theta_1) added symmetrically. Intervention: sweep K from 0 to above K_c=|omega_1-omega_2| and measure phase-locking onset; also test whether a signal injected into oscillator 1's phase appears (with delay) in oscillator 2's phase only when K>K_c. Null twin: replace the sine-coupling term with independent additive noise of matched variance added to both oscillators (common noise, not phase-difference-dependent), which can raise coherence somewhat but shows no sharp K_c-like transition and does not transfer an injected signal from one oscillator's phase to the other's.

statement: Two or more tensors that share a common mode are constrained to use the identical factor matrix for that mode (coupled [X]), creating a pressure toward representations of that mode that are useful simultaneously across all coupled tensors rather than optimized for any single one.
what exists: two or more tensors with at least one mode in common; a shared factor matrix for the common mode; private factor matrices for the non-shared modes of each tensor
what changes: the shared factor matrix is updated using gradients pooled across all tensors that use it; private factors are updated using only their own tensor's error.
what persists: the shared factor matrix persists as a single object referenced by multiple tensors.
what is selected: shared representations that reduce joint error summed across all coupled tensors survive; representations useful for only one tensor but harmful to another are suppressed by the pooled gradient.
what can reproduce: the shared factor matrix can be exported and coupled into a introduced tensor that includes the same mode.
what can learn: a single latent code for the shared mode that is predictive across multiple distinct relations/outcomes.
what can transfer: knowledge learned about the shared mode from a data-rich tensor transfers immediately to a data-poor tensor coupled to it.
distinguishing observable: prediction accuracy on the data-poor tensor for entries involving under-sampled shared-mode-values should be higher under coupling than under independent per-[X], with the advantage disappearing as the data-poor tensor's own sample size grows.
minimal world: Two tensors, A (many samples) and B (few samples), both indexed in part by the same 'agent' mode but otherwise independent modes/outcomes, generated from a true shared agent-factor plus tensor-specific factors. Fit jointly with a shared agent factor matrix versus fitting each tensor independently. Measure B's held-out error. The null twin couples the tensors by sharing a factor matrix for a mode that, in the true generative process, is actually independent between A and B (a mode with matching cardinality and marginal [X] but no real shared structure), so coupling can only hurt or have no effect, isolating whether coupling per se (vs. any shared-parameter regularization) produces the transfer benefit only when true shared structure exists.

what exists: species states x_i; realized edge flux phi_ij(t)=a_ij*h(x_i,x_j); total system throughput Phi_total(t); slowly adapting coefficient a_ij(t)

what is selected: none; this is a law, not a selection process.
what can reproduce: standard population growth continues at the x_i level.
what can learn: coupling coefficients adapt toward flux-homeostatic targets within a lifetime, distinct from cross-generational mutation.
what can transfer: the hysteresis signature in a_ij vs. history should reappear in the same motif embedded in different larger networks.
distinguishing observable: the community Jacobian's dominant eigenvalue at a fixed state x* should differ depending on the flux-history path taken to reach x*, unlike fixed-coefficient models which predict identical Jacobian at identical x.
minimal world: 2-species predator-prey motif with adaptive a_ij(t), driven along two different trajectories converging on the same x* with different flux histories; intervention measures Jacobian eigenvalues at x* on both paths. Null twin: fixed-coefficient model parameterized at the time-averaged a_ij value across both trajectories; the null predicts identical Jacobian at x* regardless of path.

nearest_priors.explains: Per-capita coefficients a_ij become slow state variables that adapt within a lifetime. nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The specific adaptation target. Adaptive foraging climbs a fitness or gain gradient, not a flux set-point. It also has no explicit dependence on system-wide throughput Phi_total.

The claimed 'history dependence of the Jacobian' holds only for the Jacobian restricted to x. The full (x, a) Jacobian is an ordinary state-dependent Jacobian, so the novelty is largely representational. statement: The correctness of an agent's application of a rule to a case is not fixed by any fact intrinsic to the agent (such as an internal representation of the rule's full extension) but is settled by whether the agent's response is brought into line with the corrective responses of a surrounding community of practice. Finite individual training data underdetermines the rule's extension on inputs; community-level correction is what fixes which continuation counts as 'going on in the same way.'
what exists: a population of agents each with an internal rule-approximation g_i(x) trained on finitely many examples that underdetermine the intended rule on inputs; a community interaction protocol where agents observe peers' responses to cases; a corrective feedback signal based on majority/modal response
what changes: On a input x_, agents produce individually divergent responses (since training underdetermines g); a corrective update step nudges divergent agents' functions toward the modal community response.
what persists: Once a stable majority response pattern emerges for a class of inputs, it persists as the binding 'correct' continuation for future agents entering the population.
what is selected: Response patterns matching the emergent community norm are reinforced; idiosyncratic extensions are corrected away, not falsified by any fact about original intention.
what can reproduce: agents enter the population with only finite training data plus exposure to current community interaction, inheriting the extant norm.
what can learn: Each agent's g_i is refined not only from its own training examples but from social correction signals, making learning partly social rather than purely evidential.
what can transfer: The community-fixed rule extension transfers to joining agents purely through interaction, without access to the original training data.
distinguishing observable: Seed two independent sub-populations with training data compatible with multiple distinct rule-extensions; after within-group correction, check whether each group converges to a single, possibly different, stable norm on large inputs, versus a null where correctness is fixed by an internal 'true rule' each agent already individually possesses (correction being inert), predicting identical convergence across isolated groups.
minimal world: Agents trained on finite (x,y) pairs from an arithmetic rule ambiguous beyond the training range (consistent with multiple distinct continuations). Agents in small interacting groups observe peers' answers on large x and adjust toward the group's modal answer over repeated rounds. Null twin: identical training and testing but no inter-agent interaction (independent isolated extrapolation). Measurement: within-group variance and between-group divergence on inputs, distinguishing socially-fixed convergence from chance/prior-driven independent convergence.
