nearest_priors.name: Kripke's Wittgenstein community view of rule-following (Kripkenstein 'quus' skeptical paradox and skeptical solution)
nearest_priors.field: philosophy of language / philosophy of mind
nearest_priors.explains: Finite training underdetermines the rule's extension (plus vs quus beyond the trained range); correctness is fixed by agreement with community correction rather than by any intrinsic fact about the agent; idiosyncratic continuations are corrected, not falsified; new members acquire the norm through participation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It gives no dynamical update rule (modal-response nudging), no convergence model, and no prediction that isolated groups diverge. It is a conceptual account, not a runnable population model.

nearest_priors.name: Naming game / conformist-biased social learning (Steels naming game; Boyd-Richerson conformist transmission; voter/majority-rule opinion dynamics)
nearest_priors.field: language evolution / cultural evolution / statistical physics of social dynamics
nearest_priors.explains: Agents update toward the modal peer response over repeated rounds; within-group consensus emerges as an arbitrary but stable convention; separate groups converge to different conventions (symmetry breaking); newcomers inherit the existing norm; the norm is maintained without access to any original data.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard versions assume discrete labels rather than function extrapolation from ambiguous training data. They also lack the normative framing (what 'correctness' consists in).

nearest_priors.name: Lewis conventions / iterated learning of underdetermined generalizations (Kirby-Griffiths iterated learning; ensemble disagreement under underspecification)
nearest_priors.field: game theory / cognitive science / machine learning
nearest_priors.explains: Multiple equilibria are compatible with the same data, so the selected equilibrium is arbitrary and self-perpetuating. Underspecification means independently trained learners extrapolate differently off-distribution, and transmission to new generations stabilizes one continuation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Iterated learning is vertical transmission and does not by itself include horizontal majority correction. Lewis conventions do not model function learning.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little. The mechanism is Kripke's skeptical solution operationalized as a conformist opinion-dynamics / naming-game model over learned functions under underspecification. The only novel element is applying modal-consensus dynamics to continuous function extrapolation, which is a straightforward combination.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Run the minimal world with a manipulation. Introduce a single agent whose internal extrapolation is deliberately set to a different continuation but who has high social influence, or seed groups with a prior bias. If correction (not intrinsic rules) fixes correctness, the group norm tracks the social manipulation and diverges between groups. If agents carry a shared inductive bias, isolated (no-interaction) groups also converge identically and interaction adds only variance reduction. Also compare within-group variance with and without interaction, holding the prior fixed, to separate conformity dynamics from shared-prior convergence.

blind_text:
statement: A recurrent map f_theta is built to be a contraction (Lipschitz constant L<1), so by the Banach fixed-point theorem iteration converges from any starting point in its basin to a attractor. Storing a pattern means parameterizing theta so a fixed point sits there; recall is iterating f_theta from a noisy cue until convergence. Multiple non-overlapping basins give discrete, content-addressable memories from pure contraction geometry.
what exists: state vector s in R^d; parameterized map family f_theta; enforced contraction constant L<1 (e.g., via spectral normalization)
what changes: theta is updated when storing a pattern; s updates as s_{t+1}=f_theta(s_t) during recall
what persists: the fixed point s*=f_theta(s*) as long as theta is unchanged
what is selected: patterns whose basins remain non-overlapping (sufficient fixed-point separation relative to L) are retained
what can reproduce: a stored attractor's theta can be copied into another contraction-map instance
what can learn: theta is learned via gradient or [X]-like rule to place a fixed point at a target pattern
what can transfer: the same contraction operator transfers to storing pattern sets
distinguishing observable: recall distance-to-attractor decreases geometrically with iteration count matching ||s_t-s*||<=L^t||s_0-s*||; a null twin with L>=1 diverges or wanders instead of showing guaranteed geometric convergence
minimal world: 5 patterns stored as fixed points of contraction maps sharing one recurrent layer; corrupt cues with varying flip-noise and measure convergence trajectories/basin boundaries. The null twin uses identical architecture and stored patterns but weights rescaled so spectral radius exceeds 1, matching parameter count but lacking the contraction guarantee.

nearest_priors.name: Hopfield network / attractor associative memory (Hebbian-stored fixed points, recall by iteration from a noisy cue)
nearest_priors.explains: Patterns are stored as fixed points by setting the weights (the missing [X] is almost certainly 'Hebbian'). Recall iterates the recurrent map from a corrupted cue. There are multiple discrete basins giving content-addressable memory, capacity limits when basins overlap, and flip-noise experiments measuring basin boundaries.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Hopfield multi-attractor dynamics are not globally contractive. They need expansive directions and a spectral radius above 1 between basins. So the claimed global geometric convergence bound L^t from any start does not hold across basins.

nearest_priors.name: Banach contraction mapping / contractive implicit layers (deep equilibrium models and monotone-operator equilibrium networks with spectral normalization)
nearest_priors.explains: The enforced L<1 via spectral normalization, the fixed-point iteration s_{t+1}=f(s_t), the geometric error bound ||s_t-s*|| <= L^t ||s_0-s*||, learning theta by gradient to place the fixed point, and divergence or wandering once L>=1.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Banach's theorem guarantees a unique fixed point on all of R^d. A single global contraction therefore cannot hold 5 separate attractors with non-overlapping basins, so this prior refutes the multi-memory claim rather than explaining it.

nearest_priors.name: Echo state property / fading-memory reservoir (contractive recurrent dynamics)
nearest_priors.explains: A contractive recurrent layer (spectral radius or norm below 1) forgets initial conditions and converges to an input-determined trajectory. It also shows the stable versus chaotic contrast when the weights are rescaled above 1.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Contraction erases the cue. All initial states converge to the same state, which is the opposite of content-addressable recall of multiple stored patterns.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Nothing novel is left over. The central claim is internally contradictory. A map with global Lipschitz constant L<1 on R^d (as enforced by spectral normalization on one shared recurrent layer) has exactly one fixed point, so 'multiple non-overlapping basins from pure contraction geometry' cannot happen. Multiple attractors need the map to be non-contractive somewhere, such as on basin boundaries. Separate maps per pattern would instead need an external selector. The null twin (spectral radius >1) is closer to what a working multi-attractor Hopfield net needs, which inverts the proposed control. A repaired version (locally contractive within each basin, expansive at the boundaries) is just a standard Hopfield or attractor network with local stability analysis.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Store 5 patterns in the single spectrally normalized (L<1) layer and iterate from each clean pattern and from random starts. If Banach holds, every trajectory converges to the same single s*, so recall is not pattern-specific. A Hebbian Hopfield net with the same patterns instead recovers distinct attractors, with trajectories that stall or bifurcate near basin boundaries where the local Jacobian norm exceeds 1. Measuring the local Jacobian norm along recall trajectories distinguishes a true global contraction from locally contractive multi-attractor dynamics.

blind_text:
statement: Each unit locally adjusts its own activation threshold based on a short window of its own recent activity: thresholds rise slightly after firing and decay slowly toward a baseline when quiescent, without any global signal. This local homeostatic pressure, applied independently at every unit, drives the whole network toward a self-tuned point where the average number of units triggered by triggering one other unit is close to 1 (branching ratio ~1), rather than a value set by an experimenter.
what exists: units with continuous activation and adjustable threshold; local recent-firing-rate estimate per unit; network connectivity
what changes: Threshold(t+1) = Threshold(t) + eta*(firing_indicator - target_rate); activation propagates to neighbors if it exceeds threshold.
what persists: Each unit's threshold value persists and slowly drifts, encoding a local estimate of its own operating point.
what is selected: Units whose threshold trajectory stabilizes near the branching-ratio-1 regime persist in an active, cascading dynamic; units that saturate (threshold too high/low) effectively drop out of avalanche participation.
what can reproduce: N/A - no unit-level reproduction, only threshold adaptation.
what can learn: The network as a whole 'learns' its own operating point (branching ratio) via distributed local adaptation, without any global objective function.
what can transfer: The self-tuned branching ratio should transfer across changes in network size and input drive rate, i.e., the system re-equilibrates to near-critical regardless of these nuisance parameters.
distinguishing observable: Measured branching ratio (average number of downstream units triggered per upstream trigger) converges to ~1 across varied drive rates and network sizes; a system with fixed (non-adapting) thresholds instead shows branching ratio that varies systematically and monotonically with drive rate.
minimal world: A small random directed graph (50-200 nodes) with binary/continuous activation, local adaptive thresholds as described, driven by sparse random external pulses; measure branching ratio and avalanche exponents across 5x variation in external drive rate. The null twin uses the same graph and drive but with static thresholds tuned once at initialization to match the mean firing rate of the adaptive version, then held fixed — matching first-order [X] but not reproducing branching-ratio invariance under drive-rate changes.

nearest_priors.name: Self-organized criticality via homeostatic plasticity / adaptive thresholds in neural networks (Levina–Herrmann–Geisel 2007; Zierenberg–Wilting–Priesemann 2018; Magnasco et al. 2009; Rohlf/Bornholdt local-rule criticality)
nearest_priors.explains: Per-unit threshold or excitability adaptation toward a target firing rate, with no global signal, driving the network near branching ratio m≈1. Avalanche statistics as the measured observable. Comparison against a static-parameter null.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The claimed invariance of m under drive-rate changes. In rate-homeostasis models, m ≈ 1 − h/r* (drive h, target rate r*), so m falls as drive rises unless h/r* is small. The claim holds only in the separation-of-timescales limit.

nearest_priors.name: Intrinsic plasticity / adaptive threshold homeostasis (Triesch 2005; SORN, Lazar et al. 2009; spike-frequency adaptation)
nearest_priors.explains: The exact update rule θ ← θ + η(spike − target_rate): a local, persistent threshold encoding each unit's own operating point.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Does not by itself predict the network-level branching ratio of 1 or power-law avalanches. That requires the SOC framing.

nearest_priors.name: Classical self-organized criticality with slow drive and dissipation (Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld sandpile, Olami–Feder–Christensen, Drossel–Schwabl)
nearest_priors.explains: Criticality reached without experimenter tuning, through slow local loading and fast relaxation. Avalanche exponents. Robustness to system size.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It has no explicit per-unit homeostatic threshold with a target rate. Drive-rate dependence (finite drive breaks criticality) is again the caveat.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Nothing mechanistic is unexplained. One predicted behaviour conflicts with the closest prior: robust invariance of m≈1 across a 5x drive variation. Rate-target homeostasis theory predicts m = 1 − h/r*, a systematic decrease with drive. The 'units drop out' selection framing is a relabelling of saturation. The masked [X] is presumably 'statistics' or 'firing rate'.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Sweep external drive h over 5x at fixed target rate r*. Fit the measured m (e.g. with the MR estimator for subsampled data) against 1 − h/r*. If m tracks 1 − h/r*, this is standard rate homeostasis. If m stays pinned at 1 independent of h, some additional term is sensing the branching ratio itself (e.g. an update that uses correlations between upstream and downstream firing), which would go beyond the known prior.

blind_text:
statement: An inhibitor field, sourced by the local magnitude of recent [X] weight change and diffusing faster than the activator (which is sourced by activity), creates Turing-style 'plasticity islands': zones where weight updates are permitted alternate with frozen zones, with island spacing set purely by the diffusion-length ratio, independent of input correlation structure.
what exists: activator field A(r,t) sourced by |Δw|; inhibitor field I(r,t); per-synapse gate g(r)=Heaviside(A(r)-I(r)); weights w
what changes: standard two-species [X] dynamics for A,I; gate g recomputed each step; dw=η·g(r)·[X]_term applies only where gated
what persists: the periodic plasticity-island pattern partitioning the network into freely-learning vs. frozen modules
what is selected: synapses currently inside active islands accumulate learning; islands can drift, giving different modules turns
what can reproduce: the island spatial pattern can seed a network as scaffold
what can learn: only gated subpopulations learn at any time, implementing a spatial learning-rate schedule
what can transfer: frozen (consolidated) modules can be reused unchanged while other islands learn a task
distinguishing observable: island spacing scaling with sqrt(D_inhibitor/λ) and remaining unchanged when input correlation length is varied, versus spacing tracking input correlation length in a correlation-clustering null
minimal world: A 2D neuron sheet is run under two input correlation-length regimes with fixed [X] diffusion parameters, compared against a null where 'islands' are instead assigned directly from local input-correlation magnitude (no [X]), matched in average island size/count at baseline. Doubling input correlation length should leave true-mechanism spacing unchanged but shift null-mechanism spacing.

nearest_priors.name: Turing / Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor reaction–diffusion pattern formation (local activation, lateral inhibition)
nearest_priors.explains: Periodic island pattern arising from a fast-diffusing inhibitor and slower activator; intrinsic wavelength set by diffusion lengths and decay rates rather than by input structure; island drift and pattern persistence; using a pattern as a template or scaffold.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Why the pattern gates synaptic plasticity, the Heaviside gate on Hebbian updates, and the feedback in which the inhibitor is sourced by |Δw| that is itself gated by the pattern.

nearest_priors.name: Masked or gated plasticity for continual learning (PackNet, hard attention to task, XdG context gating, synaptic consolidation / EWC-style freezing, progressive and modular nets)
nearest_priors.explains: Only gated subsets of synapses learn; frozen, consolidated modules are reused unchanged for transfer; a spatial learning-rate schedule; modules taking turns.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Masks that self-organise spatially through reaction–diffusion, and island spacing independent of the input.

nearest_priors.name: Diffusible-messenger or neuromodulator-gated plasticity (NO volume learning, Montague–Gally–Edelman; GasNets; three-factor learning rules)
nearest_priors.explains: Spatially diffusing fields that are sourced by activity and multiply the Hebbian term (dw = η·gate·Hebb); a plasticity window that is local but spread by diffusion.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Two-species Turing instability that yields periodic islands with an intrinsic spacing.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. The novel element is the specific coupling: the inhibitor is sourced by gated weight change, which creates plasticity–pattern feedback that could shift or destabilise the Turing wavelength. The claim that spacing depends 'purely' on sqrt(D_I/λ) is an idealisation. Standard Turing wavelength depends on both diffusivities and on the reaction kinetics. Because the sources depend on activity, input statistics could leak into the source terms.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Hold diffusion parameters fixed and double the input correlation length. Also clamp the gate open so there is no Δw feedback, then compare the island wavelength with the linear Turing prediction computed from the A/I kinetics alone. If the spacing matches the pure reaction–diffusion prediction and ignores both the input correlation length and the plasticity feedback, the mechanism reduces to an uncoupled Turing mask over three-factor learning. If the spacing shifts when the Δw feedback is enabled, the coupling is doing real work.

blind_text:
statement: A representation is built by averaging a function's output over the orbit of a finite group action on the input, producing a feature that is exactly invariant (or covariant) to that group's transformations without requiring any labeled transformed examples. Invariance is enforced structurally by the averaging operator itself, not learned statistically.
what exists: input x; finite group G with action g.x; base function f; symmetrized function f_sym(x) = (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} f(g.x)
what changes: f is optimized for a task while f_sym is used at inference/output; the averaging operator itself is fixed
what persists: the invariance identity f_sym(g.x) = f_sym(x) for all g in G, for any choice of f
what is selected: underlying functions f whose symmetrization retains task-discriminative information are selected by downstream performance
what can reproduce: identical output is reproduced for every member of a group orbit
what can learn: f (the pre-symmetrization function) can be trained by gradient descent on task loss with the averaging held fixed
what can transfer: the invariant representation transfers directly to inputs related by any group element, with zero additional training
distinguishing observable: task accuracy under group transformation of the input for f_sym versus unsymmetrized f (matched parameter count and training data) — f_sym shows zero performance drop under transformation while f degrades
minimal world: World: 2D points with a cyclic group of 8 rotations acting on them; task is to classify shape identity. Intervention: compare f_sym built from an 8-element rotation average against a bare classifier f trained on the same non-augmented data. Null twin: f trained with data augmentation (rotated copies added to training set, matching the amount of 'exposure' to rotations) but without structural averaging at inference; it approximates invariance statistically but shows residual variance across orbit members that f_sym does not.

nearest_priors.name: Reynolds operator / group-averaging symmetrization (Haar-measure projection onto invariants), as used in invariant neural networks and frame averaging (Puny et al. 2022)
nearest_priors.explains: Exact invariance f_sym(g.x)=f_sym(x) for any f; the fixed averaging operator; training f through the average by gradient descent; identical outputs across an orbit; zero-shot transfer to transformed inputs; the covariant variant via averaging g^{-1} f(g.x).
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The idea that downstream performance selects f whose symmetrization stays discriminative is just ordinary task-loss training through the projection.

nearest_priors.name: Test-time augmentation averaging over a transformation group (e.g. rotation TTA, averaging over the 8 dihedral or rotation copies)
nearest_priors.explains: Averaging predictions over a finite set of transformed inputs at inference, and robustness under those transformations.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Training f end-to-end through the average. Standard TTA applies the average only post hoc and does not guarantee a group structure.

nearest_priors.name: Group-equivariant CNNs with invariant pooling over the group (Cohen & Welling 2016); Deep Sets / Janossy pooling for permutation groups
nearest_priors.explains: Invariance enforced by architecture rather than by data; orbit pooling; comparison against data augmentation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: They impose weight sharing inside the layers, whereas here an arbitrary unconstrained f is wrapped in an external average.

parsed.unexplained_residual: None substantive. The augmentation-vs-structural-invariance comparison is a standard ablation in the invariant-networks literature. The 'selection' framing is plain gradient-based training through the Reynolds projection.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: No mechanism distinction is really possible, because the description is the Reynolds operator. To separate it from post-hoc TTA (the second prior), train f with the average included in the loss versus train f bare and average only at test time. Then compare accuracy and orbit variance. Both give exact invariance, but only end-to-end training changes the learned f.

statement: At fixed compute, only a limited total interval width budget can be propagated through the abstract interpreter across all tracked variables; the system must allocate this budget by choosing which variables to represent precisely (narrow, costly) versus abstract away coarsely (wide, cheap). The bottleneck is defined on abstraction width rather than on mutual information, producing an allocation problem absent from either [X] or [X] alone.
what exists: a set of k variables each with an assignable precision level (bits of interval width) drawn from a shared budget B; an abstract interpreter whose propagation cost scales with precision level; a downstream sensitivity query on a designated output
what changes: the allocation of budget B across the k variables' precision levels is updated to minimize the resulting output bound width subject to the fixed total budget
what persists: the total budget B and the [X] structure persist across allocation updates
what is selected: precision allocations that most reduce output bound width per unit budget spent are favored, an implicit marginal-value ranking
what can reproduce: N/A within a single agent; the allocation policy can be copied across agents facing the same [X]
what can learn: the allocation policy learns which variables are output-critical purely from repeated abstract propagation, without ever executing the concrete program
what can transfer: the learned allocation pattern transfers to perturbation budgets on the same [X], requiring only rescaling
distinguishing observable: under a fixed total budget, output bound width achieved by the learned allocation is strictly smaller than that from a uniform allocation across variables, with the gap widening as the [X]'s sensitivity structure becomes more heterogeneous
minimal world: A [X] with one output-critical variable and four irrelevant ones under a shared precision budget; intervention: vary which variable is critical across trials; null twin: a uniform-allocation policy that splits the same total budget equally across all variables regardless of [X], matched in total compute, which achieves a strictly wider output bound.

statement: Deviations of the local order parameter from its critical value are corrected by triggering avalanches whose size scales with the magnitude of the deviation, so that small errors are fixed by small cascades and large errors by large ones. This produces scale-free homeostasis: an error-correcting process whose corrective 'kick' size distribution is itself a power law, unlike either fixed-gain [X] or undirected [X].
what exists: order parameter deviation ε_i = φ_i - φ_c per site; [X] height h_i; a coupling that raises local height proportional to |ε_i| before relaxation
what changes: at each step, h_i += α|ε_i|; sites topple by standard [X] rule; each topple locally resets ε toward zero at the toppled site by a fixed fraction.
what persists: the mapping α from error magnitude to injected height persists as a fixed system parameter (the homeostatic gain).
what is selected: no discrete selection; the joint (error, avalanche-size) [X] are shaped by dynamics toward a scale-free correction regime.
what can reproduce: not applicable.
what can learn: not applicable directly (α is fixed here, distinguishing it from mechanism 5's learnable gain).
what can transfer: the exponent relating error magnitude to corrective avalanche size should be invariant across lattice sizes, testable as a transferable homeostatic scaling law.
distinguishing observable: a power-law relation between error magnitude and the size of the avalanche that corrects it, with corrected-error relaxation time distributed as a power law; null twin uses a fixed-gain (non-avalanching) proportional controller that corrects error directly without cascading, producing exponential relaxation times instead.
minimal world: [X] order-parameter system with error-proportional height injection; null twin replaces the [X]/avalanche correction with a simple linear controller φ_i -= β·ε_i applied directly (same mean correction rate, no cascade); compare relaxation-time distributions and error-vs-correction-size scaling between the two.

nearest_priors.name: Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld sandpile / self-organized criticality with state-dependent driving
nearest_priors.explains: Height variables, the standard toppling rule, power-law avalanche size and duration distributions, and the lattice-size-invariant exponents tested by finite-size scaling. Here the drive is simply made proportional to a local error |ε_i|.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The coupling back to a second field φ, where each topple resets ε by a fixed fraction, and the specific claim that avalanche size scales with the size of the error that triggered it. In BTW, the size of a triggered avalanche is largely independent of how much grain is added.

nearest_priors.name: SOC as an absorbing-state transition tuned by feedback (Dickman–Vespignani–Zapperi; Sornette's 'SOC as feedback control')
nearest_priors.explains: Interpreting avalanching as a feedback mechanism that holds an order parameter at its critical value. The 'homeostasis' reading of criticality, including a fixed feedback gain, is standard in this literature.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The explicit per-site error-to-drive mapping α, and the proposed joint error–correction-size scaling law as the main observable.

nearest_priors.name: Homeostatic plasticity driving networks to criticality (Levina–Herrmann–Geisel dynamic synapses; criticality-homeostasis models) contrasted with a proportional (P) controller
nearest_priors.explains: An error-correcting process that produces scale-free neuronal avalanches. It also explains the null twin: a linear P-controller relaxes deviations exponentially with characteristic time 1/β.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: A fixed sandpile toppling rule serving as the corrective actuator. The neural models adapt couplings rather than injecting height proportional to error.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The claimed monotone power-law mapping from error magnitude to the size of the avalanche that corrects it is not a standard sandpile property. In BTW, the size of a triggered avalanche is mostly decoupled from the drive increment, so this scaling is an asserted prediction rather than something any prior guarantees. Apart from that, the construction combines a sandpile with error-proportional drive and a P-controller null.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Run the coupled sandpile and a plain BTW sandpile that receives the same total drive but is randomized, i.e. decoupled from ε. Then regress avalanche size on the triggering |ε| across several lattice sizes L. If the conditional avalanche-size distribution P(s | |ε|) is independent of |ε| (standard SOC), the claimed homeostatic scaling law is absent. If the conditional mean shows a size-invariant exponent that is absent in the decoupled control, the error-to-cascade coupling is real. The P-controller comparison alone cannot tell these apart, because any SOC system beats a P-controller on relaxation-time tails.

statement: The internal model is maintained as a colimit of local linear patches glued along overlap regions rather than as one global parameter vector. When prediction error on the current patch exceeds threshold, a pushout operation adds a patch glued to existing ones along shared boundary states, expanding the atlas instead of overwriting it. Old patches remain available and are re-activated when their domain recurs.

what persists: previously created patches and their gluing maps, retained indefinitely unless pruned by disuse
what is selected: patches with low residual on their domain and glue maps that keep neighboring triangles commuting are kept; inconsistent patches are merged or discarded
what can reproduce: a sub-atlas (patch plus its glue maps) can be forked to seed a model for a related plant sharing that operating regime
what can learn: per-patch parameters via [X]; atlas [X] via pushout/merge events
what can transfer: shared patches reused across tasks/plants that revisit the same operating regime, without retraining
distinguishing observable: performance retention when returning to an old regime after visiting a one, compared against a single monolithic global adaptive model (plain [X]) which should show catastrophic forgetting of the old regime
minimal world: A 1D piecewise-linear plant that switches among several regimes over time. Intervention: revisit an earlier regime after a long excursion elsewhere. Null twin: identical regime-switch schedule and total adaptation steps, but the patches are forced to share a single global parameter vector (no gluing/pushout), matching switch [X] while removing compositional memory.

statement: A controller's functional identity is defined by its response profile to a fixed set of canonical probe trajectories (its representable [X] Hom(-,C)), not by its raw parameter vector. Two controllers are treated as interchangeable for transfer purposes exactly when their probe-response profiles are naturally isomorphic across probe compositions, even if their underlying parameters differ substantially.

what changes: internal controller parameters adapt online via a standard control law; independently, the probe-response signature is recomputed periodically
what persists: the compressed probe-response signature, carried forward as the controller's portable identity
what is selected: for any transplantation/transfer decision, the controller whose signature is nearest (Yoneda-distance) to a target signature is chosen
what can reproduce: a signature can be reinstantiated in a fresh controller instance by fitting parameters to reproduce the same probe responses
what can learn: the probe-to-response mapping is learned online via active probing
what can transfer: swapping one controller implementation for another with matching signature should preserve task performance despite differing parameters
distinguishing observable: task performance after controller-swap-by-signature versus swap-by-raw-parameter-nearest-neighbor, tested on a plant with parameter redundancy (multiple gain vectors giving identical probe behavior)
minimal world: A linear plant with a redundant/non-identifiable gain parameterization (several distinct gain vectors yield identical closed-loop behavior on the probe set). Null twin: same plant, probes, and redundancy, but controller selection/transfer decisions made by raw parameter-space distance rather than probe-signature distance, matching computational budget while ignoring the representable-[X] structure.

blind_text:
statement: The natural-parameter tensor is constrained to Tucker form Θ = G ×1 A ×2 B ×3 C with a small core G, forcing all cross-mode interaction information through a fixed-size bottleneck before expansion back to full variable dimensions. Varying core size traces a rate-distortion curve between bottleneck capacity and achievable entropy-maximizing fit to target marginals.
what exists: k discrete variables, per-mode factor matrices, a small core tensor G, and a target set of marginal constraints.
what changes: At each core size, core and factor matrices are optimized via dual ascent to maximize entropy subject to constraint violation below tolerance; core size is then swept.
what persists: The mode-to-factor assignment and the requirement that interactions route through G persist across optimization.
what is selected: Core entries and factor columns carrying constraint-relevant information are retained; irrelevant entries are driven toward zero (self-pruning).
what can reproduce: A well-fit small core can be transplanted as an initialization seed for a related problem with the same number of modes.
what can learn: The system learns the minimum core size needed to satisfy a target constraint set, i.e. a compressed representation of required interactions.
what can transfer: A fitted core G can be moved into a variable triple with different alphabets ( A,B,C), testing whether the abstracted interaction pattern is variable-independent.
distinguishing observable: The entropy-vs-core-size curve shows a sharp elbow at a core size equal to the true number of independent hidden interaction channels, plateauing above it; a raw moment-based MaxEnt model has no core-size notion at all and thus no elbow to exhibit.
minimal world: Three 4-state variables generated from a true rank-2 Tucker-core interaction structure. Intervention: fit Tucker-core MaxEnt models with core dimension swept 1..4 to empirical low-order marginals, recording entropy/violation. Null twin: permute which marginal value applies to which variable pair before fitting (same numbers, destroyed structure); this should yield a smooth, elbow-free entropy-vs-core curve.

blind_text:
statement: Early in an agent's lifetime, it uses a coarse, cheap, and highly sound abstract domain (wide boxes) to bound sensitivity, guaranteeing safety but yielding little actionable precision. As experience accumulates, the domain is progressively refined toward tighter representations (octagons, then zonotopes) that trade some soundness margin for completeness, mirroring a maturation curve in precision without ever violating the original coarse bound. Refinement rate is itself governed by how much the tighter domain's predictions have been empirically corroborated.
what exists: an agent with a domain-refinement stage variable d starting at coarsest level; an abstract interpreter parameterized by d; an empirical corroboration counter tracking how often tighter predictions matched concrete outcomes
what changes: d increases (domain refines) when corroboration counter exceeds a threshold; d can also regress if a refined-domain prediction is later violated
what persists: the coarsest-level bound remains valid as an enclosing invariant at every developmental stage, regardless of d
what is selected: refinement stages that survive repeated corroboration checks are retained; those that produce violations are reverted
what can reproduce: the developmental schedule (rate function relating corroboration to refinement) can be inherited by offspring agents
what can learn: the agent learns an environment-specific refinement rate, refining faster in low-variance environments and staying coarse longer in high-variance ones
what can transfer: a refinement schedule tuned in one environment transfers as a useful prior schedule (rate, not endpoint) to a structurally similar environment
distinguishing observable: the trajectory of bound width over developmental time shows a monotone-with-occasional-reversion pattern tied to corroboration events, distinguishable from a fixed-schedule refinement (time-based only) which shows no sensitivity to environmental violation events
minimal world: An agent maturing in an environment whose noise variance changes partway through its lifetime; intervention: switch the environment's variance and observe whether refinement rate slows or reverts; null twin: an agent with a fixed time-based refinement schedule identical in final domain type and total refinement steps, which fails to revert or slow upon the variance switch.

blind_text:
statement: Variation is introduced into a factor matrix not by adding dense elementwise noise but by adding a random rank-one perturbation (an outer product of two random vectors scaled by a small step size), biasing exploration to stay within the low-rank manifold of representable structures rather than exploring the full ambient parameter space.
what exists: a factor matrix for some mode; a rank-one perturbation generator (two random vectors and a step size); a fitness/error signal
what changes: at each mutation event, a fresh rank-one perturbation is drawn and added to the factor matrix; the mutated matrix is evaluated and kept or discarded based on fitness.
what persists: the accepted factor matrix persists as the base for the next round of mutation.
what is selected: mutated factor matrices with equal or better fitness (lower error, or higher task reward) than the pre-mutation matrix are retained.
what can reproduce: an accepted mutated matrix becomes the parent for subsequent mutation rounds, i.e. the lineage of matrices reproduces with variation.
what can learn: a trajectory through factor-matrix space that improves fitness while remaining low-rank-structured relative to its recent history.
what can transfer: the rank-one perturbation operator itself (not any specific factor matrix) transfers unchanged to mutate factor matrices of entirely different tensors.
distinguishing observable: over many generations, the singular value spectrum of the accumulated change in the factor matrix should remain concentrated in a few dominant directions (low effective rank of the total drift) compared to dense-noise mutation, which produces drift with a flatter, higher-rank spectrum; final task fitness reached per number of mutation trials should also differ.
minimal world: Start from a random factor matrix for one mode of a [X] model reconstructing a target low-rank tensor; run a simple hill-climbing loop using rank-one mutations versus dense i.i.d. Gaussian mutations of matched total perturbation norm, tracking fitness-over-generations and the rank of cumulative drift. The null twin uses the identical accept/reject hill-climbing loop and matched perturbation norm but draws mutations as full dense Gaussian noise (not constrained to rank-one), isolating whether the low-rank-biased mutation shape (versus mere presence of variation-selection) accounts for faster convergence or different drift spectra.

blind_text:
statement: Growth cones follow a [X] gradient to a coarse target zone (chemoaffinity) before any activity-dependent refinement occurs; only within that zone does [X] competition refine fine connectivity. The gradient thus causally restricts the set of eligible partners available to [X] competition, independent of what activity [X] later occur.
what exists: growth cone positions p(t); fixed guidance gradient M(x); candidate synapse set S formed within a gradient-tolerance band; weights w(s) for s in S
what changes: p(t) moves deterministically along M; S is fixed once cones halt; dw(s)/dt evolves by normalized [X] competition within S only
what persists: the coarse topographic map (which cone lands in which zone) is fixed early and persists regardless of later activity
what is selected: within S, subsets of synapses win or lose via correlation-based competition (e.g., winner-take-all normalization)
what can reproduce: the coarse map is deterministically reproducible from the gradient alone across different activity-seed runs
what can learn: fine receptive-field structure within each topographic zone is learned from activity
what can transfer: the coarse map transfers across any activity [X] (invariant); fine structure is activity-specific and does not transfer
distinguishing observable: shuffling activity correlation structure while holding the gradient fixed changes only within-zone fine structure and leaves the coarse map intact; a pure-[X] null model without a guidance gradient would show the coarse map itself reorganizing when activity [X] are shuffled
minimal world: A layer of source neurons projects growth cones toward a target sheet under a fixed guidance gradient, forming candidate zone-restricted synapse sets; [X] competition then refines weights within each zone under one of several different activity-correlation regimes. Intervention: gradient present, guiding zone assignment. Measure zone assignment stability and within-zone fine structure across activity regimes. Null twin: same target sheet, same number of candidate synapses and same activity regimes, but zone assignment is instead randomized independent of any gradient (matched [X] of connections per zone) — coarse map should then vary across activity regimes since nothing anchors it.

nearest_priors.name: Two-stage retinotectal map formation: Sperry chemoaffinity (Eph/ephrin gradients) followed by activity-dependent Hebbian refinement (e.g., Whitelaw & Cowan 1981; Goodhill & Xu 2005; Simpson & Goodhill 2011)
nearest_priors.explains: Growth cones follow a molecular gradient to a coarse topographic zone. Correlation-based competition with normalization then refines fine connectivity. The coarse map is invariant to activity manipulations, while fine receptive-field structure depends on activity statistics. This matches the classic experiments where TTX or retinal-wave manipulations leave the coarse map intact but degrade refinement.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The strict gating, where the candidate set S is frozen once cones halt, is a simplification relative to models in which gradient and activity terms act concurrently.

nearest_priors.name: Hebbian competitive map formation with synaptic normalization (von der Malsburg 1973; Willshaw & von der Malsburg 1976; Miller, Keller & Stryker 1989 ocular dominance)
nearest_priors.explains: Correlation-based winner-take-all refinement within a fixed arbor or candidate set. Fine receptive-field structure is learned from activity correlations and is activity-specific.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The gradient-determined coarse map. Without a guidance cue (or 'polarity markers'), the global orientation and placement of the map depend on activity and initial conditions, which is exactly the described null model.

nearest_priors.name: Sperry chemoaffinity hypothesis / Gierer gradient-matching models (Sperry 1963; Gierer 1983; Prestige & Willshaw 1975)
nearest_priors.explains: Deterministic, activity-independent coarse topography that is reproducible from gradients alone.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Within-zone fine structure learned through correlation-based competition, and its dependence on the activity regime.

parsed.unexplained_residual: No new mechanism is present. The strict sequential gating (gradient first, then a frozen candidate set, then competition confined to S) is a stylized version of the standard concurrent gradient-plus-activity models. The null twin is also internally questionable. If randomized zone assignments are fixed and competition is confined within zones, the coarse map would not reorganize with activity either; that prediction holds only if the null allows competition across zones.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Run concurrent-term models (gradient and Hebbian terms acting simultaneously, e.g., Goodhill-type energy models) against the strictly gated version under strong, spatially shifted activity correlations, or with a partially flattened gradient such as an ephrin knockout. The concurrent model predicts that activity can shift coarse zone boundaries when the gradient is weak (duplicated or shifted maps, as in Isl2-EphA3 knock-in). The gated model predicts that zone assignment is fixed by the gradient regardless of activity strength.

blind_text:
statement: When multiple attractors coexist in the same [X], noise-driven fluctuations occasionally push the state across a basin boundary; a bias term that scales with an external fitness signal deepens the basin of the higher-fitness attractor, making escape from it less likely and entry into it more likely. Over repeated stochastic excursions, the population of trajectories increasingly concentrates in the fitness-favored attractor—selection acting on basin geometry rather than on individual trajectories.
what exists: state x with multi-well potential V(x); fitness signal F(basin) attached to each attractor; noise amplitude D
what changes: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta*grad[V(x_t) - kappa*F(basin(x_t))] + sqrt(D)*noise
what persists: the identity and location of each attractor persists; only relative basin depth/width changes with kappa
what is selected: the attractor with higher F is selected for over many stochastic realizations
what can reproduce: an ensemble of independent trajectories can be run in parallel as a population, each subject to the same selection bias
what can learn: kappa (selection strength) can be adapted online based on observed occupancy [X]
what can transfer: the same fitness-biasing rule transfers to any multi-well system with labeled basins
distinguishing observable: track occupancy fraction across the population over time as kappa is turned on vs off; true attractor-selection shows occupancy shifting toward the higher-F basin at a rate dependent on D and kappa, whereas a system with no fitness bias shows occupancy fractions set only by relative basin volume (unresponsive to F)
minimal world: A symmetric double-well potential (equal basin volumes) with noise, run as an ensemble of 1000 independent trajectories; assign F_left=1, F_right=0 and apply the bias term. Intervention: sweep kappa from 0 upward and measure occupancy fraction shift toward the left basin. Null twin: apply the same average leftward drift as a constant additive force (not tied to basin identity or F) matched in mean magnitude, which shifts occupancy similarly at kappa=0 baseline but does not adapt if F values are swapped mid-run, unlike the true mechanism which would reverse selection direction.

nearest_priors.name: Noise-driven attractor selection (Kashiwagi, Yomo et al. 2006 adaptive attractor-selection model: dx/dt = f(x)·A(fitness) + noise)
nearest_priors.explains: Coexisting attractors, noise-driven switching between them, and a fitness or activity signal that stabilises the higher-fitness attractor. Population occupancy concentrates in the fit basin. The mechanism reverses if fitness labels are swapped. It transfers to any multistable system. Selection acts on attractor stability rather than on individual trajectories.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: In the original model, fitness modulates the deterministic drift term multiplicatively and effectively lowers noise; it does not add an explicit additive kappa·F potential tilt. It also has no online adaptation of kappa from ensemble occupancy.

nearest_priors.name: Overdamped Langevin dynamics / Kramers escape in a tilted multi-well potential (Boltzmann-weighted occupancy exp(-(V - kappa F)/D))
nearest_priors.explains: The update rule is exactly Euler-Maruyama discretisation of Langevin dynamics on the effective potential V - kappa·F. The basin-depth change follows directly. Kramers rates set the occupancy shift rate, which depends on D and kappa. Stationary occupancy follows the Boltzmann ratio exp(kappa ΔF / D). With kappa = 0, occupancy is set by basin volume and depth alone.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not interpret the tilt as selection or fitness. It does not adapt kappa from occupancy. It says nothing about F being tied to basin labels: a piecewise-constant F(basin(x)) has zero gradient inside basins, so it must be smoothed to act.

nearest_priors.name: Fitness-landscape selection with mutation (quasispecies / Wright-Fisher on a rugged landscape; Wright's shifting balance; Gibbs sampling with fitness as negative energy)
nearest_priors.explains: An ensemble concentrates on higher-fitness peaks, with noise or mutation enabling peak shifts. Selection strength (inverse temperature) controls the concentration. The same logic transfers to any labelled landscape.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Trajectories here are independent, with no reproduction or differential replication. Selection enters only through potential bias, not through birth and death. The online kappa adaptation is closer to adaptive tempering than to standard evolutionary models.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The only addition is online adaptation of kappa from observed occupancy, a standard adaptive-temperature or adaptive-bias control loop comparable to metadynamics or adaptive simulated tempering. There is also a technical gap: grad of a basin-indexed step function F is zero almost everywhere. The description implicitly requires a smoothed basin-indicator bias, as in umbrella or metadynamics collective-variable bias.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Swap F_left and F_right mid-run while holding the rest fixed. Also compare the stationary occupancy ratio against the Boltzmann prediction exp(kappa·ΔF/D). If occupancy matches the tilted-potential equilibrium and reverses on the swap at the Kramers rate, the system is plain Langevin dynamics with a fitness-labelled bias. If the rule works multiplicatively on drift or noise instead, as in the Kashiwagi model, the rate scales with activity rather than with exp(kappa ΔF / D).

what changes: fitness recomputed each generation as hypotheses mutate; selection probability proportional to fitness.
what persists: the weight vector (w1,w2,w3) across generations unless itself evolved.
what is selected: hypotheses maximizing composite fitness, i.e. broad, simple, cheaply-decidable explanations.
what can reproduce: top-fitness hypotheses crossover/mutate into next generation's pool.
what can learn: the weight vector can be learned via meta-selection to match downstream task success.
what can transfer: the fitness function transfers across domains where verification cost scales similarly with structure.
distinguishing observable: population converges toward hypotheses that are checkably cheap even at slight cost to scope, a bias absent when verification_cost is excluded from fitness (pure [X]/scope selection produces larger, expensive-to-check but equally accurate hypotheses).

Null twin: identical evolutionary loop with fitness = scope+simplicity only (verification run for measurement but excluded from selection); the twin evolves toward expensive-to-check hypotheses at equal accuracy, unlike the true mechanism.

Convergence toward cheaper-to-evaluate individuals when cost is penalised, and toward larger, bloated individuals when it is not. The null twin is a standard ablation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The cost term here is specifically model-checking time/space, not execution runtime. Nothing about formal verification is inherent to plain GP.

nearest_priors.name: Model-checking-based genetic programming / search-based synthesis with a verifier in the loop (e.g., Katz & Peled MCGP; CEGIS-style synthesis)
nearest_priors.explains: A model checker is used inside the evolutionary loop to evaluate candidate automata or programs. The checker supplies fitness-relevant signals such as state-space size and decision cost.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Those systems usually use the checker's verdict (correctness) rather than its time/space as an explicit penalty term. They also have no meta-learned weights.

nearest_priors.name: Speed prior / Levin search (Kt complexity) and Bayesian model selection with complexity-plus-computation penalties; meta-evolution of fitness weights (hyperparameter optimisation)
nearest_priors.explains: Preferring hypotheses that are simple AND cheap to compute or decide, trading slight scope for tractability. Learning the weight vector via outer-loop selection against downstream success.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The population-based evolutionary dynamics. The specific use of verification cost rather than generation or run time.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little. The claim that the fitness landscape is 'emergent only from the triple combination' just means verification cost requires running the checker. That is a measurement dependency, not a new mechanism. Nesting depth driving exponential checking cost is standard state-explosion behaviour.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Replace measured model-checker time/space with a static structural proxy, such as state count times an exponential in nesting depth, used as the penalty term. If convergence and final hypothesis distributions are unchanged, the mechanism reduces to ordinary parsimony-pressured GP. If they differ, the empirical verifier cost carries unique information. An example is hypotheses whose checking cost depends on the checker's heuristics (partial-order reduction, BDD variable ordering) rather than on syntactic size.

blind_text:
statement: Feature-encoding units carry both an amplitude (feature intensity) and a phase (grouping tag); units representing features that belong to the same object become phase-coupled via a Kuramoto-like coupling rule, so that binding information is carried independently of feature content. Downstream readout uses relative phase, not amplitude, to determine which features belong together.
what exists: oscillatory units with amplitude a_i and phase theta_i; a coupling weight matrix K_ij learned from task feedback; a downstream relational readout comparing phase differences
what changes: theta_i <- theta_i + dt * sum_j K_ij * sin(theta_j - theta_i) (phase dynamics); K_ij updated by gradient of a downstream relational task loss (e.g. correct grouping/query answer) with respect to coupling weights.
what persists: The coupling matrix K persists across trials, encoding which feature-pairs tend to co-occur as parts of the same object.
what is selected: Coupling configurations that produce phase clusters matching ground-truth object boundaries are reinforced by task reward/loss.
what can reproduce: Coupling matrices can be copied into a agent's oscillator population as a prior.
what can learn: Which feature co-occurrences imply common object membership, learned purely from downstream binding-task error.
what can transfer: Learned binding rules generalize to objects composed of familiar features in combinations, tested via correct grouping on unseen composite stimuli.
distinguishing observable: Downstream task accuracy should collapse when phases are experimentally scrambled while amplitudes are held fixed, but remain intact when amplitudes are scrambled and phase relations preserved; a rate/amplitude-only encoding model (null) is insensitive to phase scrambling by construction and instead degrades only under amplitude scrambling — the double-dissociation is the key signature.
minimal world: A synthetic scene with multiple objects, each defined by 2-3 co-occurring features (color, shape, position) rendered as unit activations; task is to answer relational queries (e.g. 'what shape is the red object'). Intervention: after training, independently scramble phase-only vs amplitude-only across units and measure query accuracy in each condition. Null twin: a matched-capacity model that encodes objects purely via amplitude/rate patterns with no separate phase variable (binding done implicitly via a learned combined amplitude code), tested under the same two scrambling interventions, which should show no phase-specific vulnerability since it has no phase variable to scramble in the first place (scrambling a dummy phase variable added post-hoc has no effect on its output).

nearest_priors.name: Binding-by-synchrony / temporal correlation hypothesis (von der Malsburg; Singer & Gray), implemented as oscillatory networks such as LEGION (Wang & Terman), and modern complex-valued / Kuramoto binding networks (Complex AutoEncoder, Löwe et al. 2022; Artificial Kuramoto Oscillatory Neurons, Miyato et al. 2024)
nearest_priors.explains: Units carrying amplitude for feature presence and phase for grouping. Kuramoto phase dynamics. Same-object features synchronising. Readout from relative phase. Coupling weights trained end-to-end on a downstream loss (AKOrN, CAE). Predicted sensitivity to phase scrambling.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Explicitly framing the amplitude/phase double-dissociation against a rate-only null as the key test. Copying the coupling matrix into another agent as a prior, which is trivial weight transfer.

nearest_priors.name: Tensor-product / conjunctive-coding binding and slot-based object-centric learning (Smolensky; Slot Attention, Locatello et al. 2020) as the rate-code alternative
nearest_priors.explains: The null twin: binding carried implicitly in amplitude/rate patterns. Compositional generalisation to novel feature combinations. Relational query tasks such as CLEVR-style 'what shape is the red object'.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Phase as a variable separate from content, and the Kuramoto dynamics.

nearest_priors.name: Hebbian / gradient-learned coupling in oscillator associative memories (Hoppensteadt–Izhikevich oscillatory neurocomputers; phase-oscillator Hopfield nets)
nearest_priors.explains: A persistent coupling matrix K that encodes feature co-occurrence statistics and drives synchronisation clusters that act as learned attractors.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Learning K from a downstream task-loss gradient rather than a Hebbian correlation rule. The relational readout.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially nothing mechanistic. The 'reproduction' of copying K as a prior and the selection framing are relabelings of weight initialisation and gradient descent. The double-dissociation protocol is a well-motivated experimental design, not a new mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare against a complex-valued or Kuramoto binding network such as AKOrN or CAE, trained identically. Scramble phase with amplitude fixed, and amplitude with phase fixed. If both show the same double dissociation, the described mechanism is identical to that prior. A difference would only arise if, for example, amplitude modulates effective coupling in one model but not the other; test this by scaling the amplitudes and checking whether the synchronisation clusters change.

blind_text:
statement: A pair of conjugate hyperparameters can serve as a complete, fixed-size memory of an arbitrarily long history of binary observations. Each observation updates the hyperparameters by a simple increment, and the resulting posterior predictive distribution is identical to what would be computed from the full raw history. Hyperparameters from independent observers can be merged additively to pool evidence.
what exists: hyperparameters alpha, beta of a Beta distribution; incoming binary observations x_t
what changes: alpha += x_t, beta += (1-x_t) after each observation
what persists: the pair (alpha,beta), which fully encodes all history relevant to future prediction under the Beta-Bernoulli model
what is selected: not applicable (deterministic update)
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: the implied estimate of the underlying success rate p = alpha/(alpha+beta)
what can transfer: two agents' (alpha,beta) memories can be summed to combine independently gathered evidence without exchanging raw data
distinguishing observable: predictions made from (alpha,beta) alone exactly match predictions made from the full observation history; an agent restricted to a fixed-length sliding window of recent observations diverges from the true posterior as evidence accumulates over long runs
minimal world: a sequence of Bernoulli trials with a fixed true rate; intervention: interleave and then merge the (alpha,beta) memories of two independently updating agents observing disjoint subsequences; null twin: an agent maintaining a fixed-length raw window of the last k observations instead of the sufficient hyperparameters, matched on memory size.

nearest_priors.name: Beta-Bernoulli conjugate Bayesian updating (Bayes/Laplace rule of succession, Raiffa-Schlaifer conjugate priors)
nearest_priors.explains: The (alpha,beta) state, the increment update alpha+=x, beta+=1-x, the posterior predictive alpha/(alpha+beta), and exact equality with full-history computation for exchangeable Bernoulli data.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The additive merge is standard, but the description omits one detail: summing two posteriors counts the shared prior twice, so one copy of the prior pseudo-counts must be subtracted to recover the pooled posterior exactly.

nearest_priors.name: Sufficient statistics / Fisher-Neyman factorization and Pitman-Koopman-Darmois theorem for exponential families
nearest_priors.explains: Why a fixed-size summary (the success and failure counts) losslessly encodes all history relevant to inference. It also explains why the summaries of disjoint samples combine by addition.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not specify the Beta prior or the particular predictive formula; it gives the general principle only.

nearest_priors.name: Mergeable summaries / count-based sketches and distributed sufficient-statistic aggregation (e.g. MapReduce combiners, federated counts)
nearest_priors.explains: The fixed-memory streaming update, merging agents without exchanging raw data, and the comparison against a sliding-window baseline of equal memory.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The Bayesian posterior-predictive interpretation and the role of the prior pseudo-counts.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The only gap is a minor imprecision: a naive additive merge double-counts the prior unless one copy of it is subtracted (or the prior is Haldane Beta(0,0)).
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Merge two agents that each start from a Beta(1,1) prior. Compare the naive sum (alpha1+alpha2, beta1+beta2) against the posterior computed from the pooled raw data. If the described mechanism is exactly conjugate updating, the naive sum will be off by one extra prior pseudo-count per parameter; subtracting the prior makes the two match exactly. Any residual discrepancy after that correction would indicate something beyond standard conjugacy. Also test with a drifting true rate p, where the sliding window should beat the sufficient statistic, confirming that the claimed advantage depends on stationarity.

statement: Transporting a controller from task A to task B along morphism f is permitted in full only if the transported constraint formula on B remains satisfiable; when it does not, the minimal unsat core names exactly the parameter subvector that must be re-adapted online, while all other components stay frozen from the source task.

what changes: [X]-check C_B(f#(K_A)); if [X], extract core, apply adaptive update only to core-indexed indices online; else deploy transported gain unchanged.
what persists: Non-core components remain frozen post-transfer.
what is selected: Which indices receive plasticity is determined purely by core membership.
what can reproduce: Repaired controllers seed further transfers along composite morphisms f∘g.
what can learn: A predictor of which morphism types produce which core patterns, built from repeated transfer events.
what can transfer: The core-pattern signature itself transfers as a prior for future similar morphisms.
distinguishing observable: Parameter-update footprint size and settling time vs. a baseline that always fully re-adapts from scratch after any transfer, with no [X] gating.
minimal world: Chain of pendulum-control tasks generated by successive scaling/rotation morphisms; intervention varies morphism magnitude from small (empty core) to large (near-total retune). Null twin: fixed-fraction re-adaptation heuristic (always retunes top-k parameters) without [X]/core computation; compare footprint to actual necessity.

blind_text:
statement: Two initially nearby continuous latent states, filtered through the same [X]-plus-[X] system, can be driven onto different discrete active supports purely because independent process noise pushes one but not the other across an activation threshold. Once on different supports, their subsequent trajectories decouple even if the underlying continuous states re-converge, producing support-level pattern separation that is history-dependent rather than a direct function of current state alone.
what exists: two parallel latent trajectories x_t^(1), x_t^(2); independent process noise per trajectory; shared dictionary and threshold rule; support histories s_t^(1), s_t^(2)
what changes: each trajectory's support switches independently based on its own noise realization crossing threshold, even under identical mean dynamics
what persists: the shared threshold and dictionary structure
what is selected: divergent support trajectories from initially similar states
what can reproduce: the bifurcation dynamic reappears for any pair of nearby states passing near a threshold boundary
what can learn: the threshold sharpness can be tuned to control the rate of spontaneous support divergence
what can transfer: the same bifurcation law applies regardless of dictionary size once threshold and noise scale are fixed
distinguishing observable: measure support overlap between the two trajectories over time after their continuous states re-converge: a nonzero mechanism shows persistent support divergence (hysteresis) even at convergence, while a memoryless threshold-on-current-state-only rule shows immediate support re-merging
minimal world: Two copies of a single latent variable are run with shared mean dynamics but independent process noise, near a fixed activation threshold. Intervention: measure the fraction of time their supports differ, before, during, and after a period where their continuous state estimates converge. Null twin: a memoryless variant where support is recomputed purely from current state each step with no persistence, matched for the same noise variance, which will show support re-merging immediately upon state convergence.

nearest_priors.name: Hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) thresholding under stochastic forcing: noise-induced switching in a bistable element
nearest_priors.field: Electronics / stochastic dynamics (Kramers escape, stochastic resonance)
nearest_priors.explains: Nearby inputs landing in different discrete states because independent noise pushes one across the switching threshold. Persistence of the chosen state after the inputs re-converge, which is hysteresis inside the dead band. History-dependent output. Threshold sharpness and dead-band width setting the spontaneous divergence rate. The memoryless comparator null showing immediate re-merging.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The multi-atom dictionary support structure. Coupling of the discrete support back into the continuous latent filter, so that trajectories decouple rather than only their read-outs.

nearest_priors.name: Dynamic sparse coding / support-aware recursive estimation (e.g. LCA with internal state versus thresholded output, modified-CS / support-prior Kalman filtering, switching linear dynamical systems)
nearest_priors.explains: Filtering a continuous latent through a dictionary-plus-threshold (sparse) system with active supports. A support prior carried across time, which creates support persistence and makes the active set depend on history. Support switches driving different subsequent dynamics. Independence of the bifurcation law from dictionary size once threshold and noise scale are fixed.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not by itself frame the effect as noise-driven divergence of twin trajectories. Its analysis is usually single-trajectory estimation accuracy, not pairwise support overlap.

nearest_priors.name: Pattern separation via sparse thresholded coding / attractor basins (dentate gyrus expansion recoding, winner-take-all attractors)
nearest_priors.field: Computational neuroscience (hippocampal memory models, Marr / Treves–Rolls)
nearest_priors.explains: Similar inputs mapped to dissimilar discrete sparse codes. Attractor versions add history dependence, since the pattern falls into and stays in a basin. Noise at the basin boundary determines which code wins.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The classic account is state-driven (orthogonalisation of current input), not noise-driven divergence with independent process noise. It does not specify tunable threshold sharpness as the learning knob.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is left over. The mechanism is noise-induced symmetry breaking at a hysteretic threshold, applied to the support of a dynamic sparse coder. One gap: the description never states the persistence rule, i.e. how support memory is implemented (dead band, support prior, or feedback into the dynamics). The claimed hysteresis is asserted rather than derived from the 'threshold rule'. It must come from support-dependent dynamics or a support prior, otherwise it reduces to the memoryless null.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Clamp both continuous latents to exactly the same value, removing all noise, for a period, then release. A pure Schmitt-trigger read-out keeps divergent supports only while the state stays inside the dead band. Supports re-merge once the shared state leaves the band on either side. If the supports instead feed back into the latent dynamics (the switching / support-prior coder), divergence persists and the continuous trajectories re-separate after release. Sweep the dead-band width against the support-feedback gain to attribute persistence to each.

blind_text:
statement: A representation layer is forced through a channel of limited capacity (bits or dimensions) positioned between input and a downstream task signal, with an explicit pressure to minimize mutual information with the input while maximizing mutual information with the task label. This produces representations that discard input variance uncorrelated with any future task, i.e. invariances emerge from compression, not from architecture.
what exists: input variable X; bottleneck variable Z with a capacity budget; task variable Y; an encoder p(Z|X) and decoder p(Y|Z)
what changes: encoder/decoder parameters update to trade off I(Z;X) against I(Z;Y) via a Lagrange-weighted objective
what persists: the minimal sufficient [X] of X for predicting Y, once capacity is low enough to force compression
what is selected: encodings that lie on the information-bottleneck frontier for the current task distribution
what can reproduce: a trained bottleneck encoder can be cloned as an initialization for a downstream task
what can learn: the sufficient-[X] mapping X→Z for whatever Y is currently supervising it
what can transfer: Z transfers to tasks Y' whenever Y' is predictable from the same sufficient [X] as Y, but not otherwise
distinguishing observable: sweeping the capacity budget downward should produce a measurable, monotonic drop in nuisance-variable decodability from Z while task-relevant decodability stays flat until a sharp threshold — a plain [X] (no task term) would show nuisance decodability staying high regardless of capacity
minimal world: Inputs are images of a shape (task-relevant) rendered with random background color (nuisance). Train an encoder-bottleneck-decoder to predict shape identity under a shrinking bottleneck width. Intervention: vary bottleneck width and measure a linear probe's ability to recover background color from Z. Null twin: an [X] with the same bottleneck width trained to reconstruct the full image (no task supervision), matched in width and training data, which should retain background decodability at all widths since it has no pressure to discard task-irrelevant information.

blind_text:
statement: Synaptic changes are gated not by the instantaneous reward but by an eligibility trace that marks recently active synapses, decaying exponentially, so that a delayed scalar reward can retroactively credit the specific state-action pairing that caused it. This solves temporal credit assignment without backpropagation through time or a value function.
what exists: synapses with weight w; an eligibility trace e per synapse; a global delayed scalar reward signal r(t)
what changes: e updates each step by e ← λe + (pre-activity × post-activity); w updates by Δw = η × r(t) × e(t) whenever reward arrives
what persists: weight changes only where trace and reward temporally overlap; traces from irrelevant events decay to near-zero before reward arrives
what is selected: synapses whose activation reliably precedes reward by less than the trace decay window
what can reproduce: not applicable at synapse level; at population level, trace-decay time constants can be duplicated across successful agents
what can learn: state-action associations spanning delays up to roughly 1/(1-λ) timesteps
what can transfer: the learned association transfers to any task sharing the same delay structure between cue and reward
distinguishing observable: varying the cue-to-reward delay should produce a sharp learning-curve degradation once delay exceeds the trace time constant 1/(1-λ), whereas a model using only instantaneous [X] updates (no trace) should fail to learn at any nonzero delay, not show a graded threshold
minimal world: A corridor task: agent presses a lever at position A, reward delivered k steps later at position B, k varied across trials. Intervention: sweep k and measure learning success with the eligibility-trace rule. Null twin: identical network with the trace term removed (Δw = η × r(t) × instantaneous activity only), matched in learning rate and architecture, which should learn only at k=0 and fail catastrophically for any k>0 rather than degrading gradually.

nearest_priors.name: Three-factor reward-modulated Hebbian learning with synaptic eligibility traces (Barto, Sutton & Anderson 1983 Associative Search Element; Izhikevich 2007 'distal reward' R-STDP with dopamine gating)
nearest_priors.explains: Everything central. It has a per-synapse trace that decays exponentially (e ← λe + pre×post), a global scalar reward that gates weight change (Δw = η r e), and no critic or BPTT. It solves distal credit assignment, bridging delays up to about the trace time constant, and learning fails without the trace when reward is delayed.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing substantive. The claim of a 'sharp' degradation at 1/(1-λ) is stronger than the prior predicts: an exponential trace gives a graded, roughly λ^k falloff in effective learning rate. The population-level 'duplication of time constants' is a separate evolutionary add-on, not part of the rule.

nearest_priors.name: TD(λ) / actor-critic with eligibility traces (Sutton 1988; Sutton & Barto)
nearest_priors.explains: It shares the accumulating trace with decay λ, the retroactive credit assignment, and the effective horizon of 1/(1-λ).
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The description explicitly excludes a value function and TD error. Here r(t) is raw reward, not a prediction error, so the method cannot chain credit beyond the trace window through bootstrapping.

nearest_priors.name: REINFORCE / node-perturbation policy gradient with eligibility (Williams 1992), and Klopf's drive-reinforcement / Hedonistic neuron
nearest_priors.explains: It shares scalar global reward multiplied by a locally computed eligibility, giving credit assignment without backprop. It also shares the idea of synapses as eligibility-marked, reward-seeking units.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: REINFORCE's eligibility is the log-policy gradient (correlated with noise), not a pure pre×post Hebbian product. Without a baseline it has variance issues that the description does not address.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Two minor points remain. First, the prediction of a 'sharp' threshold at delay 1/(1-λ) does not follow from an exponential trace, which predicts smooth exponential degradation (modulated by noise and learning rate). Second, the population-level inheritance of trace time constants is an evolutionary-selection overlay not present in the standard rule. Neither is novel machinery.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Sweep delay k finely and fit learning success versus k. The standard eligibility-trace rule predicts a smooth, roughly exponential decline (effective gain ∝ λ^k, rescuable by increasing η or the number of trials). A true sharp step at 1/(1-λ) would indicate an additional nonlinear gate. Also compare against a TD(λ) actor-critic: with an intermediate cue inserted mid-delay, TD chains credit beyond 1/(1-λ), while the described critic-free rule should not.

blind_text:
statement: Fitting under a combined loss of data-fit plus a penalty on parameter magnitude creates a pressure toward biased-but-lower-variance estimates whenever the penalty strength is tuned by held-out risk. This produces a characteristic U-shaped generalization-error curve as a function of penalty strength, with a nonzero optimum whenever noise is present relative to signal.

what changes: gradient descent on L(w)+lambda||w||^2 updates w; lambda is itself adjusted by minimizing validation risk across a grid or via cross-validation
what persists: the shrunk estimate w-hat(lambda) across the optimization
what is selected: the value of lambda minimizing held-out risk
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: the mapping from noise-to-signal ratio to optimal shrinkage intensity
what can transfer: an optimal lambda* learned on one dataset transfers to datasets with matched dimensionality and noise level
distinguishing observable: test error vs lambda traces a U-shape with a nonzero minimum under noise, whereas an unregularized (lambda=0) fit shows monotonically worsening generalization as feature dimension approaches or exceeds sample size
minimal world: linear regression with p close to or exceeding n, where most features are pure noise and a few carry signal; intervention: increase the noise variance of the response; null twin: the same setup fit by unregularized least squares (or pseudo-inverse), matched on training loss but lacking the shrinkage penalty.
