blind_text:
statement: Each postsynaptic unit has a fixed total synaptic weight budget (sum of weight magnitudes capped at a constant), so [X] potentiation of the most correlated inputs necessarily forces [X] that weakens less-correlated inputs, compressing many possible input channels into a sparse subset of retained, highly informative connections.
what exists: a postsynaptic unit with N incoming synapses; a weight vector w under a fixed total-magnitude budget; input lines with varying correlation to a target/output signal
what changes: weights update by a [X] term (dw = eta*x*y) then are renormalized every step so their total magnitude equals the fixed budget
what persists: the final sparse subset of retained high-weight synapses persists as the unit's effective, compressed input channel
what is selected: the subset of inputs most correlated with the unit's own output is selected to retain weight; weaker competitors are driven toward zero by the shared budget constraint
what can reproduce: the surviving sparse weight pattern can be copied onto a fresh unit to reproduce equivalent selective responses to the same inputs
what can learn: the unit learns to compress a high-dimensional correlated input space into a low-dimensional informative subset (implicit feature selection)
what can transfer: the compressed selection pattern transfers to correctly filter input vectors drawn from the same correlational structure, ignoring uninformative dimensions
distinguishing observable: the number of retained non-negligible weights should stay roughly constant even as the number of input lines N grows (compression ratio scales with N), and retained inputs should be exactly the most-correlated ones; an unbudgeted [X] rule without [X] would show weight growth spreading across all correlated inputs rather than concentrating into a fixed-size sparse subset
minimal world: a single unit receiving a growing number of input lines with varying pairwise correlation to a target signal; intervention: increase N while holding the total weight budget fixed; null twin: an identical [X] update rule without the fixed-budget [X] step (weights instead clipped only by a generous ceiling), compared for the sparsity/selectivity difference as N grows.

nearest_priors.name: Hebbian learning with synaptic normalization (von der Malsburg 1973; Miller & MacKay 1994, subtractive/multiplicative constraint)
nearest_priors.explains: The Hebbian term dw = eta*x*y followed by renormalization to a fixed total weight. It explains competition among synapses, where the most correlated inputs win and the rest are driven toward zero, especially under subtractive normalization. It explains sparse, selective receptive fields. It also explains the null-twin contrast: unconstrained Hebbian growth spreads across all correlated inputs and diverges.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Miller & MacKay show that multiplicative L1/L2 renormalization gives graded, PCA-like weights rather than a hard sparse subset. So the claim that the number of retained weights stays roughly constant as N grows depends on the form of the constraint and on the correlation structure; it is not guaranteed. The copy-to-fresh-unit 'reproduction' is trivial, not mechanistic.

nearest_priors.name: Oja's rule / Hebbian PCA with weight normalization
nearest_priors.explains: A Hebbian update with implicit normalization to a fixed norm. The unit extracts the dominant correlational direction, which gives dimensionality reduction and transfer to new inputs with the same covariance structure.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It uses an L2 constraint and converges to the principal eigenvector, which is generally dense rather than sparse. It gives no fixed-size subset selection.

nearest_priors.name: Heterosynaptic plasticity / synaptic scaling with resource-limited competition (including the BCM sliding threshold as a relative)
nearest_priors.explains: A biological account of a fixed synaptic resource budget: potentiation at some synapses forces depression at others. This produces selectivity and pruning, as in ocular dominance development.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: BCM uses a sliding threshold rather than a sum constraint. It gives no precise prediction that the retained count is independent of N.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Only one claim is left unexplained: that the number of retained synapses stays constant as N grows. In the standard analysis, this holds for subtractive normalization with sufficiently spread correlations. It does not hold in general for multiplicative L1 renormalization. The 'reproduce' and 'transfer' clauses are trivial restatements of copying a learned weight vector.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Run the same Hebbian rule under three constraints: subtractive L1 normalization, multiplicative L1 renormalization, and multiplicative L2 (Oja). Sweep N while keeping the budget fixed. Then compare the count of non-negligible weights and the overlap with the top-k correlated inputs. Sparsity with a constant count that appears under all normalization types would go beyond Miller & MacKay's predictions. Sparsity that appears only under the subtractive constraint confirms the known prior.

blind_text:
statement: When the overcomplete dictionary admits multiple sparse supports that reconstruct the current prediction equally well, the support actually adopted is the one whose one-step-ahead predicted covariance (computed by running the [X] prediction step forward under each candidate support) is smallest. what changes: the active support switches to s* whenever a tie in reconstruction is detected and future uncertainty differs across candidates
what persists: the selection criterion (minimize predicted trace covariance)
what is selected: one support among several equally-valid [X]
what can reproduce: the tie-breaking selection rule generalizes to any overcomplete basis with redundant atoms
what can learn: the criterion weighting (e.g. trading current accuracy against future certainty) can be tuned via reward
what can transfer: the rule transfers to dictionaries with different redundancy structure
distinguishing observable: under repeated exposure to ambiguous inputs, this mechanism converges to a consistent preferred support across trials, whereas a mechanism that breaks ties randomly or by atom index shows no consistent preference and higher long-run estimation error
minimal world: A dictionary with two atoms nearly parallel (same reconstruction, different noise coupling) is used to encode a repeating ambiguous stimulus. Intervention: measure which atom is chosen across 100 repeated presentations and track subsequent estimation error. Null twin: identical setup but ties broken by fixed atom-index priority, matched for the same average reconstruction error on first presentation, which shows no consistent future-uncertainty-minimizing preference and accumulates higher long-run error.

nearest_priors.explains: The state tracked by a Kalman filter over an overcomplete dictionary, with a sparse support that can switch over time. It also covers computing the predicted covariance P_pred conditional on a chosen support.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not use future-uncertainty minimisation as the rule for breaking ties among equally accurate supports. Standard KF-CS picks supports by residual or thresholding.

nearest_priors.name: A-optimal sensor/measurement selection in Kalman filtering (trace-of-covariance minimisation, active sensing)
nearest_priors.field: optimal experiment design / control / target tracking
nearest_priors.explains: The selection criterion argmin trace(P_pred), evaluated by running the Riccati/prediction step forward under each candidate configuration. It also explains the information-seeking framing and the tunable accuracy-versus-certainty weighting.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It selects sensors or measurements, not representational supports within an overcomplete code. It has no notion of ties in reconstruction accuracy.

nearest_priors.name: Active inference / expected-information-gain tie-breaking (epistemic value in the free-energy framework)
nearest_priors.explains: Choosing among equally good explanations by minimising expected future uncertainty. It also covers tuning the pragmatic-versus-epistemic weighting by reward.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not specify the sparse-dictionary support structure or the specific trace-of-Kalman-covariance criterion.

A minor flaw: the null twin's fixed atom-index tie-break would also produce a perfectly consistent preference, so 'no consistent preference' is misstated. Only the higher long-run error distinguishes the two.

The described mechanism's choice should follow the lower-trace(P_pred) atom. An index-priority or residual-only KF-CS tracker should keep choosing the same index. Also compare against an A-optimal selector applied without the tie condition: the described mechanism should never sacrifice current reconstruction accuracy unless the criterion weighting is tuned to allow it.

blind_text:
statement: Each unit in a recurrent network is permanently fixed as either strictly excitatory or strictly inhibitory (the sign of all its outgoing weights is fixed at initialization and enforced by projection after every update), while weight magnitudes remain trainable. This constraint reduces the effective solution space available to learning and is expected to bias the network toward different, more structurally interpretable and differently robust solutions than an unconstrained network of equal size.
what exists: recurrent network units each tagged excitatory or inhibitory; trainable weight magnitudes; sign-projection operator applied post-update; task loss
what changes: Standard gradient update on weight magnitudes each step, followed by a projection step that clips any weight whose sign would flip back to zero (or its minimum magnitude with correct sign), enforcing the fixed-sign constraint throughout training.
what persists: The excitatory/inhibitory identity of each unit and the resulting motif [X] (e.g., E/I ratio, characteristic connection patterns) remain fixed while magnitudes adapt.
what is selected: Among all networks that could solve the task, only those reachable within the sign-constrained subspace are found by gradient descent; this constrains which dynamical solutions (e.g., specific oscillatory or attractor structures) are discovered.
what can reproduce: Not applicable directly.
what can learn: The network learns to perform the task using only weight-magnitude adjustments within the fixed sign structure.
what can transfer: Solutions found under the constraint may generalize differently to task variants or perturbations than unconstrained solutions, due to their different inductive bias.
distinguishing observable: For networks trained to matched task performance, targeted lesioning of inhibitory units produces a qualitatively different (typically more catastrophic, less graceful) degradation pattern in the sign-constrained network than in a null twin (identical architecture, same training procedure, but no sign constraint, i.e., weights free to take any sign) lesioned at matched-magnitude units; the resulting weight-magnitude distributions also differ systematically (e.g., heavier tail in constrained case).
minimal world: World: a small recurrent network trained to perform a working-memory or oscillation task via gradient descent, with half its units pre-designated excitatory and half inhibitory. statement: A process or store counts as part of an agent's cognitive system if and only if it is reliably, causally integrated into the agent's real-time control loop in the functional role internal memory/computation would occupy, regardless of whether it is physically internal or external to the organism. what exists: agent body with internal state buffer I of limited capacity; an external artifact/store E readable and writable by the agent during task execution; a task requiring information across time exceeding I's capacity; a coupling channel (read/write latency and reliability) between agent and E
what changes: At each step the agent consults or updates I or E based on availability and cost; task performance depends on the effective combined I∪E loop.
what persists: The functional role assignment (which store carries which information) persists across a task episode and can be reassigned across episodes.
what is selected: Over many trials, coupling strategies (what to offload to E, when to trust it) that improve performance are reinforced.
what can reproduce: Successful coupling policies can be copied to agent instances in a population.
what can learn: The agent learns when to rely on E versus I, and, if E is agent-modifiable, learns to construct and maintain informative external marks.
what can transfer: A coupling policy learned with one external store can transfer to a structurally different external store serving the same functional role.
distinguishing observable: Corrupt E versus corrupt an equal-information-content amount of I and compare performance-degradation curves; the mechanism predicts closely matching degradation across both, whereas a 'mere tool' null (E is uninformative sensor input, not loop-constitutive) predicts no degradation from corrupting it.

After training the agent to use E, run matched-magnitude corruption experiments (randomly flip k internal entries vs. k external entries) and compare failure rates. Null twin: an agent given a static, uninformative landmark it never actually writes to; 'corrupting' this landmark produces no performance change, contrasting with the true loop-integrated E.

statement: A bistable (or multistable) system stores information as which basin it currently occupies; once settled, it remains there after the input that pushed it there is removed. Switching basins requires input to exceed a threshold that itself depends on the currently occupied basin (hysteresis), so the same input can produce different outputs depending on history—memory without any separate storage register.

what changes: x_{t+1} = x_t - eta*grad V(x_t) + I(t) + noise; basin recorded whenever the system settles
what persists: the occupied basin persists across time steps once I(t) returns to zero, as long as I never exceeded the switching threshold
what is selected: no selection; this is a passive storage mechanism
what can reproduce: the potential shape V(x) can be copied to instantiate independent memory cells
what can learn: the well depths/threshold can be reshaped slowly to change memory capacity or retention
what can transfer: the same bistable unit can be reused to store different bits sequentially by re-driving it
distinguishing observable: apply the identical input pulse sequence with different histories and check output depends on prior state (hysteresis loop in input-output plot); a non-memory system (e.g., a monostable relaxation system) would show identical output regardless of history
minimal world: A 1D double-well x'=-dV/dx+I(t)+noise, driven by pulses of varying sign and magnitude. blind_text:
statement: A fast system stores single episodes instantly in rapidly modifiable weights and tags the associated slow-system synapses; during offline replay events, tagged synapses capture consolidation resources only if reactivated, converting transient traces into stable long-term weight changes. Consolidation strength thus depends on tag strength at encoding and cumulative replay, not on one-shot storage into the slow system.

what changes: At encoding, fast weights update instantly and tags are set proportional to salience; during replay, buffered sequences are reactivated and tagged slow synapses capture resources, incrementally strengthening slow weights; tags decay over time if not captured.
what persists: Consolidated slow-system weights that remain after the fast buffer is erased or overwritten.
what is selected: Episodes with stronger tags (higher salience/reward) or more frequent replay are preferentially consolidated over weakly tagged, rarely replayed ones.
what can reproduce: Buffered sequences are reinstated during replay, generating repeated training signal for the slow system.
what can learn: The slow system extracts generalized/schema-level structure across many replayed episodes, beyond any single episode.
what can transfer: Consolidated generalized representations support performance on related tasks without access to the original episodic buffer.
distinguishing observable: Recall becomes robust to buffer deletion only gradually, with robustness scaling with replay count/tag strength and disrupted by blocking the capture step, unlike direct one-shot storage into the slow system, which would be immediately buffer-independent regardless of replay count.
minimal world: A small world where a fast weight matrix stores a trajectory instantly on first exposure and a slow weight matrix updates only during discrete replay events sampled from the fast buffer, with tag-decay dynamics. Intervention: delete the fast buffer at varying delays post-learning and measure slow-system recall accuracy as a function of delay/replay count. Null twin: a model where slow weights are updated identically and instantly at encoding (no replay/tag step), matched for final asymptotic weight magnitude but showing no delay-dependence or replay-count sensitivity in buffer-lesion tests.

blind_text:
statement: When one agent adopts another's reported belief, the received confidence is multiplied by a per-source discount factor that is itself updated over time based on the retrospective accuracy of that source's past reports. what exists: multiple agents with belief stores and confidences; a communication channel between agent pairs; a per-pair discount factor; periodic ground-truth reveals

what persists: Discount factors persist as relational state between agent pairs, encoding accumulated social trust across rounds.
what is selected: Communication influence is effectively selected toward reliable informants as unreliable sources accrue low discount factors.
what can reproduce: Agents can be added or removed from the population; agents start with a default discount and calibrate through interaction.
what can learn: Discount factors and, optionally, which agents to query at all (active source selection).
what can transfer: A calibrated discount toward a source can transfer across content domains if tested for domain-general versus domain-specific reliability.
distinguishing observable: After introducing a confidently-wrong agent into the network, population accuracy over subsequent rounds recovers toward truth-tracking as that agent's discount decays, versus a fixed-discount population whose accuracy is pulled toward the confident liar and stays degraded.

what can reproduce: not applicable at the synapse level; across an agent population, the parameters γ and η could be varied and selected by task fitness

what can transfer: learned value estimates generalize to states sharing predictive features with previously experienced states
distinguishing observable: track the trial-by-trial location of the peak δ response across training and test reward omission: the mechanism predicts the response migrates backward to the earliest predictive cue and produces a below-baseline (negative) response when an expected reward is omitted; a reward-only (non-bootstrapping) model predicts the response stays locked to reward delivery and shows no anticipatory migration or omission response.

The mechanism model uses full [X] bootstrapping (δ includes V(s_{t+1})); the null twin uses a reward-only delta (δ = r_t − baseline, no bootstrapped future value term), matched in overall reward [X] and cue timing. The diagnostic is whether the peak response migrates to the predictive cue and produces omission-triggered dips, which occurs only in the [X] model.

nearest_priors.explains: Error-driven, prediction-error-proportional learning. This is the null twin (delta = r - baseline).
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Within-trial backward migration of the response to earlier cues, second-order conditioning via bootstrapping, and the omission dip timed to the expected reward.

parsed.discriminating_intervention: Record trial-by-trial phasic responses during cue-cue-reward conditioning. Then run: (a) reward omission, (b) a shift in reward timing, and (c) a blocking/second-order conditioning test. TD(lambda) predicts all of the following: gradual backward migration, whose intermediate-time propagation depends on lambda; a dip locked to the expected reward time; and responses to earlier cues without direct reward pairing. A Rescorla-Wagner-type model shows none of these timing effects. To separate the described mechanism from textbook TD, vary lambda by manipulating the eligibility-trace decay: an agent whose behaviour deviates from TD(lambda) trajectories would indicate a novel mechanism.

blind_text:
statement: The parameter update combines two distinct error signals simultaneously: the closed-loop tracking error (as used in reference-model adaptation) and a separate prediction error generated by a parallel serial-parallel predictor model driven by the same input stream, both weighted and summed into a single composite update. This combination accelerates parameter convergence beyond what either error alone achieves, without requiring deliberate probing.
what exists: tracking error e; prediction error epsilon (from a parallel predictor sharing theta); parameter theta; weighting constants gamma1, gamma2
what changes: theta_dot = gamma1*e*phi1 + gamma2*epsilon*phi2, where phi1, phi2 are the regressors from the closed-loop path and predictor path respectively
what persists: the parallel predictor model structure, running continuously alongside the main control loop
what is selected: not applicable
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: true plant parameters, faster and under weaker excitation requirements than tracking-error-only adaptation
what can transfer: the composite update law transfers to any plant parametrization admitting both a reference-model tracking formulation and a serial-parallel predictor formulation
distinguishing observable: under weak excitation, convergence rate of theta to theta_star is strictly faster with composite adaptation than with tracking-error-only adaptation (mechanism 1) on identical input realizations; additionally the prediction error epsilon decays to zero even while e is still nonzero, since epsilon reflects instantaneous parameter mismatch rather than integrated closed-loop dynamics -- the relative decay timing of e versus epsilon distinguishes composite from single-error adaptation
minimal world: Identical plant/reference-model setup as mechanism 1, plus an auxiliary predictor y_hat = theta*phi(u) trained on the same input stream, contributing epsilon = y - y_hat into the update alongside e. Null twin: mechanism 1 alone (gamma2 = 0, tracking-error-only) run on the identical input realization. Compare time for theta to enter an epsilon-ball around theta_star under a weakly-exciting reference; composite adaptation should converge measurably faster than the null twin.

nearest_priors.name: Composite adaptive control (Slotine & Li, 1989), combining a tracking-error-driven and a prediction-error-driven parameter update
nearest_priors.explains: Covers nearly everything. The update sums a tracking-error term and a prediction-error term (theta_dot = -P[phi1*e + phi2*epsilon]). The prediction error comes from a filtered serial-parallel estimation model that runs alongside the control loop. It explains the faster, smoother convergence than tracking-error-only (MRAC-style) adaptation without extra probing signals, and the fact that epsilon reflects parameter mismatch directly while e passes through closed-loop dynamics. It also explains transfer to any linearly parametrised plant that admits both a tracking formulation and a predictor formulation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not guarantee convergence to theta_star under genuinely weak excitation. Parameter convergence still needs some persistent excitation, so 'weaker excitation requirements' and 'strictly faster on every realization' are stronger than the standard results support.

nearest_priors.name: Combined direct/indirect adaptive control (Duarte & Narendra, 1989)
nearest_priors.explains: Uses both the output (tracking) error of direct MRAC and the identification error of an indirect series-parallel identifier to update shared controller and plant parameters simultaneously. This gives better transients and faster convergence than either scheme alone.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Its parametrisation couples controller and identifier parameters through a matching condition rather than sharing a single theta in a simple weighted sum. Otherwise it is essentially the same mechanism.

nearest_priors.name: Concurrent learning / data-driven adaptive control (Chowdhary & Johnson), and gradient series-parallel identification (Lyapunov/MIT-rule identifiers)
nearest_priors.explains: Adds a prediction-error term alongside the tracking error to relax persistent-excitation requirements. This matches the 'weaker excitation' claim.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It uses recorded data stacks rather than a continuously running parallel predictor on the current input stream.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The only gaps are the stronger claims of strictly faster convergence under weak excitation on every input realization, and epsilon decaying while e is nonzero. These are empirical tendencies of composite adaptation rather than guaranteed properties, and standard composite adaptation does not remove the excitation requirement for parameter convergence.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Run the scheme and a textbook Slotine-Li composite adaptive controller (same plant, filtered prediction error, same gains) on identical weakly-exciting reference realizations. Compare the parameter trajectories and the relative decay timing of e and epsilon. If they coincide, the mechanism is composite adaptation. Then remove excitation entirely (constant reference): if theta still converges to theta_star, the mechanism exceeds composite adaptation (e.g. uses stored data as in concurrent learning); if not, it matches the prior.

blind_text:
statement: The environment provides two resource types whose spatial abundance is anti-correlated, and intake follows diminishing returns for any single trait allocation. This rule alone, without any social interaction, creates selective pressure for organisms to specialize their intake-trait allocation to local resource ratios rather than remaining generalists.
what exists: 2D grid; resource fields [X](x,y), [X](x,y) anti-correlated in space; agent traits (e1,e2) with e1+e2 fixed budget; agent position and energy
what changes: energy(t+1) = energy(t) + sqrt(e1*[X](x,y)) + sqrt(e2*[X](x,y)); agents move toward higher local energy gradient; traits mutate slightly at reproduction.
what persists: the anti-correlated spatial resource structure across generations.
what is selected: trait pairs (e1,e2) whose match to local resource ratio maximizes intake are favored in reproduction.
what can reproduce: agents reproduce proportional to accumulated energy, offspring inherit (e1,e2) with mutation.
what can learn: individuals can additionally learn a movement policy that follows the local resource gradient within a lifetime.
what can transfer: specialization pattern (bimodal trait distribution) transfers to landscapes sharing the same anti-correlation structure, even with different absolute abundances.
distinguishing observable: the population trait distribution becomes bimodal (specialists) under spatial segregation of resources but stays unimodal (generalist) when the identical total resources are mixed uniformly at every location — same total resource budget, different spatial layout.
minimal world: A grid where two resources are placed either in separated patches (test) or uniformly interleaved at every cell (null twin), with total resource mass held equal between conditions. Agents with mutable (e1,e2) forage, gain energy via diminishing-returns intake, and reproduce. Measure trait-distribution modality after many generations in both layouts.

nearest_priors.name: Levins' fitness-set theory of niche breadth (coarse- vs fine-grained environments)
nearest_priors.explains: The core prediction. Fixed allocation (e1+e2 constant) is a trade-off, and sqrt intake is a concave payoff. In a fine-grained, uniformly mixed environment every agent sees the same resource ratio, so the optimum is a single interior generalist (e1 = R1/(R1+R2)) and the trait distribution stays unimodal. In a coarse-grained, segregated environment the local optima sit at opposite extremes, favouring specialists and a bimodal distribution. It also covers the 'same total resources, different grain' null twin.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Explicit agent movement, the within-lifetime learned gradient-following policy, and energy-proportional reproduction dynamics on a grid.

nearest_priors.name: Levene multiple-niche polymorphism / spatially heterogeneous (disruptive) selection with habitat choice
nearest_priors.explains: How divergent selection in distinct patches, plus limited mixing, maintains a stable polymorphism (bimodality). Directed movement toward the matching patch acts as habitat choice, which strengthens local adaptation and keeps the two modes separate.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The specific square-root allocation trade-off and transfer across landscapes with different absolute abundances. The latter follows from optima depending only on resource ratios.

nearest_priors.name: Baldwin effect / learning-evolution interaction in artificial-life foragers (e.g., Ackley–Littman)
nearest_priors.explains: Individuals learning a gradient-following movement policy within a lifetime, which lets genotypes reach matching patches and shapes selection on the inherited traits.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The bimodal-versus-unimodal outcome itself, which comes from the trade-off geometry and environmental grain.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. The one subtlety is that the claim 'this rule alone creates specialization' needs spatial segregation strong enough relative to movement and dispersal. If agents traverse both patch types within a lifetime, the environment becomes effectively fine-grained and generalists win again. This dependence on dispersal scale is itself standard Levins/Levene migration–selection theory.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Keep the segregated layout but vary patch size relative to agent lifetime movement range (and offspring dispersal distance). Levins/Levene predicts a threshold: bimodality should collapse to unimodality once agents integrate over both patch types, even though the layout is still 'segregated'. Separately, disable the learned movement policy (random walk). Habitat-choice theory predicts weaker bimodality; if bimodality is unchanged, movement plays no role beyond grain.

statement: A representation is compressed by retaining only those latent dimensions whose perturbation produces an output change above a fixed threshold (high-sensitivity directions), while dimensions whose perturbation leaves the output nearly unchanged are marginalized out, yielding a minimal representation sufficient for predicting intervention outcomes rather than for reconstructing raw input.
what exists: high-dimensional latent z; decoder producing output y=g(z); per-dimension sensitivity score computed by perturbing each z_i and measuring output change; retained subset R of dimensions
what changes: periodically recompute per-dimension sensitivity scores; update R to keep only dimensions above threshold tau; retrain/re-fit decoder using only R, discarding the rest
what persists: the retained dimension index set R persists between recompression cycles unless re-triggered by distribution shift
what is selected: among candidate thresholds tau, the one yielding smallest R that still predicts held-out intervention outcomes within tolerance is selected
what can reproduce: the compressed representation and its retained-dimension set can be copied into a downstream model trained on a related task
what can learn: the threshold tau and the encoder mapping input to z can be jointly learned via gradient descent using the sensitivity-based masking as a differentiable relaxation
what can transfer: the compressed sensitivity-selected representation transfers to a task that depends on the same underlying causal generative factors, while discarding nuisance factors that never mattered
distinguishing observable: compare downstream prediction accuracy on interventional (do-perturbed) test data between the sensitivity-thresholded representation and a same-size representation chosen by highest reconstruction variance (standard [X]-like compression); the sensitivity-thresholded one should predict intervention outcomes better at matched representation size
minimal world: A generative world with 10 latent factors, 3 of which causally drive a downstream output and 7 of which are nuisance factors with large marginal variance but no causal effect; intervention directly manipulates the output-relevant latents at test time. Null twin: a compression scheme retaining the 3 highest-variance latent dimensions (standard variance-based bottleneck) matched in compressed dimensionality to the sensitivity-based method, but which — because nuisance factors have higher variance — ends up keeping non-causal dimensions instead.

statement: Before any concrete perturbation trial is run, an abstract interpreter propagates a declared misspecification set (parameter intervals) through the causal [X]'s transfer functions to compute a sound over-approximate output range. Any input variable whose removal from the perturbation set cannot shrink this abstract output range is provably causally inert under the stated misspecification, and is screened out before sampling begins. This differs from correlation-based screening because it certifies irrelevance rather than merely failing to detect relevance.
what exists: arithmetic [X] nodes [X]..Xn with declared parameter interval ranges; abstract interval/zonotope semantics for each node's transfer function; a concrete simulator with fixed true parameters; a misspecification set (box) over parameters
what changes: each round, the abstract interpreter re-propagates the current misspecification box through the [X]; the screening set of 'possibly relevant' inputs is updated by comparing abstract output width with and without each input's perturbation channel active
what persists: the [X] [X] and the current misspecification box persist across screening rounds until explicitly refined
what is selected: downstream costly concrete sensitivity trials are allocated only to inputs that survive the abstract screen
what can reproduce: the screening procedure itself can be applied unchanged to structurally isomorphic [X]
what can learn: the misspecification box can be tightened online as concrete trials reduce parameter uncertainty
what can transfer: the certified-irrelevant input set transfers to any [X] sharing the same subgraph structure, independent of parameter values
distinguishing observable: zero false-negative rate on causally relevant inputs even under adversarial nonlinear cancellation, compared to a correlation-based screen run on the same finite sample which exhibits nonzero false negatives
minimal world: A [X] with 5 nodes where [X] affects Y only through a term that exactly cancels with [X] at the sampled parameter values but not across the whole misspecification box; intervention: shrink or widen the misspecification box and observe screening set changes; null twin: a screen that thresholds empirical correlation on the same finite sample set, matched in sample count and noise [X], which incorrectly drops [X] because cancellation holds at the sampled point but not across the certified range.

nearest_priors.field: Formal verification / static analysis / verified numerics
nearest_priors.explains: Propagating a parameter box through node transfer functions with interval or zonotope semantics to get a sound over-approximate output range. Comparing output widths with and without an input's perturbation channel, as in interval-based influence bounding. Refining the box, and certification rather than detection.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The staged allocation of costly concrete trials, and the causal-graph framing of relevance. It also does not justify the 'no shrink implies inert' inference, since over-approximation can hide real influence through wrapping or dependency effects.

nearest_priors.name: Factor screening before global sensitivity analysis (Morris elementary effects, sequential bifurcation, group screening, then Sobol trials on the survivors)
nearest_priors.explains: A cheap screen that removes inputs before expensive sensitivity trials are allocated to the survivors. Online tightening of parameter uncertainty as trials accumulate. The contrast with correlation-based screens, which miss inputs with cancelling or nonmonotone effects.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Soundness guarantees. Classical screens are sample-based and can produce false negatives.

nearest_priors.name: Structural causal model irrelevance (d-separation / graphical ancestry and do-calculus identification of null effects)
nearest_priors.explains: Certifying causal inertness from graph structure alone. Transfer of the irrelevant set to any model with the same subgraph, independent of parameter values. The distinction between structural (faithfulness-violating) cancellation and true absence of effect.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Parameter-box-dependent relevance, where cancellation holds at some points of the box but not others. Also the numeric width comparison.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Nothing substantive is new: the mechanism is abstract-interpretation-based certified screening feeding a sensitivity-analysis budget. There are two internal tensions. (1) Over-approximate width non-shrinkage does not soundly certify zero influence. Sound irrelevance needs an upper bound on influence that equals zero, for example via symbolic or affine forms showing zero coefficients, not a width comparison. (2) The claim that the irrelevant set transfers 'independent of parameter values' contradicts the minimal world, where relevance depends on the box.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Build a model where input X has a genuine nonzero effect that interval arithmetic masks through the dependency problem, such as f = X*A - X*A' with correlated A and A' that are treated independently. Check whether the width-comparison screen wrongly certifies X as inert. Then compare against an affine/zonotope variant that tracks symbolic coefficients of X. Separately, vary the box on a fixed graph to test whether the certified set really is parameter-independent, as the prior claims, or box-dependent, as the minimal world implies.

statement: Genomes evolve under a mutation operator combining point mutation with occasional segmental duplication, where duplicated segments can subsequently diverge independently of the original. what can reproduce: Standard sexual/asexual reproduction with the mutation operator applied each generation.
what can learn: The population's evolvability increases over generations (facilitated variation): a population-level capacity to respond faster to future environmental shifts.
what can transfer: Duplicated, diverged modules can be recombined or co-opted (exapted) to build phenotypic functions when needed.
distinguishing observable: Following a sudden environmental shift that requires a function, populations with duplication-enabled mutation show a shorter and less variable time-to-adaptation than a null twin; measured via distribution of generations-to-fitness-recovery.

Intervention: run [X] with the duplication+point-mutation operator and record time-to-recovery of peak fitness after the shift. Null twin: identical genome length distribution and total mutation-rate variance, but using point mutation only (mutation rate rescaled so total per-generation phenotypic variance matches the duplication condition, no duplication events); compare post-shift adaptation-time distributions between the two.

statement: Before each true observation arrives, the filter generates a synthetic expected observation by applying a known transform to its own prior prediction, and compares this to the actually-transformed incoming observation; the mismatch is used to correct the [X] and gain preemptively, prior to and in addition to the standard update step. what changes: a'_t = a_t|t-1 - eta*grad(||T(y_hat)-T(y_actual)||^2) is computed as an anticipatory correction, then the standard [X] update is applied on top of a'_t.
what persists: the anticipatory-correction step recurs identically at every cycle regardless of whether a violation is detected (though its magnitude may be zero).
what is selected: correction step sizes eta that reduce two-stage residual (anticipatory + posterior) more than single-stage residual are reinforced.
what can reproduce: none.
what can learn: the correction step size eta and which transform(s) are worth checking anticipatorily.
what can transfer: an anticipatory-correction policy tuned for one transform schedule should reduce transient error spikes when a structurally similar (but not identical) schedule is introduced.
distinguishing observable: measure the peak transient error immediately after an abrupt regime change; the two-stage anticipatory-correction filter should show a smaller peak than a filter that only performs the standard posterior update, at matched total computation.
minimal world: World: state space with a scheduled, known transform (e.g., periodic input scaling) applied to observations. Intervention: compare filters with and without the anticipatory pre-update correction step, both receiving identical transform schedules. Null twin: a filter that performs an extra update computation of equal cost (e.g., a second redundant posterior update using the same y_t twice) instead of the anticipatory transform-based correction, matching compute but not using transform-derived information.

The mechanism is a Kalman filter plus a test-time-training-style auxiliary gradient step with a transform-consistency loss, combined with meta-learned step sizes. There is also a tension in the description. The step is called 'anticipatory' (it happens before y_t arrives), yet it uses T(y_actual). If T is known and invertible, the transform-space residual carries no information beyond y_t. In that case the step reduces to an extra, reweighted update on the same observation, which is nearly identical to the null twin. Any novelty depends on T being non-invertible or on T being applied before y_t arrives (for example, via the known schedule), and the description leaves this unspecified.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Use an invertible, full-rank T and compare three conditions under abrupt regime changes: (1) the anticipatory filter, (2) an iterated Kalman filter doing a second gradient or Gauss-Newton step on y_t with eta tuned equally, and (3) a Kalman filter with the known schedule injected as a feedforward input. If (1) does not beat both (2) and (3) in peak transient error, then the effect is just iterated updating or known-input feedforward. Also test with a non-invertible T (a projection), where the transform-space residual could weight directions differently.

statement: A locally driven, locally relaxing lattice ([X]-like) spontaneously organizes into a critical state where perturbations propagate as avalanches with no characteristic scale. This scale-free branching allows a single small input to trigger effects ranging from local to system-wide, providing a substrate for long-range coordination without any global controller tuning a parameter.
what exists: 2D grid of cells with integer stress value; slow random external drive adding units to random cells; fixed toppling threshold; toppling rule redistributing stress to 4 neighbors
what changes: Each step: add drive; any cell above threshold topples, distributing stress to neighbors, which may cause cascading topples (an avalanche) until all cells are subcritical.
what persists: The statistical stationary distribution of avalanche sizes/durations ([X]), independent of initial condition.
what is selected: No agents are selected; the process selects a stationary attractor distribution of configurations, not entities.
what can reproduce: None directly; the lattice state is not a reproducing unit.
what can learn: A readout layer sampling lattice states can learn to exploit the long-range temporal/spatial correlations generated by avalanches (reservoir-style learning).
what can transfer: The avalanche correlation structure generalizes across different readout tasks fed from the same lattice, since it is task-independent.
distinguishing observable: Avalanche size distribution follows a power law with a stable exponent across drive rates; a null twin using the same threshold rule but with toppled stress randomly reassigned (breaking the branching neighbor structure) instead of redistributed to neighbors produces an exponential (not power-law) size distribution.
minimal world: World: an NxN grid with integer stress, slow uniform random drive, threshold-4 toppling to von Neumann neighbors, periodic boundary. Intervention: measure avalanche size distribution over 10^5 drive steps and its dependence on grid size (finite-size scaling). Null twin: identical drive and threshold, but on toppling, the excess stress is deposited on four uniformly-random cells anywhere in the lattice rather than the four physical neighbors, preserving mean stress and toppling frequency but destroying local branching geometry; this twin yields exponential avalanche [X] with no finite-size scaling collapse.

nearest_priors.explains: Everything central. It covers the 2D integer-height lattice, the slow random drive, threshold-4 toppling to von Neumann neighbours, and cascading avalanches that run until every cell is stable. It also covers the attractor to a stationary critical state regardless of initial condition, power-law avalanche size and duration distributions, and finite-size scaling. The masked [X] is 'sandpile' in the first instance and 'distribution' in the later ones.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The reservoir-style readout layer and the cross-task transfer claim. The BTW model also contradicts two details of the minimal world. First, it needs dissipation at open boundaries. With periodic boundaries and conservative toppling, total stress grows without bound, so there is no stationary state and avalanches eventually never end. Second, its random-neighbour variant does not give an exponential distribution.

nearest_priors.name: Random-neighbour / mean-field sandpile (Manna-type annealed SOC, critical branching process)

nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The claimed result for the null twin. The known outcome is still a power law with mean-field exponents, not an exponential distribution. Randomising neighbours changes the exponents, but it does not destroy criticality.

nearest_priors.explains: A fixed dynamical substrate with a trained linear readout. Its task-independent correlation structure can be reused across readout tasks. BTW theory predicts runaway, non-terminating avalanches under periodic boundaries. It predicts a 2D power law with finite-size scaling under open boundaries. It predicts a mean-field power law (tau = 3/2) for the random-neighbour twin. A stationary power law under periodic conservative dynamics, or an exponential distribution in the random twin, would be genuinely non-BTW behaviour. statement: For a controller to achieve zero asymptotic error against a class of disturbances or references, it must contain an internal replica of the dynamic generator of those signals (e.g. an integrator for constant offsets, an oscillator model for sinusoids). This is the Internal Model Principle: necessary and sufficient for offset-free regulation in linear feedback systems, and it works by structural duplication of the exosystem inside the controller, not by high gain.
what exists: plant state x; controller state z containing embedded generator matrix S; exogenous disturbance/reference generator state w with dynamics S; error e = reference minus output
what changes: controller state updates as z_{t+1} = S z_t + K e_t, embedding the same S that drives the disturbance/reference; plant control uses feedback of [x,z]
what persists: the embedded copy of S persists as a permanent structural component of the controller, independent of the particular disturbance realization
what is selected: controllers whose internal dynamics include S are selected under long-horizon zero-steady-state-error criteria; controllers lacking S are excluded
what can reproduce: the same embedded-S structure can be reinstantiated in any controller facing signals from the same generator class
what can learn: online identification of an unknown S (e.g. unknown disturbance frequency), effectively learning which internal model to embed
what can transfer: the identified generator model S transfers unchanged to plants that face the same disturbance/reference class
distinguishing observable: steady-state error goes to exactly zero under persistent structured disturbance only when S is embedded; a feedback-only controller without embedded S shows a nonzero residual error scaling with disturbance amplitude
minimal world: A 1D integrator plant perturbed by an unknown-but-structured sinusoidal disturbance at fixed frequency. Intervention: controller A embeds an oscillator mode matched to the disturbance frequency in its own dynamics. Null twin B uses high-gain feedback tuned to match A's transient rise-time and noise sensitivity but has no embedded oscillator mode. Measure asymptotic error: A converges to zero; B settles to a bounded nonzero ripple at the disturbance frequency despite matched gain margins.

nearest_priors.name: Internal Model Principle (Francis & Wonham 1975-76; Davison's robust servomechanism problem)
nearest_priors.field: Linear control theory / robust output regulation
nearest_priors.explains: Everything central. It covers the exosystem w with dynamics S and the controller state z updated by z+ = S z + K e. It covers stabilizing feedback on the augmented state [x,z], so the embedded copy of S acts as a servocompensator. It gives necessity and sufficiency of the embedded copy for robust zero steady-state error. The integrator case (constant disturbances) and the oscillator case (sinusoids) are its standard examples. It also predicts that finite high gain without the embedded model leaves a residual error proportional to disturbance amplitude and inversely related to loop gain at the disturbance frequency, which is the A-vs-B minimal world.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Online identification of an unknown S is not part of the classical fixed-S principle. The description also leaves out standard technical conditions: stabilizability/detectability of the augmented system, and no plant transmission zeros at the eigenvalues of S. Without these, the 'sufficient' claim is overstated.

nearest_priors.name: Adaptive internal model / adaptive output regulation (Serrani-Isidori-Marconi; Marino-Tomei; Bodson adaptive disturbance cancellation)
nearest_priors.explains: The 'what can learn' clause: estimating an unknown disturbance frequency online and tuning the embedded oscillator so the controller asymptotically contains the correct generator. It also covers reinstantiation of the identified model across controllers facing the same signal class.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It adds nothing to the core fixed-S structure. It is an extension layered on the internal model principle rather than a separate account.

nearest_priors.name: Repetitive control / resonant (PR) controllers and disturbance observers
nearest_priors.field: Control engineering (servo drives, power electronics, disk drives)
nearest_priors.explains: These are concrete instances of embedding a generator in the loop: a delay-line model of all periodic signals, or a resonant term at a known frequency. They reject periodic disturbances exactly, whereas pure high-gain feedback does not.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: They are special cases. They do not state the general necessity result and do not cover arbitrary generator matrices S.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The 'selection', 'reproduction' and 'transfer' framing is a relabelling of the observation that the servocompensator depends only on the exosystem class. The learning clause is covered by the adaptive internal model literature.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: There is no substantive distinction to test, since the description is the Internal Model Principle itself. The one check worth making: place a plant transmission zero at the disturbance frequency. Francis-Wonham predicts that no stabilizing controller with the embedded oscillator achieves regulation, so the 'sufficient' claim fails. Alternatively, perturb the plant parameters: A's zero error should be robust to this, while a feedforward-cancellation controller without an internal model would lose its zero error.

statement: Local redundancy (number of parity checks touching a site) is a mutable trait: it increases when a site's recent avalanche history shows frequent large cascades and decreases during long zero-participation streaks, with edges rewired to random neighbors on each change. This turns code rate into an evolving trait shaped by realized avalanche [X] rather than by directly measured noise, producing self-tuned, spatially heterogeneous redundancy with no global objective.
what exists: sites with local redundancy r_i; per-site avalanche-participation counters; toppling dynamics as in the base dynamical law
what changes: every window of W steps, r_i is incremented with probability proportional to recent large-avalanche participation and decremented after long inactivity, adding/removing a randomly-placed parity edge accordingly
what persists: total system size; redundancy budget may float or be capped
what is selected: checks embedded in appropriately-sized (neither vanishing nor runaway) avalanches are reinforced; unused or catastrophically overloaded check placements are pruned or amplified respectively
what can reproduce: individual parity checks are duplicated onto neighboring fragile sites, giving checks a literal birth-death/copy dynamic
what can learn: the population-level redundancy profile converges toward a spatially-varying allocation matched to local noise exposure, learned without central computation
what can transfer: a redundancy profile equilibrated under one noise environment should retain adaptive advantage (faster re-stabilization) when transplanted into a environment with similar avalanche [X] but a different exact noise trace
distinguishing observable: the lag/hysteresis structure between noise injection and redundancy change is mediated by avalanche propagation delay; contrast with a null twin where redundancy responds directly to locally measured noise rate, which should equilibrate similarly under simple noise but diverge when noise and realized impact decouple spatially
minimal world: a ring of N sites with baseline checks, heterogeneous noise injection, and the mutation operator applied every W steps. Null twin: identical ring and toppling rule, but redundancy mutation driven directly by locally measured noise-injection frequency rather than realized avalanche size, matched under simple noise but diverging when a site is protected by a distant neighbor's redundancy.

nearest_priors.name: Self-organized criticality in adaptive networks (Bornholdt–Rohlf activity-dependent rewiring; Bornholdt–Röhl, Meisel–Gross)
nearest_priors.explains: Local connectivity (here r_i, the number of parity edges) is a mutable per-node trait. It is updated on a slow timescale from each node's recent dynamical activity. Edges are added or removed to random partners. The network self-tunes to a heterogeneous structure without any global objective.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The rule direction is reversed: Bornholdt–Rohlf removes links from active nodes and adds them to frozen ones, whereas here large-avalanche participation adds links. It also has no parity-check or code-rate interpretation and no copying of checks onto fragile neighbours.

nearest_priors.name: Homeostatic / Hebbian plasticity driving neuronal avalanches to criticality (Levina–Herrmann–Geisel dynamical synapses; de Arcangelis–Herrmann Hebbian SOC)
nearest_priors.explains: Coupling is adjusted by realized avalanche activity rather than by raw input. The slow adaptation loop is layered on sandpile toppling. It selects for avalanches that are neither vanishing nor runaway. It produces hysteresis and lag set by propagation delay, and learns local structure without central computation.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It gives no error-correction or redundancy semantics. It also lacks the discrete birth–death duplication of checks and the transplant/transfer prediction framed as code-rate adaptation.

nearest_priors.name: Highly Optimized Tolerance (Carlson–Doyle) combined with adaptive-rate / locally adapted LDPC redundancy allocation
nearest_priors.explains: Protection is allocated in a spatially heterogeneous way matched to local hazard exposure, which yields cascade-size statistics. Redundancy is treated as a code-rate resource. It covers the contrast between protection placed where noise lands and protection placed where damage propagates.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: HOT optimizes a global objective by design, while this mechanism is decentralized and evolutionary. Adaptive coding usually measures channel noise directly rather than using realized cascade impact.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The only novel element is the relabeling of sandpile edges as parity checks, so that code rate becomes an evolving trait. Duplicating checks onto neighbouring fragile sites is a mild variant of preferential or copy-based link growth. The line 'catastrophically overloaded placements pruned or amplified respectively' is internally ambiguous. None of this adds a mechanism beyond activity-dependent adaptive rewiring on SOC dynamics combined with hazard-matched redundancy allocation.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Use the ring with a noise source at site A whose avalanches deposit their damage mainly at a distant site B. The described mechanism should grow redundancy at B, or wherever cascades pass, with a lag set by avalanche travel time. The Bornholdt–Rohlf activity rule should instead prune links at highly active sites. The noise-rate null should grow redundancy at A. Then flip the sign of the activity-to-link rule and check which direction still yields bounded, non-runaway avalanche distributions.

blind_text:
statement: Each site retains a decaying trace of how recently and how strongly it participated in a past avalanche; this trace additively lowers the site's effective threshold for a limited window, meaning avalanches leave transient scars that bias where future avalanches are more likely to propagate. This creates path-dependent avalanche [X] (temporal correlations, 1/f-like spectra) beyond what a memoryless threshold model produces.
what exists: sites with scalar state and threshold; an additional decaying 'recent activity trace' variable per site
what changes: After a site topples, its trace jumps up and then decays exponentially each timestep; effective threshold = base threshold - trace, so recently active sites topple more easily for a while.
what persists: The trace values persist across drive/relaxation cycles with a characteristic decay time, functioning as a short-term memory of local avalanche history.
what is selected: N/A directly, though regions with elevated persistent trace effectively become temporarily 'selected' as preferential avalanche pathways.
what can reproduce: N/A.
what can learn: The spatial pattern of traces amounts to a learned short-term map of high-activity regions, shaping subsequent dynamics without any explicit objective.
what can transfer: The temporal autocorrelation structure (power spectrum shape, e.g., 1/f vs white noise) of global activity should be a transferable signature across drive rates and system sizes if trace-based memory is the generating mechanism.
distinguishing observable: Global activity time series shows long-range temporal correlations (1/f-like power spectrum, non-exponential autocorrelation decay) that persist as trace decay time constant is varied predictably; a memoryless threshold model (mechanism 1) instead produces near-white or short-correlation-time activity spectra.
minimal world: Same base lattice/threshold model as mechanism 1, with an added exponentially-decaying trace per site that lowers threshold as described; measure the power spectrum of total system activity for several trace decay time constants. The null twin adds an equivalent-magnitude but spatially-random (non-history-linked) threshold perturbation each timestep, matched in variance to the trace-based one, so mean threshold [X] match but perturbations are decoupled from each site's own toppling history — this should fail to produce the long-range temporal correlation structure.

nearest_priors.name: Sandpile / threshold SOC models with history-dependent weakening (BTW/Manna/OFC variants with site 'damage', fatigue or facilitation that temporarily lowers local threshold and heals over time; e.g., damage-and-healing earthquake models)
nearest_priors.explains: The per-site scalar load with a threshold. Toppling-induced threshold reduction that relaxes exponentially back to baseline. Transient 'scars' that channel later avalanches. Aftershock-like clustering and temporal correlations beyond those of the memoryless BTW model.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not guarantee that the result is a 1/f spectrum robust across decay times. The specific variance-matched, spatially random null twin is a design choice rather than part of the prior.

nearest_priors.name: Activity-dependent facilitation / eligibility trace in neuronal avalanche models (short-term synaptic facilitation, dynamic thresholds; the facilitating counterpart of Levina–Herrmann–Geisel depressing synapses)
nearest_priors.explains: The trace variable itself: it jumps on firing and decays exponentially, is additive with drive, and lowers the effective firing threshold. The resulting 'short-term memory map' of recently active regions and the path-dependent propagation of avalanches.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard LHG uses depression, not facilitation. The model does not by itself predict long-range 1/f correlations. Facilitation can instead push the system supercritical rather than keep it at criticality.

nearest_priors.name: Epidemic-type aftershock / self-exciting (Hawkes) point processes with exponential kernel
nearest_priors.explains: Past events raise the near-term probability of future events locally, with an exponentially decaying excitation. This produces temporal clustering and non-white activity spectra.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It has no lattice threshold-redistribution dynamics or avalanche propagation. An exponential kernel alone gives a finite correlation time, not genuine 1/f, unless kernels are superposed or the process sits near criticality.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The claim that a single exponential trace with one time constant produces 1/f-like, non-exponential autocorrelation that persists across decay constants is not explained by any listed prior. A single timescale normally imprints a Lorentzian corner, so long-range correlation would have to emerge from the interaction between critical avalanche statistics and the memory. That emergence is asserted rather than derived. Everything else is standard.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Sweep the trace decay constant tau over a decade and fit the activity power spectrum. The alternatives predict different spectra. (a) If the spectrum is a Lorentzian whose corner frequency is about 1/(2π·tau) and moves with tau, the system is simple exponential-kernel facilitation, i.e. Hawkes-like clustering. (b) If the spectrum is a 1/f^α power law whose exponent stays fixed, with only its cutoffs shifting, and it vanishes both in the history-decoupled variance-matched null and in the memoryless sandpile, the claimed emergent long-range memory is supported. A second check is to shuffle trace assignments across sites while preserving each site's own trace statistics, which tests whether it is the spatial path channeling or merely the temporal self-excitation that is required.

statement: A diffusible trophic resource is produced at a constant background rate and consumed by synapses in proportion to their activity-driven uptake; a synapse can only grow in weight if local resource exceeds a threshold. Because active synapses locally deplete the resource, this produces long-range effective inhibition through diffusion-limited competition alone, without any dedicated inhibitory molecule, and predicts a minimum spacing between surviving strong synapses.
what exists: resource field R(x,t); synaptic uptake u(x,t) = c(x,t)*w(x,t); weight field w(x,t)
what changes: dR/dt = sigma - kappa*u*R + D*Laplacian(R) ; dw/dt = eta*c*R*(1-w) - decay
what persists: a minimal exclusion distance between mature high-weight synapses, set by D/kappa, robust to changes in correlation magnitude
what is selected: synapses that first draw down local resource suppress nearby competitors from crossing the growth threshold — a first-past-the-post selection among near-equal initial competitors
what can reproduce: the exclusion-zone spacing tiles identically if the tissue area is expanded
what can learn: the system organizes spatial winner placement from initial correlation noise, not stimulus content per se
what can transfer: the minimum-spacing [X] transfers across different absolute correlation magnitudes, depending only on D/kappa
distinguishing observable: pairwise distance distribution of surviving strong synapses shows a hard minimum-distance exclusion zone, versus a null model with resource-independent competitive normalization (e.g., plain Oja's rule) where spacing instead scales with correlation/noise magnitude rather than a fixed diffusion-set minimum
minimal world: A line of candidate synapses with near-identical initial weights and matched independent activity-correlation noise competes for a shared diffusing resource. Intervention: resource field as above. Measure nearest-neighbor spacing distribution of final strong synapses across many noise seeds and varying correlation magnitude. Null twin: same activity/noise [X] and same mean total 'inhibitory budget', but competition implemented as instantaneous non-diffusing normalization (weights renormalized to fixed sum at each step, no spatial R field) — spacing should then depend on noise magnitude rather than being pinned to a fixed diffusion-length minimum.

blind_text:
statement: Memory stores per-subprogram abstract sensitivity summaries, computed once via [X] as functions from an input-perturbation set to an output bound, rather than storing concrete execution traces. This produces zero-shot sound sensitivity bounds for compositions.

what changes: when a subprogram is encountered for the first time, its summary is computed and cached; when a composite program is assembled, cached summaries are composed algebraically to yield the composite's bound
what persists: cached summaries persist unchanged as long as the underlying subprogram and its declared perturbation interface are unchanged
what is selected: subprograms whose summaries compose to tight bounds under frequent compositions are prioritized for caching over rarely reused ones (a cache-eviction pressure)
what can reproduce: cached summaries can be copied wholesale into library instances
what can learn: the library's coverage of composition patterns improves reuse rate over time, reducing average bound-computation cost per composite
what can transfer: summaries transfer across any composite program using the same subprogram interface, regardless of the rest of the composite's structure
distinguishing observable: bound tightness and compute cost for a composite made entirely of cached subprograms match those obtained by full re-analysis from scratch, while compute cost is substantially lower — a gap not observable if memory instead cached only concrete execution traces, which cannot be composed algebraically and require full re-execution for any composite
minimal world: A library of 4 arithmetic subprograms combined into never-before-seen composites of length up to 6; intervention: assemble a composite and compare bound and cost from cached-summary composition vs. from-scratch [X]; null twin: a memory that caches concrete execution traces of each subprogram at fixed sample points, matched in storage size, which cannot produce a sound bound for the composite without re-executing it.

nearest_priors.explains: The [X] is abstract interpretation. Each subprogram's abstract transfer function is computed once and cached. Summaries are reused at every call site regardless of context. Composite results come from composing summaries, not re-analysing bodies. A summary stays valid while the procedure and its interface are unchanged. It is sound, and much cheaper than whole-program re-analysis. Concrete traces cannot give sound bounds; abstract summaries can.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The frequency-driven cache eviction, and the 'learning' of coverage over time. Both are ordinary memoization policy rather than part of the analysis. It also does not guarantee the claimed equality of tightness with from-scratch analysis, since summary composition generally loses precision.

what persists: the control-design map f(.) and the estimator recursion structure, unchanged across the run
what is selected: the parameter estimate value most consistent (least-squares optimal) with observed input-output data
what can reproduce: the two-stage pipeline (estimator + design map) can be instantiated on different plant classes without modification
what can learn: unknown plant coefficients (order, gain, pole locations) purely from input-output data
what can transfer: the estimator and design map are plant-generic and transfer across different physical plants sharing the same model structure

blind_text:
statement: Mutation acts on the abstraction level used to represent a program's parameters, not on concrete parameter values: a mutation event can widen a point value into an interval, narrow an interval, or switch the represented domain from box to zonotope. what exists: programs represented as abstract-domain objects rather than scalars (interval bounds, zonotope generators); an abstract interpreter that propagates these objects to output bounds; a compute budget limiting propagation cost per domain type
what changes: mutation operators probabilistically widen, narrow, or change the domain type (box to octagon to zonotope) of a randomly chosen parameter; the resulting output bound and its compute cost are recomputed via [X]
what persists: the underlying concrete parameter distribution being approximated persists unchanged; only its abstract representation mutates
what is selected: abstraction configurations that achieve output bound width below a target at lowest compute cost
what can reproduce: surviving abstraction configurations are copied with further domain-level mutation to offspring
what can learn: the population converges on domain types matched to the true dependency structure (e.g., zonotopes selected when parameters are correlated, boxes selected when independent)
what can transfer: a domain-type choice learned on one program transfers as a prior domain choice for structurally similar programs
distinguishing observable: populations evolve toward domain types whose tightness/cost ratio matches the true correlation structure of the underlying parameters, a pattern absent when mutation instead perturbs concrete parameter values directly
minimal world: A 2-parameter linear program with parameters that are either independent or strongly correlated across environments; intervention: switch the true correlation structure and observe which abstract domain type gets selected; null twin: a control population where mutation only perturbs concrete point values and abstraction domain is fixed to boxes throughout, matched in generation count and population size, which cannot express the correlation-tracking advantage of zonotopes.

nearest_priors.name: Evolutionary / genetic-algorithm search over abstract-domain configurations (abstraction refinement as search, cf. learned or adaptive abstract-domain selection, e.g. DeepPoly/ERAN domain choice, learned widening/refinement policies)
nearest_priors.field: abstract interpretation / program analysis, neural network verification
nearest_priors.explains: The genome is a per-parameter choice of domain and precision (interval width, box, octagon, zonotope). The abstract interpreter [X] propagates it. Fitness is a multi-objective trade-off between bound width and compute cost. Selecting zonotopes when parameters are correlated follows directly, because affine forms capture linear correlations and boxes do not.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It gives no special name to the heritable-granularity framing. Transfer of domain priors across structurally similar programs requires an added meta-learning component.

nearest_priors.name: CEGAR / adaptive precision tuning and mixed-domain selection (e.g. Precision tuning, partitioning and domain-selection heuristics, Astrée domain parameterisation)
nearest_priors.explains: It refines or coarsens abstraction granularity based on precision needs under a cost budget, and chooses a relational domain only where correlations matter.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It uses deterministic, counterexample-guided refinement rather than a population with mutation, selection and inheritance, so there is no population convergence dynamics.

nearest_priors.name: Genetic programming / evolution of representations (evolvability, meta-evolution of encodings) plus mixed-precision or AutoML search with transfer as warm-start priors
nearest_priors.explains: The representation itself mutates, rather than the values it holds. Configurations are selected against a cost-accuracy Pareto front. Transfer works as warm-starting priors on similar tasks, and the null twin mirrors fixed-encoding versus evolvable-encoding comparisons.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not by itself supply the soundness semantics of abstract domains.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is left unexplained. The combination is evolutionary search over abstract-domain and precision configurations with a bound-width/cost fitness, and the correlation-tracking result follows from known zonotope properties. Framing this as 'heritable abstraction granularity' is renaming. One point is loose: it is not stated whether the 'point value' option inside a sound analysis stays sound when the concrete parameter is a distribution.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare the evolutionary population against a deterministic CEGAR-style refinement, or a simple greedy per-parameter domain selection guided by estimated correlation, on the 2-parameter program when the correlation switches. If greedy or analytic selection matches the evolved configurations and adapts as fast at equal compute, the evolutionary mechanism adds nothing beyond known domain-selection heuristics. Population-level effects that greedy selection cannot reproduce, such as retention of standing variation enabling faster readaptation after the switch, would distinguish it.

blind_text:
statement: Multiple strategy types compete for a shared, finite, replenishing resource, and each type's growth rate is proportional to its resource-conversion efficiency minus a competition term from co-occurring types. This resource-mediated competitive dynamic selects for efficient or niche-differentiated strategies without any explicit fitness function beyond the shared resource constraint.
what exists: set of strategy types with population density; shared resource pool with replenishment rate; per-type resource uptake and conversion efficiency; competition/interaction coefficients
what changes: Each step, resource is replenished, consumed by types proportional to density and uptake rate, and each type's density updates via a Lotka-Volterra-style growth term scaled by resource availability and interaction coefficients.
what persists: Either a single dominant type (competitive exclusion) or a stable coexistence equilibrium, determined by the niche-overlap structure of interaction coefficients.
what is selected: Types with higher resource-conversion efficiency relative to competitors, or with reduced niche overlap, are selected for persistence.
what can reproduce: Each type reproduces proportional to its resource-scaled growth rate (birth-death process).
what can learn: No individual learning; the population-level outcome (which strategies persist) is the selection-driven inference of which strategies fit the resource landscape.
what can transfer: A winning strategy's parameters can seed populations in structurally similar resource environments and predictably succeed if niche overlap with residents is low.
distinguishing observable: Time-to-fixation or coexistence outcome depends systematically on the efficiency/niche-overlap parameters; a null twin using a neutral (Moran-process) model where all types have identical growth rates regardless of efficiency shows fixation time scaling only with population size, uncorrelated with efficiency parameter, distinguishing selection from drift.
minimal world: World: two to four strategy types sharing one resource pool with logistic replenishment; efficiencies and interaction coefficients set experimentally. Intervention: vary the niche-overlap matrix and measure whether coexistence or exclusion results, and correlate fixation probability with efficiency rank. Null twin: identical population sizes and resource replenishment, but growth increments assigned by a neutral Moran process (random type chosen to reproduce/die each step regardless of efficiency); compare fixation-time distributions and their correlation (or lack thereof) with the efficiency parameter between the two systems.

what is selected: organisms robust across the [X] ensemble, not merely point-optimal to the one shock sequence that actually occurred
what can reproduce: organisms above ensemble-fitness threshold, passing π with mutation
what can learn: policy parameters adjust via gradient/evolutionary updates on ensemble loss
what can transfer: robust policies transfer to realized perturbations absent from the training ensemble, tested by generalization to held-out shocks
distinguishing observable: variance and worst-case fitness under held-out shocks, compared between ensemble-selected and realized-trajectory-selected populations at matched total simulation budget
