Variance and worst-case metrics are standard robustness observables.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Explicit do-operator (counterfactual) framing of the shock clamp. Slow meta-level evolution of the plausibility weights over P. The specific trophic-ecology setting.

nearest_priors.explains: Objective is the expectation over a plausibility-weighted scenario set rather than a single realized path. Out-of-sample evaluation on held-out scenarios. Comparing expected, variance and worst-case performance against a nominal (single-scenario) solution.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Population-level reproduction with mutation. Evolution of the scenario weights as a persistent heritable or meta state.

nearest_priors.field: causal inference / model-based RL / open-ended evolution
nearest_priors.explains: Clamping an intervention variable in a learned or known dynamical model to generate imagined rollouts. Requires a clampable model. The environment or scenario distribution itself adapts slowly at a meta level.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Plain averaging (not adversarial regret) as the fitness rule. The evolutionary-threshold reproduction scheme. Curriculum methods typically push weights toward hardness, not plausibility.

Its update rule is not given, and it resembles adaptive or automatic domain randomization or curriculum learning. The 'counterfactual do()' vocabulary is a relabeling of simulated perturbation sampling in a known simulator.

If evolving the weights yields distinctive gains or shifts in which shocks are covered, the meta-level component is the novel part.

statement: Coefficients currently at zero (inactive) maintain a hidden scalar accumulator that integrates unexplained residual correlated with their dictionary atom, decaying slowly over time. When this accumulator crosses a reactivation threshold, the coefficient re-enters the active set with an initialized variance proportional to accumulated evidence, rather than being reactivated from a naive default. This gives 'off' units a persistent latent memory of near-relevance invisible in the current [X] itself.

what changes: a_i decays by factor gamma each step and increments by (d_i . r_t); when a_i > tau, x_i reactivates with variance set by a_i's magnitude
what persists: accumulator values across many steps while a unit remains nominally 'off'
what is selected: which inactive units are primed to reactivate soonest
what can reproduce: the accumulator mechanism generalizes to any number of inactive units
what can learn: the decay rate gamma and threshold tau can be tuned to balance false-reactivation rate against detection latency
what can transfer: the accumulator-based reactivation rule transfers to dictionaries without retraining decay/threshold parameters
distinguishing observable: reactivation latency after a cause reappears is shorter when the cause was recently active-then-silenced (accumulator still elevated) than when it has been silent for a long time — a naive reactivate-from-zero model shows constant latency regardless of recent history
minimal world: A latent cause is switched on, off, then on again after variable silent durations, with several other unrelated causes active throughout. Intervention: measure reactivation latency as a function of the silent duration. Null twin: a model with no hidden accumulator, where inactive coefficients simply retest a fixed reactivation criterion from a reset state each step, matched for the same steady-state false-positive rate, which shows latency independent of prior silent duration.

nearest_priors.name: Locally Competitive Algorithm (Rozell et al. 2008): leaky 'membrane potential' u_i thresholded to give sparse coefficients
nearest_priors.explains: The hidden accumulator. Each inactive unit keeps a sub-threshold internal state that leakily integrates its atom's correlation with the unexplained residual (d_i·r minus lateral inhibition), invisible in the output code. It re-enters the active set when this state crosses the threshold lambda. With warm-started or streaming LCA across frames, elevated sub-threshold potentials from recent activity give shorter reactivation latency, which is the predicted history dependence.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Initializing a variance, rather than a point amplitude, from the accumulated evidence. It also does not cover the explicit framing of tuning gamma/tau for false-reactivation versus latency.

nearest_priors.name: Sparse Bayesian learning / ARD with fast marginal-likelihood basis re-addition (Tipping & Faul 2003)
nearest_priors.explains: Pruned basis functions re-enter the model when their residual-correlation statistic (q_i^2 > s_i) exceeds a criterion. On re-entry the prior variance (1/alpha_i) is set in closed form from that evidence, giving an evidence-proportional variance initialization.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It has no leaky temporal integration across time steps. The statistic is recomputed from the current residual, so latency does not depend on silence duration.

nearest_priors.name: CUSUM / leaky evidence accumulation (sequential change detection, drift-diffusion, leaky integrate-and-fire)
nearest_priors.explains: A decaying accumulator of a correlation statistic triggers a detection at a threshold. Gamma and tau trade false-alarm rate against detection delay (ARL tradeoff). Residual accumulator state after recent activity shortens detection delay compared with a reset or fresh start.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The dictionary / sparse-code context and the variance initialization upon reactivation.

parsed.discriminating_intervention: In a streaming task, reactivate the same cause after identical silent durations but with differing accumulated evidence magnitudes, for example by varying the cause amplitude before silencing. Separately, resetting the internal states u between frames (cold-start LCA) should abolish the latency-versus-silence curve, identifying the accumulator as the source.

what changes: connection gain scales up when a unit's variance falls below target and down when above target, each timestep, driving the global spectral radius toward [X]
what persists: the self-tuned spectral radius, which stabilizes near a critical value regardless of initial conditions
what is selected: connectivity configurations whose resulting activity variance matches the homeostatic target
what can reproduce: the tuning rule itself can be copied unchanged to any recurrent module regardless of its size

blind_text:
statement: In iterated [X] whose parameter space contains a fractal escape/bifurcation boundary (e.g. quadratic maps z→z²+c), the local sensitivity of a soundly-computed abstract classification (bounded vs escaping, via interval [X] with widening) scales as a power law in perturbation radius r, with exponent equal to the local box-counting codimension of the boundary. Regions near the boundary amplify perturbations self-similarly at every abstraction-refinement depth, directly coupling [X] [X] to the [X] of the classified set.
what exists: complex parameter grid c; iterate z_{n+1}=z_n^2+c; interval-box abstract domain of resolution rho; sound escape/bounded classifier L(c,rho); measured local sensitivity S(c,r) = fraction of label flips within radius r
what changes: as rho is refined and r shrinks, the classification stability of each c updates; S(c,r) is recorded as a function of r
what persists: the power-law exponent linking S(c,r) to r near the boundary is invariant across refinement scales once rho << r
what is selected: no explicit selection; the 'surviving' distinctions are parameter regions whose label remains constant under refinement (stable interior/exterior), while boundary points never stabilize
what can reproduce: the boundary reproduces its own statistical scaling law under magnification (self-similarity), not a reproducing agent
what can learn: an observer fitting the exponent from a few scales learns the local fractal dimension without needing infinite refinement
what can transfer: the fitted exponent transfers to predict sensitivity at unmeasured, finer scales without further simulation
distinguishing observable: S(c,r) vs r forms a single scale-invariant power law across ≥3 decades of r near the boundary (fractal law) versus saturating/exponential behavior for a system with a smooth, non-fractal bifurcation set
minimal world: World: 2D grid of complex c, quadratic map iterated with a sound interval/widening escape test at resolution rho. Intervention: sample c_i at varying distances from the true boundary and measure S(c_i,r) over shrinking r. Null twin: replace the map with a linear contraction z_{n+1}=a z_n+c (smooth, 1-D bifurcation curve), matched in grid density, resolution schedule, and escape-radius threshold; its S(c,r) should saturate rather than obey a stable power law, isolating the fractal boundary as the cause of amplification.

nearest_priors.name: Uncertainty exponent / final-state sensitivity (Grebogi, McDonald, Ott & Yorke 1983; McDonald et al. 1985)
nearest_priors.explains: The central claim. The fraction of perturbed initial conditions or parameters whose final state (bounded vs escaping) is uncertain at radius r scales as f(r) ~ r^alpha, with alpha = D - d_boundary, the box-counting codimension of the basin or parameter boundary. It also covers fitting alpha from a few scales and extrapolating it to finer ones, and it covers smooth boundaries giving alpha = 1 versus fractal boundaries giving alpha < 1.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The sound interval abstract-domain classifier with widening. It also says nothing about the 'abstraction-refinement depth' framing that couples abstract-interpretation precision to the fractal geometry.

nearest_priors.name: Rigorous interval-arithmetic / distance-estimate computation of the Mandelbrot set and Julia sets (e.g. Milnor-Thurston-style escape tests, validated numerics, abstract interpretation with interval domains à la Cousot)
nearest_priors.explains: The sound three-valued labelling (bounded, escaping, unknown) at resolution rho. It explains why points near the boundary never stabilise under refinement while interior and exterior points certify at finite depth. The unknown region shrinks with the boundary's box-counting scaling.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The perturbation-radius sensitivity statistic S(c,r). It does not supply the explicit power-law exponent prediction.

nearest_priors.name: Box-counting / Minkowski dimension via epsilon-neighbourhood volume scaling
nearest_priors.explains: The volume of the r-neighbourhood of a set scales as r^(D - d). The fraction of label flips within radius r is exactly this neighbourhood measure, so the exponent is the codimension. The same scaling holds for self-similar reproduction under magnification.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The dynamical origin of the boundary and the sound-classifier machinery.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Only the packaging of the uncertainty exponent inside a sound abstract-interpretation classifier with widening is new, and widening there is dubious because it would inflate the unknown set. Two claims in the description are wrong. First, the null twin should not 'saturate': a smooth boundary gives a clean power law with exponent 1 (codimension 1), so the discriminator is the exponent value, not power law versus saturation. Second, the Mandelbrot boundary has Hausdorff dimension 2 (Shishikura), so the local exponent near much of it approaches 0 with slow corrections, making the 3-decade fit hard.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Measure S(c,r) near the Mandelbrot boundary and in the linear-map null twin over at least 3 decades of r. Under the uncertainty-exponent prior, both give power laws: the null twin with alpha = 1 and the quadratic map with alpha = 2 - d_box (at or near 0). Recompute alpha using exact point evaluation instead of the interval/widening classifier. If alpha is unchanged, the abstract-interpretation layer adds nothing beyond the GMOY uncertainty exponent. Any rho-dependent deviation would be the only novel content.

nearest_priors.name: Turing reaction-diffusion instability (Gierer-Meinhardt short-range activation, long-range inhibition)
nearest_priors.explains: A locally self-enhancing variable coupled to a faster-spreading inhibitor yields a stable periodic pattern from a uniform state. The intrinsic wavelength is set by the inhibitor length scale sqrt(D/beta). The pattern is independent of initial noise and self-tiles as the domain grows (peak insertion). A non-diffusing global inhibitor gives winner-take-all or a single blob rather than a wavelength.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: On its own it says nothing about synapses, Hebbian coincidence detection, or entraining the pattern's phase through structured input.

nearest_priors.name: Swindale / von der Malsburg Hebbian cortical map models (ocular dominance and orientation columns via Mexican-hat lateral interactions)
nearest_priors.explains: Hebbian (correlation-driven) weight growth combined with short-range excitation and longer-range suppression produces periodic stripes or patches of strong and weak synapses. The period is set by interaction range rather than input statistics. Structured early input can bias the map's layout.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Lateral suppression is usually a fixed kernel rather than an explicit diffusing chemical field with its own synthesis and decay dynamics.

nearest_priors.name: Heterosynaptic plasticity via diffusible retrograde messengers (e.g., nitric oxide, BDNF/proBDNF competition) and synaptic tagging/clustering
nearest_priors.explains: Activity-triggered local synthesis of a diffusible factor that affects nearby synapses. It gives a biological basis for the spatial spread of plasticity effects.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not by itself predict a Turing instability or a characteristic spatial wavelength.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is unexplained. As written, the activator w does not diffuse and the inhibitor is driven by c rather than by w. Unless c depends on w (post-synaptic activity depending on weights), a uniform input gives a uniform c and hence a uniform I, so no instability would arise. With a non-diffusing activator, Turing selection can also push toward the grid scale rather than giving a clean band. The claim that the wavelength depends only on D/beta and is invariant to correlation magnitude is stronger than standard Turing theory, where the selected wavenumber generally depends on the reaction-term gains as well. These are specification gaps, not novel mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Two tests separate this from the fixed-kernel Swindale model. First, vary the inhibitor decay beta and the diffusion D independently while holding the correlation strength fixed, then check whether the dominant wavelength scales as sqrt(D/beta). Second, block inhibitor synthesis transiently: in the reaction-diffusion model the pattern should relax with a timescale of 1/beta, whereas a fixed lateral-kernel map shows no such dependence. Separately, sweep the correlation amplitude to test the claimed invariance of wavelength; the Turing prior predicts some shift in wavelength with the activation gain.

blind_text:
statement: Stress can pass from a site to a neighbor only across an edge belonging to a currently-violated parity check; satisfied checks act as insulators blocking propagation entirely rather than merely attenuating it. Because check-satisfaction status changes moment-to-moment as an avalanche proceeds, the effective propagation [X] fluctuates on top of a fixed underlying graph, and this predicts that critical exponents of the resulting transition depend on code parameters rather than being fixed by lattice dimensionality alone.
what exists: fixed Tanner graph with edges labeled satisfied/violated at each instant; stress values at variable nodes
what changes: at each propagation step stress moves only across currently-violated edges, after which satisfied/violated status of all touched checks is recomputed, opening or closing paths for the next step within the same avalanche
what persists: the underlying fixed graph, whose edges are only gated open/closed and never structurally added or removed
what is selected: no explicit agent selection; avalanche paths are moment-to-moment selected by which checks happen to be violated, producing a path-dependent effective [X]
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: none intrinsic; this is a bottom-level interaction primitive on which mutation, memory, and developmental mechanisms above can be built
what can transfer: the quantitative relationship between code rate/degree distribution and resulting critical exponents should be a transferable, class-universal law testable across different codes sharing graph connectivity
distinguishing observable: critical exponents (e.g., avalanche size-duration scaling) shift systematically with code rate/degree distribution at fixed lattice connectivity, whereas a null twin with edges gated open at a matched average fraction independent of real check status shows exponents fixed by lattice dimensionality alone
minimal world: a fixed 2D nearest-neighbor lattice overlaid with an [X]-like check structure, stress propagating only through violated-check edges; vary code rate/degree distribution at fixed lattice connectivity and measure avalanche exponents. Null twin: identical lattice with the same average open-edge fraction assigned by an independent random gate each step rather than by actual check-violation status.

nearest_priors.name: Self-organized criticality sandpile / threshold-avalanche models (Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld, Olami–Feder–Christensen, Manna), including sandpiles on networks where exponents depend on degree distribution (Goh et al.)
nearest_priors.explains: Stress held at sites, threshold-triggered redistribution to neighbors, avalanches, and size-duration scaling exponents as the observable. On heterogeneous graphs the exponents depend on the degree distribution rather than on dimension alone.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Why redistribution is allowed only across edges of currently violated parity checks, and how the open/closed state of each edge is recomputed from the check syndrome during an avalanche.

nearest_priors.name: Syndrome dynamics under iterative bit-flipping decoding of LDPC / Tanner-graph codes (Gallager), and toric-code defect dynamics
nearest_priors.explains: The fixed Tanner graph, the satisfied and unsatisfied checks, and local updates driven only by unsatisfied checks, with syndrome status recomputed after each step. Behaviour also depends on code rate and degree distribution, as in density-evolution thresholds.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The conserved or transferred stress variable, the avalanche statistics, and critical exponents; decoding analysis gives thresholds, not avalanche scaling laws.

nearest_priors.name: Dynamic / annealed percolation and kinetically constrained or state-dependent-conductance models (e.g., dynamic bond percolation, facilitated / kinetically constrained models, conserved-lattice-gas absorbing-state transitions)
nearest_priors.explains: Edges on a fixed lattice that are gated open or closed moment to moment. Transport occurs only through open bonds. The distinction between gating that depends on the system's own state and gating that is independent of it (the null twin) can change the universality class, as in facilitated dynamics versus random dilution.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The specific parity-check rule that determines which edges are open, and how code rate or degree distribution would parametrize the exponents.

parsed.unexplained_residual: No single prior couples an SOC stress-transfer avalanche to gating by the Tanner-graph syndrome, where the gating feeds back on itself because moving stress changes which checks are violated. The specific claim that critical exponents are a transferable function of code rate and degree distribution at fixed lattice connectivity is a conjecture no listed prior establishes. Plausibly it reduces to a known absorbing-state or conserved-directed-percolation class with parity-constrained facilitation.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Hold the 2D lattice and the mean open-edge fraction fixed. Compare three gating rules: (a) syndrome-determined gating; (b) the independent random gating of the null twin; (c) gating by a local state-dependent rule that is not a parity check, e.g. an edge opens if its endpoint stress difference exceeds a threshold, matched in fraction and in temporal correlation. Sweep code rate and degree distribution in (a). If exponents shift in (a) but (c) reproduces the same shifts, the effect is generic state-dependent gating (the prior 3 class) rather than parity structure. If only (a) shifts, and the shift tracks code parameters and not the gating correlation length, the parity-check coupling is doing distinctive work.

blind_text:
statement: An organism maintains a small set of internal state variables (e.g. energy, damage) that must stay within a bounded viable range; action selection is driven purely by the current deviation of these variables from their setpoints, not by an externally defined reward. Behavior is instrumental to the regulation, so goal-directedness emerges from the geometry of the viability boundary rather than from a hand-coded objective.
what exists: internal state vector s with viability bounds [s_min, s_max]; an action set affecting both external position and s via consumption/cost; an environment with resource patches
what changes: s decays each timestep by a metabolic cost and jumps upward when a resource is consumed; action policy updates to reduce expected time-to-boundary-violation
what persists: policies that keep s within bounds indefinitely (viable trajectories)
what is selected: action sequences that minimize the frequency or severity of boundary excursions
what can reproduce: an organism whose s stays viable long enough can spawn an offspring policy with small perturbations
what can learn: a value estimate of state-action pairs with respect to distance from the viability boundary, without any externally specified reward scalar
what can transfer: the boundary-avoidance policy transfers to resource layouts as long as the viability geometry (bounds, decay rate) is unchanged
distinguishing observable: removing the external reward signal entirely (leaving only s-dynamics) should still produce foraging behavior with [X] matching the reward-trained condition; a reward-driven [X] agent with reward set to zero should instead show no directed behavior at all
minimal world: A grid world with energy that decays 1/step and resource tiles that add energy; agent dies if energy leaves [0,100]. Intervention: strip any external reward signal and let the agent act purely to avoid boundary violation (measured via an internal control loop, not backprop reward). Null twin: an [X] agent in the identical grid given reward = +1 for eating, trained to convergence, matched for final survival rate — behavioral divergence under resource scarcity (e.g. risk-taking near the boundary) distinguishes homeostatic control from reward-shaped policy.

nearest_priors.name: Homeostatic reinforcement learning (Keramati & Gutkin 2011/2014), rooted in Hull's drive-reduction theory
nearest_priors.explains: Internal state vector with setpoints. Metabolic decay, and upward jumps when resources are consumed. Reward defined only as a reduction in drive, meaning distance from the setpoint, so there is no external reward scalar. A learned state-action value over internal plus external state. Foraging emerges from regulation. The policy transfers across resource layouts as long as the internal dynamics are unchanged. It also predicts different risk behaviour from an externally rewarded (+1 per eat) agent under scarcity.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Reproduction of policies with perturbation. The claim of a control loop that is 'not backprop reward': in homeostatic RL the drive reduction is itself a reward signal, only computed internally. Hard viability boundaries, as opposed to smooth drive functions.

nearest_priors.name: Ashby's homeostat / ultrastability, together with viability theory (Aubin)
nearest_priors.explains: Essential variables that must stay within bounds. Behaviour that is instrumental to keeping those variables viable. Goal-directedness that arises from the geometry of the viability boundary. Selection of trajectories that stay viable indefinitely (the viability kernel). Adaptation triggered by boundary excursions rather than by any reward.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Gradual learning of state-action values. Grid-world foraging specifics. Offspring with perturbed policies.

nearest_priors.name: Evolutionary / artificial-life survival selection (e.g. Ackley & Littman's evolutionary reinforcement learning, 1991; neuroevolution in energy-based ALife worlds such as Polyworld)
nearest_priors.explains: Organisms that survive long enough spawn offspring with mutated policies. Selection acts on viability alone, with no designed reward. Foraging emerges from survival pressure. Ackley & Littman specifically combine evolved evaluation functions with lifetime learning.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Explicit setpoint-deviation control. A value estimate tied to distance from the boundary during a single lifetime.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Almost nothing is unexplained. The only open point is the claim that a value estimate can be learned with 'no reward scalar'. Any temporal-difference value learner needs some scalar signal, and here it must be the change in drive or in distance to the boundary. That makes it homeostatic RL, not something reward-free. The distinguishing observable is also partly trivial: an RL agent with reward set to zero obviously shows no directed behaviour. The informative contrast is between internal drive-reduction reward and external +1 reward.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Train two agents to matched survival rates: a homeostatic-RL agent (reward = drive reduction) and the described 'pure boundary-avoidance' controller. Then (1) shift the setpoint while keeping the bounds fixed, and (2) introduce overshoot resources that push energy above 100. Homeostatic RL penalises distance from the setpoint anywhere in the range. A pure viability-boundary controller should be indifferent within the range and respond only near the bounds. The two should therefore differ in satiation and stopping behaviour, and in risk-taking in the middle of the range. Against the external +1 reward agent, test overeating past the upper bound when food is abundant: the reward agent overeats and the homeostatic agent does not.

blind_text:
statement: A coding layer computes unit activations as linear projections of the input, but only the top-k most active units are allowed to fire (k-winners-take-all); all others are suppressed to zero via lateral inhibition. Weight updates via a [X] rule apply only to the winning units, driving them toward specialization on distinct, possibly overlapping, input clusters.
what exists: input vectors x; coding units with weight vectors w_i; pre-inhibition activations u_i = w_i·x; sparse binary/masked activation vector after top-k selection
what changes: Δw_i = η·x·u_i for i in the active top-k set only; inactive units are unchanged on that trial
what persists: once specialized, a unit's weight vector remains tuned to its preferred input cluster across further training on other patterns
what is selected: units whose weight vectors best match a particular recurring input cluster become dedicated to it, reducing representational overlap between similar inputs
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: pattern separation: highly overlapping input patterns come to activate increasingly non-overlapping [X] over training
what can transfer: separated codes learned on one set of overlapping patterns reduce interference when a downstream associative memory later learns distinct associations for those same or similar patterns
distinguishing observable: measure pairwise code overlap (cosine similarity of active units) for graded-overlap input patterns before/after training, and measure crosstalk error when a linear readout is subsequently trained to map each pattern to a distinct target; the k-[X] network shows falling code overlap and lower crosstalk error, while a dense coding layer of identical size/learning rate without inhibition shows persistent high overlap and higher crosstalk
minimal world: A set of pattern vectors generated as noisy variants of a few overlapping prototypes; train the coding layer on repeated presentations, then train a linear readout to associate each specific pattern with a distinct target output and measure interference across patterns. Intervention: increase prototype overlap. Null twin: identical layer size, learning rate, and pattern [X] but no top-k inhibition (all units update every trial, dense code).

nearest_priors.name: k-winners-take-all competitive Hebbian learning for pattern separation (dentate gyrus / hippocampal models: Marr 1971; O'Reilly & McClelland 1994; Rolls & Treves; Leabra kWTA)
nearest_priors.explains: Linear activations with top-k lateral inhibition, Hebbian updates restricted to winners, and specialization on input clusters. It also covers the core claim: overlapping inputs map to less-overlapping sparse codes, which reduces interference for a downstream associative memory (CA3 or a readout). The dense-code null comparison is standard in this literature.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The stated rule Δw = η·x·u has no normalization or decay term, so weights grow without bound. Standard versions add weight normalization, Oja-style decay, or an instar term (x − w).

nearest_priors.name: Competitive learning / soft or hard WTA clustering (Rumelhart & Zipser 1985; Grossberg instar; Kohonen without neighbourhood; online k-means)
nearest_priors.explains: Winner-only updates driving weight vectors toward distinct input-cluster centroids. Also explains why units stay stable and tuned once specialized.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The classic form uses a single winner rather than k winners. It does not by itself frame the result as pattern separation feeding a downstream linear associator with crosstalk measurement.

nearest_priors.name: Sparse expansion coding for linear readout (Marr–Albus cerebellar granule-layer codon theory; Kanerva sparse distributed memory; Babadi & Sompolinsky 2014)
nearest_priors.explains: Why sparse, decorrelated codes reduce crosstalk in a downstream linear associative readout (Willshaw/perceptron capacity arguments). Also why dense codes interfere.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Those models often use fixed random projections rather than Hebbian-learned winner specialization.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The only deviation is the unnormalized Hebbian rule, which would diverge without an implicit normalization. This is a detail, not a novel mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Compare the described network against a kWTA layer with fixed random (non-learning) weights while increasing prototype overlap. If learned competitive specialization matters beyond sparsification, the learned layer should show lower code overlap and crosstalk than random kWTA at high overlap. In parallel, test with and without weight normalization to check whether the stated unnormalized rule remains stable.

The mutation step-size itself is tuned online by an [X] law responding to recent accept/reject [X] outcomes.

what changes: Perturb a morphism; [X]-check naturality; keep if [X] or core-shrinking, else discard; update mutation step-size based on recent accept rate.
what persists: Morphisms that repeatedly pass checks accumulate into a stable category; unstable ones are pruned.
what is selected: Morphism variants are selected by naturality-square [X], a logical-coherence criterion independent of downstream reward.

blind_text:
statement: Hierarchical state estimates are updated to minimize errors between top-down predictions and bottom-up signals, where each error is weighted by an adaptively estimated precision (inverse variance) reflecting the historical reliability of that channel. Precision itself is updated online by tracking recent error variance, so unreliable channels are progressively down-weighted in the update rule. This produces context-sensitive attention allocation without any explicit attention module.
what exists: layered nodes with state x_i; top-down prediction p_i; error e_i = x_i - p_i; precision scalar pi_i per node; inter-layer weight matrices
what changes: Node states move via gradient descent on the precision-weighted sum of squared errors; precision is updated as pi_i += eta*(1/(e_i^2+epsilon) - pi_i).
what persists: Learned inter-layer weights and the converged precision estimates across episodes.
what is selected: Which error channels dominate the update, favoring high-precision (reliable) channels over noisy ones.
what can reproduce: Weight and precision parameter sets can be cloned to seed agent instances.
what can learn: Cross-layer generative weights and a reliability model (precision) of each input channel.
what can transfer: The learned precision-reallocation policy transfers to noise regimes and tasks sharing channel structure.
distinguishing observable: Regression slope of update magnitude on injected channel-noise variance: precision-weighted model shows slope approaching the inverse relationship (down-weighting noisy channels), while a fixed-gain error minimizer shows a flat slope regardless of noise level.
minimal world: Two noisy sensor channels feed a hierarchical estimator of a shared latent state. Intervention: raise noise variance on one channel mid-experiment. Null twin: identical architecture with precision frozen at 1 (fixed-gain error minimization), matched on baseline error [X] but unable to reallocate trust when channel noise shifts.

nearest_priors.name: Precision-weighted hierarchical predictive coding (Rao & Ballard 1999; Friston free-energy formulation; Feldman & Friston 2010, attention as precision)
nearest_priors.explains: It accounts for nearly everything. Layered nodes hold states, top-down predictions and prediction errors. States follow gradient descent on the precision-weighted sum of squared errors. Precision is estimated online per channel, and its effect is 'attention' without a separate attention module. Generative weights are learned across layers.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The exact precision rule pi += eta*(1/(e^2+eps) - pi) is not the standard one. Friston-style schemes update log-precision by gradient descent, which converges to 1/<e^2>. The described rule instead averages inverse squared errors, which is a biased and heavy-tailed estimator (Jensen gap), regularised only by epsilon. The cloning and seeding of agent instances is extraneous framing.

nearest_priors.name: Adaptive Kalman filter with online noise-covariance estimation (Sage-Husa / innovation-based adaptive estimation)
nearest_priors.explains: It fuses two noisy sensors of a shared latent state. It tracks innovation variance so that a channel whose noise rises gets lower gain. Its gain falls as injected noise variance rises, whereas a fixed-gain filter shows a flat response. This matches the minimal world and the null twin directly.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not use a deep hierarchical generative model with learned inter-layer weights. Its updates are closed-form gain updates rather than iterative gradient relaxation of node states.

nearest_priors.name: Inverse-variance weighted (Bayes-optimal) cue combination (Ernst & Banks 2002) with reliability learning
nearest_priors.explains: Each channel is weighted by its inverse variance. When one cue becomes noisier, weight shifts toward the reliable cue, and the weight-versus-noise relationship follows an inverse law.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It has no hierarchy, no top-down predictions, no gradient-descent state dynamics, and no learned generative weights. It does not by itself specify how reliability is learned online.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The only non-standard element is the specific precision estimator, a running mean of 1/(e^2+eps) rather than the inverse of a running mean of e^2. This makes precision estimates biased upward and sensitive to occasional near-zero errors. Otherwise nothing is unexplained.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Inject zero-mean noise of known variance sigma^2 on one channel and record the converged pi. Standard precision-weighted predictive coding and the adaptive Kalman filter converge to pi ≈ 1/sigma^2. The described rule converges to E[1/(e^2+eps)], which depends strongly on eps and exceeds 1/sigma^2. That produces a characteristic eps-dependent deviation in the slope of update weight versus noise, and heavy sensitivity to rare small-error samples. Comparing heavy-tailed and Gaussian noise of equal variance would also separate the two: the described rule responds differently, while the standard estimator does not.

statement: Each neuron's identity as excitatory or inhibitory is fixed for its lifetime, constraining all of its outgoing synaptic weights to a single sign throughout learning. This structural constraint (Dale's law) restricts the space of computations reachable by weight learning alone, forcing solutions such as explicit inhibitory populations for subtraction/normalization rather than sign-flipping excitatory weights.
what exists: neurons labeled excitatory or inhibitory; sign-masked weight matrix; activity state
what changes: Weights are updated by a learning rule ([X] or gradient-based) but are clamped to the sign dictated by each neuron's fixed identity at every update step.
what persists: Neuron-type identity remains fixed across the network's entire training and operational lifetime.
what is selected: Only weight configurations within the sign-constrained solution manifold are reachable; solutions requiring cross-sign flexibility are architecturally excluded, biasing toward paired E/I motifs.
what can reproduce: Not applicable.
what can learn: The network learns task-solving dynamics (e.g., working memory, oscillation) using distinct inhibitory subpopulations to implement operations that an unconstrained network could achieve with sign-flipping single units.
what can transfer: Solutions found under the sign constraint transfer more robustly to biologically relevant perturbations (e.g., partial neuron silencing) because functional roles map onto persistent cell-type identity.
distinguishing observable: The trained sign-constrained network requires a measurably larger or structurally distinct inhibitory subpopulation to match task performance, and shows a different lesion/perturbation robustness profile and oscillatory dynamical repertoire compared to a sign-unconstrained network matched in size and weight-magnitude [X].
minimal world: A small recurrent network trained to produce a target dynamical task (e.g., sustained oscillation or working memory) with sign masks enforcing Dale's law throughout training. Intervention: same task, same size, but train an unconstrained (sign-free) version to matched performance and weight-magnitude distribution. Null twin: the unconstrained network post-hoc matched in overall weight [X] but free to flip signs; compare robustness to random single-unit lesion and the range of achievable dynamics (e.g., oscillation stability) between the two.

what persists: The stabilized specialization pattern: which module handles which input region.
what is selected: The module that becomes locally accurate first tends to keep winning that region (rich-get-richer selection).
what can reproduce: High-performing expert parameter sets can be duplicated or split when a module covers heterogeneous subregions.
what can learn: A partition of input space by task structure without externally provided region labels.
what can transfer: A frozen expert trained on one subregion can be transplanted into gated ensembles for tasks sharing that subregion's structure.
distinguishing observable: Introduce a input region late in training and measure retention on earlier regions: the gated model shows flat loss on old regions (low interference) while a monolithic network of matched total parameter count shows rising loss on old regions (catastrophic interference) when trained on the region.
minimal world: A 2D input space partitioned into four quadrant-specific regression functions, presented quadrant by quadrant. Intervention: introduce a quadrant late and measure retention on earlier quadrants. Null twin: a single monolithic network of equal total parameter count, no gating, trained identically, which forgets earlier quadrants more.

what is selected: weak learners that reduce weighted error are given higher alpha and greater influence; poor learners are down-weighted

nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Per-lineage ecological energy flux as the control signal; directional mean bias toward particular edges

statement: Per-connection plasticity starts high and uniform, then decays as a function of cumulative usage/stability, so early-forming, well-correlated representations become locked in and resistant to later revision. what changes: eta_i(t+1) = eta_i(t) * decay(usage_i, t); connections reaching stable low-error states have eta reduced faster, locking them in
what persists: early-locked coarse representations constrain what later fine-tuning can change
what is selected: whichever representation stabilizes first for a given input class becomes entrenched, even if a later alternative would be equally good
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: coarse structure early, fine structure late, with an irreversible-like window for the coarse structure
what can transfer: early-locked coarse features transfer robustly across later task changes, but atypical input during the critical window impairs later adaptation to normal input (deprivation-like effect)
distinguishing observable: withholding a class of input only during the early window versus only later versus never (fixed total exposure budget) should produce a disproportionate, timing-dependent deficit; a constant-plasticity network shows equal final performance regardless of when the equal-duration withholding occurred
minimal world: an orientation-discrimination-like task where a subset of input values is withheld either early, late, or never within a fixed total training budget; intervention: compare final discrimination performance across withholding-timing conditions; null twin: identical network/task with constant, non-decaying plasticity rate, matched on total exposure amount but predicted to show no timing effect.

statement: The control input is augmented with an exploratory probing signal whose amplitude is scaled by the current estimator's uncertainty (e.g., the trace of its covariance matrix), deliberately trading a small amount of immediate tracking performance for information that accelerates future parameter convergence. what is selected: probing amplitude is continuously selected as a function of current uncertainty rather than fixed in advance
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: unknown plant parameters faster than pure certainty-equivalence control, especially when the nominal command alone provides little excitation
what can transfer: the uncertainty-to-probing-amplitude mapping transfers to plants unchanged, since it depends only on estimator [X], not plant identity
distinguishing observable: parameter convergence rate correlates in time with instantaneous probing amplitude, and both decay together over the run; removing probing (fixing its amplitude at zero) while keeping an identical nominal controller produces measurably slower estimator convergence under a low-excitation reference -- comparing convergence time with probing on versus off, on matched reference trajectories, isolates this causal contribution
minimal world: Plant with a constant reference command (so the nominal control alone gives little excitation); controller with uncertainty-scaled probing versus null twin = identical certainty-equivalence controller with probing amplitude fixed at zero throughout. Measure time-to-convergence of theta_hat within an accuracy band and the cumulative tracking-error cost paid along the way; dual control converges faster while incurring a short-term tracking cost, whereas the null twin converges much more slowly (or stalls) under the same constant reference.

blind_text:
statement: Growth cones ascend [X] gradients toward targets; each candidate connection's information capacity is capped by a channel-capacity estimate derived from local gradient steepness ([X]). Connections are stabilized only if the [X]-derived mutual information they carry does not exceed this local capacity cap, so pruning is triggered by capacity violation, not by correlation strength alone.
what exists: growth cone positions; [X] gradient field; per-connection mutual information estimate I_ij; per-site capacity cap C_ij = 0.5·log(1+[X]_ij)
what changes: connections with I_ij > C_ij are progressively weakened/retracted; connections with I_ij ≤ C_ij and above a keep-threshold are stabilized
what persists: the final wiring diagram consistent with local capacity constraints
what is selected: connections whose achievable information matches the local channel capacity
what can reproduce: capacity-satisfying wiring templates across developmental replicates
what can learn: the map refines over iterative growth-and-prune cycles
what can transfer: capacity-consistent subgraphs transfer to gradient geometries with similar steepness profiles
distinguishing observable: pruning that tracks local gradient steepness independent of correlation magnitude, versus pruning that tracks correlation magnitude independent of steepness
minimal world: A line of target cells with a controllable-steepness [X] gradient and correlated source neurons; locally flatten the gradient in a region while activity correlation stays high. The capacity mechanism predicts pruning there; a null pruning rule based on a fixed correlation-magnitude cutoff (matched average connection density) predicts no pruning in that region.

nearest_priors.explains: Growth cones climbing molecular gradients to targets; iterative growth-and-prune cycles; stabilization or retraction of candidate connections; reproducible wiring maps across replicates; dependence of the map on gradient geometry
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: A pruning criterion set by an information-capacity cap rather than by correlation strength or competition; pruning in regions where correlation stays high

nearest_priors.name: Shannon–Hartley channel capacity C = ½log(1+SNR), combined with gradient-sensing precision limits (Berg–Purcell; Goodhill and Urbach's growth-cone gradient-detection SNR)
nearest_priors.explains: The per-site cap C_ij = 0.5·log(1+[X]_ij), with [X] as an SNR set by local gradient steepness; flatter gradients giving lower SNR and so lower capacity
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Why connections whose estimated mutual information exceeds capacity should be retracted. True MI cannot exceed capacity, so a 'violation' can only be estimation error or a mismatch between two measures. There is no developmental update rule here.

nearest_priors.name: Infomax / efficient-coding synaptic learning under resource constraints (Linsker infomax; Laughlin/Barlow efficient coding; capacity-constrained pruning)
nearest_priors.explains: Selecting connections by information content subject to a channel constraint; learning and refinement framed as matching transmitted information to capacity
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The coupling of that constraint specifically to guidance-gradient steepness in axon pathfinding

parsed.unexplained_residual: The retraction rule 'prune if estimated I_ij > C_ij' has no standard biological or information-theoretic basis. Genuine mutual information is bounded by capacity, so the rule effectively prunes where the MI estimator is inconsistent with local SNR, i.e. where correlation is high but guidance SNR is low. This is a novel combination rule and not a known mechanism. The blank [X] also appears to do double duty as both the gradient cue and the SNR.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: In a line of target cells, locally flatten the guidance gradient while keeping source-activity correlations high and fixed. Then separately steepen the gradient while reducing correlation. The capacity rule predicts pruning that tracks steepness: retraction in the flattened region and stabilization where the gradient is steep, even at lower correlation. Correlation-cutoff Hebbian refinement at matched average density predicts pruning that tracks correlation only, with no retraction in the flattened, high-correlation region.

statement: An architecture routes each input through a small, input-dependent subset of specialized modules chosen by a learned gate, rather than processing every input through the full network. This creates localized functional specialization: each module comes to handle a specific input regime, and damage to one module degrades performance only on its regime.

what changes: gate weights and module weights are updated by gradient descent on task loss; the mask is recomputed each forward pass via top-k selection on g(x).
what persists: once formed, each module's specialization to a particular input regime is retained across further training on the same task mixture.
what is selected: modules that reduce loss for the inputs routed to them are reinforced; gate weights that route inputs to the lowest-loss module are strengthened.
what can reproduce: the whole gated architecture (not individual modules) can be copied wholesale to seed a task instance.
what can learn: a task composed of multiple discrete regimes, each requiring a different function, learned via specialization rather than one shared function approximator.
what can transfer: individual modules transfer to tasks that reuse a subset of the original regimes, without retraining the whole network.
distinguishing observable: ablating one module produces damage concentrated in the input regime it served, whereas ablating an equal-sized random weight subset of a matched-parameter dense network produces diffuse damage across all regimes.
minimal world: A synthetic regression task with 4 discrete input regimes, each generated by a different target function. Train (A) a gated module network and (B) a dense network with matched total parameter count on identical data to matched training accuracy. Intervention: ablate one module in A vs an equal-parameter-count random weight subset in B; compare per-regime loss increase. B is the null twin: same capacity, same data, no routing structure.

statement: State is carried along a 1-D chain as a sequence of small 'bond' vectors, each produced by contracting the previous bond with a local core tensor and the current input (tensor-train format). All information about everything before position t that can influence position t+1 must pass through this fixed-size bond vector.
what exists: a sequence of positions; an input value at each position; a core tensor per position (or shared); a bond vector of fixed dimension passed between adjacent positions
what changes: at each step the bond vector is updated by contracting the incoming bond, the local core, and the current input; core tensors are learned to minimize task loss.
what persists: the bond vector is the only persistent carrier of history; nothing else about earlier positions is directly accessible downstream.
what is selected: core tensors that make the bond vector predictive of the task-relevant future given the fixed bond size.
what can reproduce: a learned local core can be tiled/reused identically at every position (shared-core tensor train).
what can learn: which aspects of history to compress into the bond given the bottleneck size.
what can transfer: a shared local core learned on short sequences can be applied unchanged to longer sequences.
distinguishing observable: task performance as a function of bond dimension: a sharp knee where performance saturates below the true information rate needed for the task, distinguishing this from an unconstrained recurrent state (no such knee, or knee scales differently with sequence length rather than with intrinsic task dependency depth).
minimal world: A sequence of binary inputs where the target output at position t depends on the [X] of inputs at two positions of controllable lag k. Vary bond dimension d and measure accuracy vs (k, d). The null twin uses the same chain-contraction update rule but replaces the local core tensor with one that ignores the incoming bond (i.e. resets to a fixed vector each step, matched in output variance), producing a memoryless model with identical parameter count and output [X] but no actual bond-mediated history transfer.

statement: The recursive parameter estimator maintains a covariance/information matrix that exponentially discounts old data via a forgetting factor lambda < 1, so recent measurements dominate the estimate relative to old ones. This creates a finite, sliding memory horizon (roughly 1/(1-lambda) samples) instead of accumulating infinite, equally-weighted history, letting the estimate track slowly time-varying plant parameters.

what changes: standard [X] recursion with covariance update P_k = (1/lambda)[P_{k-1} - P_{k-1} phi phi' P_{k-1} / (lambda + phi' P_{k-1} phi)]; smaller lambda discounts older data faster
what persists: the recursive estimator structure and the value of lambda across the run
what is selected: recent data are weighted more heavily than old data in determining theta_hat
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: time-varying plant parameters theta_star(t), provided their drift rate is slower than the effective memory horizon
what can transfer: a tuned lambda transfers across tasks with similar parameter drift rates
distinguishing observable: tracking lag and steady-state estimate variance trade off systematically with lambda; with lambda<1 the estimator follows a ramping true parameter with bounded lag, while lambda=1 (infinite memory, plain least squares) shows unboundedly growing lag that never catches a persistent drift -- measuring asymptotic tracking error as a function of lambda under a drifting true parameter distinguishes finite from infinite memory
minimal world: Plant with a true parameter a_star(t) that ramps slowly and continuously over time; feed identical input/output data streams into [X] with lambda<1 versus null twin [X] with lambda=1. Measure theta_hat(t) versus a_star(t): the forgetting-factor version tracks with a bounded steady offset and noise floor, while the lambda=1 twin shows growing, unbounded lag that never converges to the moving target.

nearest_priors.field: System identification / adaptive control / adaptive signal processing

blind_text:
statement: An adaptive controller facing parameter uncertainty chooses inputs that are not purely certainty-equivalent for the current best estimate but include a deliberate perturbation component that improves future parameter estimation, trading a small immediate cost increase for reduced future cost via lower uncertainty. This dual control effect is derived by including an explicit estimation-uncertainty term in the optimized multi-step cost functional, formalizing exploration-exploitation as stochastic [X] rather than heuristic search.
what exists: unknown parameter theta with belief distribution p(theta); state x; control u; cost combining regulation error and parameter-uncertainty term weighted by lambda
what changes: u_t minimizes expected multi-step cost (future regulation cost + lambda*future estimation uncertainty), not just the current-step certainty-equivalent cost; p(theta) updates by [X] after each outcome
what persists: the belief distribution over theta persists and narrows monotonically in expectation over time
what is selected: input sequences balancing caution and probing are selected over purely greedy certainty-equivalent sequences
what can reproduce: the dual-cost optimization structure is reusable in any uncertain parametric control problem
what can learn: theta is learned with lower estimation variance at a fixed horizon than under passive control
what can transfer: the calibrated probing intensity lambda transfers to but structurally similar uncertain systems
distinguishing observable: cumulative regret over a finite horizon is lower for dual control than for certainty-equivalent control at matched instantaneous input-variance budget, and parameter estimation variance shrinks faster
minimal world: unknown-gain scalar plant with a few candidate gain values. Intervention A: dual control with an information-seeking term in the cost. Null twin B: certainty-equivalent control optimal for the current point estimate, with external dither added to match A's input variance. Measure: A achieves lower cumulative cost and faster parameter convergence than B despite identical short-run input variance.

nearest_priors.name: Feldbaum dual control (Bayesian adaptive control), in its explicit/suboptimal form with an uncertainty-penalised cost (e.g. Wittenmark's active suboptimal dual control, Milito et al. innovation dual controller, Filatov & Unbehauen bicriterial dual control)
nearest_priors.explains: Caution-plus-probing inputs, the explicit estimation-uncertainty term weighted by lambda in the multi-step cost, the Bayesian belief update over theta, faster parameter convergence than passive or certainty-equivalent control, and lower cumulative cost than CE with untargeted dither. The blanks are 'stochastic [optimal control / dynamic programming]' and 'updates by [Bayes' rule]'.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The claim that the belief narrows 'monotonically' holds only in expectation, and the claim about lambda transferring across systems is a heuristic rather than a theorem.

nearest_priors.name: Bayes-adaptive MDP / POMDP planning over belief states (Bellman-optimal exploration, Gittins-index bandits)
nearest_priors.explains: Exploration-exploitation handled by optimisation over the belief state rather than heuristics, the value of information emerging from the multi-step cost, and lower regret than greedy or dithered policies.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not use an explicit lambda-weighted uncertainty term, because it derives exploration implicitly, and it is not framed around a regulation or plant-control cost.

nearest_priors.name: Certainty-equivalence self-tuning regulator with persistent excitation dither / optimal input design for identification
nearest_priors.explains: Why injected perturbations improve estimation, and it serves as the null twin B. Optimal experiment design explains why targeted excitation beats white dither at an equal variance budget.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It does not jointly optimise control cost and information in one functional, so it has no caution effect.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The phrase 'transfers to but structurally similar' is garbled, and the idea that lambda transfers across systems is an empirical heuristic rather than part of the mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: In the scalar unknown-gain plant, compare the explicit lambda-weighted dual controller with the full Bellman-optimal dual controller computed by dynamic programming over the discrete belief. If the described mechanism is just suboptimal explicit dual control, its regret will match or slightly exceed the DP solution, and some lambda value will reproduce the DP probing profile. A cost of zero sits at the CE limit and a very large cost sits at the pure-identification limit. Also check that A's advantage over B disappears when B's dither is shaped to the optimal input-design spectrum and timed to periods of high belief uncertainty.

blind_text:
statement: A key-value memory stores traces that decay multiplicatively each timestep, but any retrieval of a trace resets its decay clock, so frequency of use rather than absolute age determines persistence. Retrieval itself is similarity-weighted pattern completion over all stored keys. This produces usage-dependent forgetting rather than fixed-rate forgetting.
what exists: memory matrix M of (key_i, value_i) pairs; decay rate lambda; last-access timestamp per trace; query vector q
what changes: each step M *= (1-lambda) unless a trace is retrieved, in which case its decay clock resets; retrieval output = softmax(sim(q,k_i)) weighted sum of v_i
what persists: traces whose retrieval frequency exceeds the decay floor
what is selected: patterns that are retrieved/rehearsed more often persist longer
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: an associative mapping from partial cues to full patterns, and an implicit importance ranking via usage
what can transfer: completion of partial cues that share key features with previously rehearsed traces
distinguishing observable: recall accuracy should depend on time-since-last-access, not time-since-encoding; rehearsed items should show flat forgetting curves relative to un-rehearsed items of the same absolute age
minimal world: a stream of key-value writes with scheduled rehearsal probes at varying intervals; intervention: rehearse a subset of items at different intervals then test recall at matched absolute age against un-rehearsed items; null twin: identical write/retrieval mechanism but decay is a pure function of absolute elapsed time since encoding (no usage-dependent reset), tuned to match the average forgetting curve overall but not the rehearsal-timing effect.

nearest_priors.name: Differentiable Neural Computer / Neural Turing Machine memory with usage-based retention (usage vector decays unless read or written) combined with content-based softmax addressing
nearest_priors.explains: The external key-value memory matrix, similarity-weighted softmax read over all slots, and per-slot usage that decays and is refreshed on access. Together these give usage-dependent persistence.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: In the DNC, usage decides which slots get overwritten (allocation), not a graded multiplicative decay of stored content. It also has no explicit per-trace decay clock reset of the (1-lambda)^(t - t_last) form.

nearest_priors.name: Modern Hopfield network / transformer attention retrieval with exponential recency decay (e.g. ALiBi-style or decayed linear attention) plus refresh-on-retrieval
nearest_priors.explains: Pattern completion from partial cues via softmax(sim(q, k_i)) over the stored keys, exponential down-weighting of traces, and transfer to cues that share key features.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard attention decay depends on absolute position or age. It does not reset when a trace is retrieved, so it lacks the rehearsal-reset dynamics.

nearest_priors.name: ACT-R base-level activation / Ebbinghaus forgetting with rehearsal (spacing effect); also LRU cache replacement
nearest_priors.explains: Retrieval refreshes memory strength, rehearsed items persist, and accessibility depends on usage history rather than encoding age. LRU gives the same persistence ranking by time since last access.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: ACT-R sums power-law decays over all uses, so frequency and spacing both matter. Here a pure reset makes only the time since the last access matter. LRU is binary eviction, not graded decay with softmax pattern completion.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Almost nothing is left over. One minor point is internal: the statement says 'frequency of use' determines persistence, but a hard reset makes strength depend only on recency of last access. Frequency matters only insofar as frequent use keeps that recency short. Nothing about this is novel beyond combining softmax key-value retrieval with LRU-style exponential decay that resets on access.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Hold time-since-last-access fixed and vary the number of prior rehearsals. For example, item A is rehearsed 10 times and item B once, and both are last accessed at the same time t_last, then tested at matched delay. Under the described hard-reset mechanism, recall is identical for A and B. Under ACT-R base-level learning, A is better retained, with a flatter power-law curve. Unequal spacing schedules with the same last-access time likewise separate the two, since spacing effects appear only in ACT-R. Against the DNC, check whether low-usage traces degrade gradually (described mechanism) or remain intact until overwritten by allocation (DNC).

what persists: the accumulated graph structure from earlier epochs, since growth is irreversible in the basic version

what changes: after every pair of successive adaptations, mu re-projects the stacked state toward the canonical single-adaptation state; adaptation-law parameters are tuned to shrink this discrepancy over time
what persists: the canonical single-adaptation manifold used as the comparison target across all curricula
what is selected: adaptation laws/lineages with low associativity-violation error are retained; high-drift lineages are pruned
what can reproduce: a canonicalized post-mu controller state can seed a training lineage
what can learn: the mu operator's parameters, learned to minimize discrepancy between staged and composite adaptation
what can transfer: final competence that is invariant to the order in which a fixed task set was presented
distinguishing observable: variance of final task performance across permutations of a fixed task curriculum for the mu-constrained scheme versus a plain sequential adaptive controller with matched total gradient steps
minimal world: A sequence of drifting linear plants (tasks A, B, C) presented in different orders. blind_text:
statement: The parameter update is multiplied by a gate that is zero whenever the tracking error magnitude is below a threshold delta, so adaptation is causally forbidden from acting once performance is judged 'good enough.' This prevents the estimator from chasing sensor noise or unmodeled high-frequency dynamics once the dominant error has been driven small.
what exists: tracking error e; dead-zone threshold delta; gate g(e) = 1 if |e|>delta else 0; parameter theta
what changes: theta_dot = g(e) * gamma * e * phi; the gate switches on and off as |e| crosses delta
what persists: the threshold value delta and the underlying base adaptation law
what is selected: only super-threshold errors are permitted to drive parameter change; sub-threshold noise cannot
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: parameter values robust to small measurement noise and unmodeled dynamics, at the cost of ignoring genuinely small true errors
what can transfer: delta can be re-scaled and transferred to noise regimes if set proportional to expected noise variance
distinguishing observable: under sustained measurement noise with no true parameter change, theta remains exactly stationary once it enters the dead zone, whereas the same law without a dead zone shows a persistent slow random-walk drift in theta over long horizons -- measuring long-horizon variance of theta under pure noise distinguishes the gated from the ungated law
minimal world: Same adaptive plant/controller as mechanism 1, driven by measurement noise but with constant true plant parameters. Run with the dead-zone gate (delta>0) versus null twin with delta=0 (continuous adaptation). Both match short-term transient [X] while far from equilibrium; they diverge specifically in long-run theta variance once near equilibrium, with the gated version flat and the null twin exhibiting unbounded random-walk growth in variance over time.

nearest_priors.name: Dead-zone modification of adaptive laws (robust adaptive control; Egardt 1979, Peterson & Narendra 1982, Ioannou & Sun)
nearest_priors.field: Robust adaptive control / model-reference adaptive control
nearest_priors.explains: Essentially all of it. The gradient/MIT-style law theta_dot = gamma*e*phi is switched off when |e| <= delta. The threshold is sized to the bound on noise or unmodeled dynamics. The stated purpose is to prevent parameter drift caused by bounded disturbances. Adaptation is frozen inside the dead zone. It trades residual tracking error of order delta for bounded parameters. Transient behaviour far from equilibrium matches the unmodified law, and long-run drift is suppressed.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing substantive. One overstatement: 'exactly stationary' holds only if the noise is bounded below delta. With unbounded (e.g. Gaussian) noise, occasional excursions still produce rare updates. Standard practice also often uses a continuous (smoothed) dead zone rather than a hard 0/1 gate.

nearest_priors.name: Leakage / sigma-modification and e-modification (Ioannou & Kokotovic; Narendra & Annaswamy)
nearest_priors.explains: Same goal of preventing unbounded parameter drift under persistent disturbance and non-persistent excitation. Also addresses the random-walk / drift behaviour of the unmodified gradient law.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Does not use a hard error threshold gate. It adds a restoring term (-sigma*theta), so theta converges to a biased point rather than freezing, and it keeps adapting on small errors.

nearest_priors.name: Epsilon-insensitive loss / margin-based (error-driven) updates, e.g. SVR epsilon-tube, perceptron/passive-aggressive updates
nearest_priors.explains: Updates are driven only by errors exceeding a tolerance epsilon. Sub-threshold residuals produce zero gradient, which gives robustness to small noise.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Not framed in continuous-time closed-loop control. It makes no claims about plant stability, unmodeled high-frequency dynamics, or closed-loop parameter drift.

parsed.unexplained_residual: None beyond renaming. The only issue is the idealised claim of exact stationarity, which requires noise bounded by delta. It is not a novel element.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: No mechanistic distinction from the dead-zone prior is expected. To distinguish it from the leakage/sigma-modification alternative, inject bounded noise with |n| < delta and then introduce a small true parameter change whose induced error stays below delta. The dead-zone law will keep theta exactly frozen and never correct the change. Sigma-modification will slowly re-adapt, with theta relaxing toward a biased equilibrium. Also compare long-run theta under noise with |n| occasionally exceeding delta: sparse updates confirm a hard gate rather than a continuous modification.

statement: A population of units receives feedforward drive and inhibits each other laterally in proportion to similarity of their feedforward weights, iterating until only the top-k most strongly driven units remain active. This produces an input-adaptive [X] without any explicit fixed threshold per unit.
what exists: unit population; feedforward drive values; lateral inhibitory weight matrix; membrane potential state per unit
what changes: potentials update each timestep as drive minus inhibition from currently active competitors; units exceeding threshold fire and suppress rivals, iterating to convergence at k active units
what persists: the lateral inhibitory weight structure persists across trials
what is selected: units with the highest initial drive (best match to the current input) win the competition
what can reproduce: not applicable; the circuit structure is fixed
what can learn: feedforward weights update via [X] restricted to winning units only
what can transfer: the target sparsity level k transfers across changes in overall input contrast/magnitude
distinguishing observable: the number of active units should remain roughly constant as input contrast is scaled, unlike a fixed independent-threshold model where active-unit count scales with input norm
minimal world: 50 units receive random feedforward projections of 2D inputs at varying overall intensity. Compare the lateral-inhibition circuit to a null twin of independent per-unit thresholds tuned to match average sparsity on the training set. Vary input contrast without retraining and measure whether active-unit count stays fixed (mechanism) or drifts with contrast (null twin).

nearest_priors.name: Locally Competitive Algorithm (Rozell et al. 2008) for sparse coding, with lateral inhibition given by the dictionary Gram matrix
nearest_priors.field: computational neuroscience / sparse coding / signal processing
nearest_priors.explains: Membrane potentials are driven by feedforward projections minus inhibition from active units. Inhibition is weighted by the similarity (inner product) of feedforward weights. Only thresholded active units inhibit their rivals, and dynamics iterate to a sparse fixed point. The learned dictionary is updated using only the active coefficients.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Standard LCA uses a fixed threshold lambda, so the number of active units grows with input contrast. It does not converge to exactly k winners.

nearest_priors.name: k-Winners-Take-All networks (recurrent k-WTA; Majani, Erlanson & Abu-Mostafa 1989; Maass 2000)
nearest_priors.explains: Recurrent lateral inhibition selects exactly the top-k most strongly driven units. It gives an input-adaptive effective threshold and keeps the active count invariant to overall input scaling, which is the distinguishing observable.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Classic k-WTA uses uniform (global) inhibition rather than inhibition weighted by feedforward-weight similarity. It does not specify winner-restricted feedforward learning.

nearest_priors.name: Competitive Hebbian learning with anti-Hebbian lateral inhibition (Rumelhart & Zipser 1985; Földiák 1990; SAILnet, Zylberberg et al. 2011)
nearest_priors.explains: Feedforward weights are updated by a Hebbian/Oja-type rule applied only to winning units. Lateral inhibition decorrelates units and enforces a target sparsity level.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Földiák and SAILnet learn their lateral weights; here they are fixed. Neither guarantees exact top-k convergence under contrast scaling.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Almost nothing. The only non-standard element is the combination: LCA-style similarity-weighted inhibition driven to a fixed cardinality k rather than a fixed lambda. This is a known variant (a k-sparse / hard-cardinality LCA, akin to k-sparse autoencoders run as recurrent dynamics). There is also a minor ambiguity: the text mentions a firing 'threshold' while claiming none is fixed per unit.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Scale input contrast by 0.25x to 4x without retraining. Compare against standard LCA with a fixed lambda. Standard LCA's active count should rise with contrast, whereas the described mechanism should hold the count at k. Next, replace the Gram-matrix inhibition with uniform global inhibition, which gives plain k-WTA. The winner set should then differ for inputs whose best-matching units share similar weights: similarity-weighted inhibition suppresses redundant winners, while uniform k-WTA does not.

what persists: the accumulated weight matrix persists across storage of many patterns
what is selected: not applicable; storage is purely additive, not competitive
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: the memory accumulates associations, with recall fidelity depending on code sparsity level
what can transfer: retrieval robustness generalizes to partial or noisy cues of any stored pattern
distinguishing observable: maximum storable patterns before recall error crosses threshold should scale favorably with decreasing sparsity level, compared to dense random patterns of the same dimensionality, which show earlier capacity collapse
minimal world: 500 binary units store patterns at varying sparsity levels (from ~50% active to ~2% active). Vary sparsity, measure recall accuracy vs. number of stored patterns. Null twin: dense random-pattern memory built the same way but matched for total information (entropy) per pattern; compare capacity curves between sparse and dense-matched conditions.

nearest_priors.field: computational neuroscience / statistical physics of neural networks
nearest_priors.explains: Additive outer-product storage of sparse binary patterns in one matrix, recurrent thresholded retrieval from partial or noisy cues, reduced crosstalk, and capacity that grows as activity level a falls (roughly p_max ~ 1/(a|ln a|) times N), exceeding the dense Hopfield limit of about 0.14N

nearest_priors.name: Willshaw-Buneman-Longuet-Higgins net (clipped binary Hebbian associative matrix with sparse codes)
nearest_priors.explains: Sparse patterns stored by summed or clipped outer products, threshold retrieval, and high capacity and information efficiency (about ln2) in the sparse regime
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The description says the summation is additive rather than clipped, and Willshaw's classic formulation is hetero-associative, one-step retrieval rather than iterated recurrence.

nearest_priors.name: Kanerva Sparse Distributed Memory / Palm's associative memory analysis
nearest_priors.explains: Sparse activation reduces interference, recall from noisy cues, and capacity scaling with code sparsity
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: SDM uses fixed hard locations with an address decoder rather than a single auto-associative outer-product matrix with recurrent dynamics.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially none. The comparison against dense patterns matched for total information per pattern is a standard analysis (Palm; Amit-Gutfreund-Sompolinsky; Tsodyks-Feigelman) rather than a new mechanism. The retrieval threshold must be tuned with sparsity, which is known.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: At N=500, measure the number of retrievable patterns p_max and the stored information per synapse against activity level a, for both additive covariance storage and clipped (Willshaw) storage. If p_max follows about N/(a|ln a|) with the covariance rule and an adaptive threshold, it matches Tsodyks-Feigelman. Next, remove the mean subtraction (a pure Hebb rule on 0/1 patterns) or fix the threshold. If capacity then collapses, that identifies the specific prior variant. Any capacity gain beyond these theoretical bounds would indicate a novel mechanism.

Null twin: identical [X], noise, and injected edges but no clamp tag (node0 treated as inferential like the rest) so both networks reach coherence but only the true mechanism keeps node0 anchored to the sensor trace.
