blind_text:
statement: The system passes through discrete developmental stages, each governed by a different universality class of [X]; transition to the next stage is triggered not by a fixed clock but by cumulative avalanche size exceeding a stage-specific threshold, so that developmental timing is itself an [X]-generated (power-law distributed) quantity rather than a deterministic schedule.
what exists: a stage index k; stage-specific dynamical rules (different threshold functions/order-parameter potentials per stage); [X] heights h_i; cumulative avalanche size counter S accumulated since last stage transition
what changes: avalanches proceed under stage-k rules; S += s for each avalanche of size s; when S exceeds a stage threshold S_k, the system switches to stage k+1's rule set and resets S=0.
what persists: the ordered sequence of stage rule-sets persists as a fixed developmental program; S resets each transition but the stage index only increases (irreversible ordering).
what is selected: no within-run selection; across many runs, the distribution of stage-transition timing itself becomes the object of study.
what can reproduce: not applicable directly, though a full developmental trajectory (sequence of stage-durations) could serve as a heritable phenotype in an outer evolutionary loop.
what can learn: not applicable at the base level; stage thresholds S_k could be made evolvable to let development learn optimal staging.
what can transfer: the shape of the stage-duration distribution (expected to be power-law due to [X]-driven triggering) should transfer across different stage rule-sets and lattice sizes.
distinguishing observable: stage-transition waiting times are power-law distributed with a slope related to the underlying avalanche-size exponent; null twin triggers stage transitions on a fixed deterministic clock matched in mean duration, giving a narrow (non-power-law) waiting-time distribution.
minimal world: [X] with 3–4 discrete rule-sets cycled via cumulative-avalanche-size triggering; null twin uses fixed-interval triggering with the same mean interval; run many replicate developmental trajectories and compare the empirical stage-duration distributions (power-law vs. peaked).

nearest_priors.name: Self-organized criticality sandpile (Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld / Manna / Zhang) with integrate-and-fire threshold on cumulative avalanche output (first passage of a renewal-reward / Lévy subordinator process)
nearest_priors.explains: [X] = SOC sandpile. It covers heights h_i, avalanches with power-law sizes, and different rule-sets giving different universality classes (BTW vs Manna vs Zhang). It also covers accumulating S as a sum of heavy-tailed i.i.d.-like increments and firing when S crosses a threshold, then resetting. The waiting time is a first-passage time of a stable-like subordinator, and its exponent is tied to the avalanche exponent tau.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The irreversible ordered sequence of distinct rule-sets. Also, the proposal assumes waiting times will be power-law. First-passage counts of a stable subordinator with tau<2 follow a Mittag-Leffler law, not a pure power-law tail. So the predicted 'power-law stage durations' is not guaranteed; it depends on the time unit, the finite-size cutoff, and whether one giant avalanche dominates the crossing.

nearest_priors.name: Punctuated equilibrium / staged evolution in SOC models (Bak–Sneppen) and record-dynamics / intermittent regime switching
nearest_priors.explains: Discrete epochs whose durations are set by critical avalanche dynamics rather than a clock. The durations are heavy-tailed, and the punctuations are triggered by accumulated activity.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The explicit stage-specific rule-set switching and the counter-reset threshold on cumulative size. Bak–Sneppen keeps one rule set throughout.

nearest_priors.name: Hybrid / switched stochastic systems with state-dependent mode transitions (piecewise-deterministic Markov processes, developmental 'sizer' vs 'timer' checkpoint models)
nearest_priors.field: control theory / developmental and cell-cycle biology
nearest_priors.explains: A mode index k that only increases, with transitions triggered when an accumulated quantity crosses a threshold (sizer/adder) rather than a fixed clock (timer). The null twin corresponds exactly to the timer model. Evolvable thresholds match checkpoint tuning.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Why the accumulated increments are critical/power-law, and the universality-class change between modes.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Little is mechanistically new. It is an SOC sandpile whose rule-set is switched by an adder-type threshold on cumulative avalanche size. The only non-standard element is the claim that stage durations inherit a power-law with slope set by the avalanche exponent. Standard first-passage theory for heavy-tailed sums predicts Mittag-Leffler / truncated distributions instead, so this claim is an asserted prediction, not an unexplained mechanism. Two further gaps: the transient after each rule switch (the system is off-critical until it re-self-organizes) is not addressed, and it may dominate the waiting times.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Replace the SOC avalanche sizes with i.i.d. draws from the same empirical size distribution (a shuffled/renewal surrogate) and keep the threshold rule. If the stage-duration distribution is unchanged, the behaviour is fully explained by first passage of a heavy-tailed renewal sum. If durations differ, especially near stage starts, the difference comes from post-switch relaxation and correlations specific to sandpile dynamics. Separately, vary S_k and lattice size L: first-passage theory predicts scaling collapse N ~ S_k^{tau-1} with a Mittag-Leffler shape and an L-dependent cutoff, rather than a fixed power-law tail.

blind_text:
statement: A population of principal units is coupled to a shared inhibitory pool whose output scales with total population activity, so each unit's net activity is its feedforward drive minus a term proportional to the summed activity of the population. This soft winner-take-all interaction yields sparse, decorrelated population codes rather than dense, correlated ones.
what exists: excitatory units with feedforward drive; one or more shared inhibitory units; coupling weights excitatory→inhibitory and inhibitory→excitatory
what changes: unit activities settle via a_i = f(drive_i − λ·Σ_j a_j) iterated to a fixed point (or via explicit inhibitory-neuron dynamics) on each input presentation
what persists: feedforward weight patterns, which are shaped over time by [X] applied to the resulting sparse activity
what is selected: for a given input, the subset of units with highest initial drive remain active while others are suppressed to near zero (a per-trial competitive selection)
what can reproduce: not applicable
what can learn: the network self-organizes distinct, non-overlapping feature detectors from unlabeled input [X] (competitive/[X] learning)
what can transfer: the resulting [X] transfers to downstream linear readouts, improving generalization relative to dense overlapping codes
distinguishing observable: measure pairwise activity correlation and linear decodability per unit across many inputs: the mechanism predicts markedly lower pairwise correlation and higher per-unit linear decodability than a matched network with independent (non-inhibited) units receiving identical feedforward weights and input [X].
minimal world: A population of units receives feedforward drive from a shared set of correlated input patterns. The mechanism model adds shared lateral/pooled inhibition; the null twin has identical units, identical feedforward weights, and identical inputs but no inhibitory coupling (units activate independently). The intervention holds feedforward [X] fixed and only toggles the inhibitory interaction; the diagnostic is pairwise correlation and downstream decodability, both altered only in the inhibited model.

nearest_priors.name: Soft winner-take-all via pooled/global feedback inhibition with Hebbian competitive learning (Rumelhart-Zipser competitive learning; Földiák 1990 anti-Hebbian decorrelation; k-WTA as in O'Reilly's Leabra)
nearest_priors.explains: Shared inhibitory pool proportional to summed activity; fixed-point settling a_i = f(drive_i − λΣa_j); per-trial selection of the most strongly driven units; Hebbian/competitive shaping of feedforward weights into distinct feature detectors; sparse, decorrelated codes
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The specific claim of improved downstream linear readout is an empirical consequence, not part of the classical formulation

nearest_priors.name: Sparse coding by lateral inhibition (Olshausen-Field; Rozell's Locally Competitive Algorithm; divisive/subtractive normalization, e.g. Heeger)
nearest_priors.explains: Inhibition-driven sparsification and decorrelation; iterated dynamics settling to a fixed point; learned dictionaries of non-overlapping features; improved linear separability
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: LCA uses pairwise feature-overlap inhibition rather than a single global pool scaling with total activity; normalization is often divisive rather than subtractive

nearest_priors.name: Expansion recoding with global feedback inhibition (Marr-Albus cerebellar granule/Golgi layer; Drosophila mushroom body Kenyon cell/APL circuit)
nearest_priors.explains: One shared inhibitory neuron (APL/Golgi) scaling with total population activity, sparsening and decorrelating codes, and improving discrimination by linear readouts (MBONs/Purkinje cells)
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Classically the feedforward weights are random or fixed, with no Hebbian self-organization of feature detectors

parsed.unexplained_residual: Nothing substantive. The masked [X] terms are Hebbian plasticity/learning and sparse code/representation. The claim that per-unit linear decodability is higher relative to the uninhibited twin is a standard empirical consequence, not a new mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Replace the subtractive global pool (λΣa_j) with divisive normalization or with pairwise overlap-weighted inhibition (LCA). Then test whether the selected active set depends only on rank of drive (global k-WTA), on drive relative to mean (divisive), or on feature overlap (LCA). Also silence the single inhibitory unit (as with APL knockdown) and check that correlations rise uniformly across all pairs, rather than selectively for overlapping-feature pairs.

blind_text:
statement: A single neuron possesses several dendritic subunits, each summing a distinct subset of synaptic inputs through a local nonlinear (sigmoidal/threshold) function before the subunit outputs are linearly combined at the soma. This two-stage nonlinear-then-linear architecture lets one neuron compute functions (e.g., feature conjunctions) that a single-compartment linear-threshold unit with the same inputs cannot.
what exists: dendritic branches each holding a synapse subset; local nonlinearity per branch; somatic linear combiner and spike threshold
what changes: branch-local weights update via a local plasticity rule gated by coincidence between branch depolarization and a global (somatic) plasticity-permissive signal
what persists: the branch-to-input wiring and the branch-local weight vectors between updates
what is selected: branch configurations whose nonlinear combination reduces somatic prediction error are reinforced; uninformative branch assignments are not
what can reproduce: not applicable to a single neuron; branch-level feature-detector motifs can be duplicated onto sibling neurons during network growth
what can learn: the neuron learns nonlinearly-separable functions (e.g., [X] of two input populations) unavailable to a point-neuron of equal input count
what can transfer: a dendritic branch's learned conjunction detector can be reused when the same dendritic tree is read out by a different somatic threshold for a task
distinguishing observable: test both models on an [X]-structured input mapping; the multi-branch neuron solves it at chance-beating accuracy while a point-neuron (single global nonlinearity, same synapse count) remains at chance regardless of weight training.
minimal world: Two binary input populations project either onto separate dendritic branches (mechanism) or onto a single global summation (null twin), with matched total synapse count and total input [X]. The task is [X]-labeled pattern classification. The intervention removes branch compartmentalization while preserving synapse number and input marginal [X]. Only the multi-branch model can reach above-chance performance, isolating the compartmentalized-nonlinearity mechanism as causal.

nearest_priors.name: Two-layer (pyramidal) neuron model with sigmoidal dendritic subunits and branch-specific plasticity (Poirazi, Brannon & Mel 2003; Legenstein & Maass 2011, 'Branch-specific plasticity enables self-organization of nonlinear computation in single neurons')
nearest_priors.explains: Branch-local sigmoidal or threshold summation followed by linear somatic combination and a spike threshold. Nonlinearly separable functions (XOR, feature binding) solvable by one neuron. Branch-local weight updates gated by the coincidence of local branch depolarization with a global somatic or plasticity-permissive signal. Reinforcement of informative branch assignments. The XOR test against a point neuron.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Duplication of branch motifs onto sibling neurons during network growth. Reuse of a trained dendritic tree by a different somatic readout. Both are speculative add-ons rather than core mechanism.

nearest_priors.name: Clusteron / structural plasticity of synapse-to-branch assignment (Mel 1992; Poirazi & Mel 2001, capacity of dendritic neurons)
nearest_priors.explains: Selection of branch-to-input wiring configurations that improve the output, with uninformative assignments dropped. Capacity advantage over a point neuron at equal synapse count.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The explicit three-factor weight rule gated by a somatic signal. The formal XOR-versus-chance contrast.

nearest_priors.name: Two-layer perceptron / sum-of-sigmoids network with a dendritic prediction-error rule (Urbanczik & Senn 2014; Minsky & Papert XOR limitation of single perceptrons)
nearest_priors.explains: The hidden layer of nonlinear units combined linearly solves XOR, which a single linear-threshold unit cannot. The update is driven by somatic prediction error. Hidden features can be transferred to a new readout.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Compartmental biophysics and the local coincidence-gating interpretation. The restriction of each hidden unit to a fixed input subset, which gives sparse, non-fully-connected hidden units.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Only the growth-time duplication of branch motifs onto sibling neurons and the transfer to an alternative somatic readout. Both are plausible extensions and neither is required by the mechanism. One minor overstatement: a point neuron on 4-pattern XOR can reach 75% (3 of 4 patterns), not strictly chance, unless the task balances the patterns so that linear readout gains nothing, e.g. by evaluating with a balanced chance-level metric.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Using the Legenstein–Maass setup, abolish the global somatic gating signal (e.g., block backpropagating APs) while keeping branch nonlinearities intact. If branch-specific learning of XOR still emerges from local depolarization alone, the described coincidence-gated rule is not the operative mechanism. Separately, abolish branch spikes pharmacologically (NMDA/Na+ block restricted to dendrites) while preserving synapse count; performance should collapse to point-neuron level in both the described mechanism and the prior.

blind_text:
statement: An organism carries an internal copy of the food-web dynamics and actively tests candidate keystone species by simulating do(species_k := 0) and measuring the resulting shift in the ecosystem's attractor, rather than relying on correlational [X] like degree or co-occurrence. The resulting keystone score is stored and updated online and used to guide foraging or protective behavior. The signal is distinguishable from correlation only because the do-rollout is actually executed against the dynamical model.
what exists: food-web graph with species nodes and weighted edges; organism's internal copy of graph and dynamics; keystone-score table; ablation routine that clamps a node and rolls forward n steps
what changes: keystone score for species k updates as divergence(factual attractor, do(k=0) attractor); organism's behavior policy weights actions by current score table
what persists: keystone-score table persists as memory, refreshed when the web is observed to change
what is selected: organisms whose ablation-derived scores predict true dynamical leverage (surviving shocks by protecting or avoiding truly critical species) over organisms using correlational proxies

nearest_priors.name: Gallager bit-flipping decoding of LDPC codes (Gallager A/B, parallel/serial bit-flip), run as continual noise-driven decoding
nearest_priors.explains: The state and update rule, with only renaming. Syndrome-load is the count of unsatisfied checks on a variable node. Toppling above threshold is flipping the bit when its unsatisfied-check count exceeds a threshold. The flip's effect reaches other nodes only through Tanner-graph edges, since it changes check parities and hence the counts of variable nodes two hops away. Cascades are the bit-flip iterations triggered by a noise event. Relaxation toward low-syndrome fixed points, and the dependence on degree distribution, code rate and distance, are standard bit-flip decoder behaviour, including thresholds analysed by density evolution.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The self-organized-criticality framing: power-law avalanche statistics, the universality of avalanche exponents across code ensembles, and the claim that the system tunes itself to the decoding threshold without external tuning.

nearest_priors.name: Bak-Tang-Wiesenfeld sandpile / SOC as a driven absorbing-state phase transition (Dickman-Vespignani-Zapperi; Manna model)
nearest_priors.explains: The slow external drive (noise flips), threshold toppling, and fast cascades. The idea that separated timescales pin the system at the critical point of an absorbing-state transition. Avalanche-size distributions with a cutoff and exponents, universality classes set by connectivity and degree statistics, and the null twin as a standard sandpile run on the same graph.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The error-correcting semantics. Toppling here is not conservative: a flip can create more violations than it removes, and there is no dissipation boundary. So criticality is not guaranteed, and nothing in SOC ties the stationary point to a code's decodability threshold or minimum distance.

nearest_priors.name: Statistical-mechanics mapping of decoding thresholds (Nishimori line / random-bond Ising for toric codes; Sourlas; spin-glass analysis of LDPC codes; k-XORSAT / WalkSAT-style focused local search)
nearest_priors.field: statistical physics of codes and constraint satisfaction
nearest_priors.explains: Why a sharp decodability phase transition exists and depends on degree distribution and rate. It also covers focused local search that flips variables in violated parity constraints, whose dynamical threshold differs from the ML/SAT threshold. The 2D lattice with a surface-code-like Tanner graph fits the toric-code / RBIM picture.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Avalanche statistics and self-organization. It also implies that the threshold where bit-flip dynamics breaks down is algorithm-specific: generally below the ML or optimal decodability boundary. So the claimed exact coincidence is not supplied by this prior and is in fact contradicted by it.

parsed.unexplained_residual: The claim that the self-organized stationary state sits exactly at the code's decodability phase boundary. Known priors predict that noise-driven bit-flip dynamics reach at best the dynamical (bit-flip) threshold of that specific algorithm, not the optimal decoding threshold. They also do not predict how a noise rate that is externally set would self-tune. In addition, because toppling is non-conservative with no dissipation, genuine SOC (power laws without tuning) is asserted rather than derived; the dynamics could instead stay subcritical or oscillate.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Take one LDPC ensemble with a fixed degree distribution. Sweep the noise flip rate and measure the stationary unsatisfied-check fraction and the avalanche-size distribution. Separately compute the bit-flip decoding threshold (via density evolution or simulation) and the ML / belief-propagation threshold. If power-law avalanches occur only near the bit-flip dynamical threshold, the system is plain Gallager bit-flip dynamics plus an absorbing-state transition. If criticality tracks the ML threshold, or changes with minimum distance at fixed degree distribution in a way the synthetic-load null twin does not reproduce, the described mechanism holds. Repeat the comparison with the threshold T varied: a threshold-dependent critical point points to the algorithmic prior.

blind_text:
statement: An internal control parameter increases monotonically over the system's lifetime (e.g., resource accumulation or an internal clock), and as it crosses a fixed sequence of bifurcation thresholds, the qualitative structure of the state's attractor changes in a predetermined order (point to cycle to multiple points, etc.). This produces discrete developmental stages driven entirely by continuous internal parameter growth, without any external stage signal.
what exists: state x; control parameter r increasing over time; dynamical map f(x;r) with known bifurcation values r1<r2<r3
what changes: r_{t+1} = r_t + growth_rate; x_{t+1} = f(x_t; r_t)
what persists: the ordered sequence of bifurcation thresholds and attractor types across the parameter axis
what is selected: the growth_rate and starting r0 select which stages are reached within a fixed lifetime
what can reproduce: offspring can inherit r0 and growth_rate, reproducing the same developmental trajectory
what can learn: growth_rate can be tuned by feedback from environment (accelerating or delaying stage transitions)
what can transfer: the staged sequence transfers to any system sharing the same map f with a slowly varying parameter
distinguishing observable: plot attractor type (period, number of fixed points) against elapsed time: true bifurcation-driven development shows sharp, discrete jumps at specific times regardless of noise level, while a system merely interpolating continuously between behaviors shows gradual smooth change
minimal world: A logistic-map-like x_{t+1}=r_t*x_t*(1-x_t) with r_t creeping upward through known bifurcation points (period-doubling cascade). Intervention: vary growth_rate to compress or stretch the developmental timeline and check the stage sequence order is preserved. Null twin: replace r_t's effect with a direct time-indexed lookup table that reproduces the same attractor-type-vs-time curve without any parameter actually crossing a bifurcation (so perturbing initial x has no qualitative effect, unlike the real bifurcation case).

nearest_priors.name: Slow passage through bifurcations / dynamic bifurcation (non-autonomous ramped-parameter map, e.g. logistic map with slowly drifting r; Baer–Erneux–Rinzel, Neishtadt, Kapral–Mandel)
nearest_priors.explains: Monotone parameter drift through an ordered sequence of bifurcation values (period-doubling cascade), producing discrete qualitative changes in orbit structure over time. The rate of drift sets when transitions occur. The stage order is preserved because it is fixed by the map's bifurcation diagram.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The biological framing (inheritance of r0 and growth_rate, environmental tuning of growth_rate). It also predicts things the description gets wrong: finite ramp rates cause a bifurcation delay, so transitions lag the static thresholds r1, r2, r3 by a rate-dependent amount, and noise shifts and blurs the transitions rather than leaving them sharp 'regardless of noise level'.

nearest_priors.name: Waddington landscape / bifurcation-driven cell-fate and developmental staging (Huang, Kauffman; slowly changing morphogen or clock parameter)
nearest_priors.explains: Discrete developmental stages arising from continuous change in an internal parameter, with no external stage signal. It also covers the heritable developmental program and the environmental acceleration or delay of stage transitions (heterochrony).
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The specific period-doubling map or attractor-period readout. That is supplied by the dynamical-systems prior.

nearest_priors.name: Quasi-static parameter sweep / adiabatic tracking of attractors (and, for timing, the heterochrony / rate-of-development concept)
nearest_priors.explains: Treating a slowly varying parameter as quasi-static, so the system occupies the attractor of f(.; r) at each moment. Scaling growth_rate compresses or stretches the timeline while keeping the order of stages.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Non-adiabatic effects such as bifurcation delay and transient memory, and the selection and inheritance framing.

parsed.unexplained_residual: Essentially nothing mechanistic. The 'reproduce' and 'learn' clauses just relabel parameter inheritance and parameter tuning. Two claims in the description are inaccurate relative to the prior: (1) noise-independent sharp jumps; in fact noise advances and smears transitions, and the ramp rate delays them. (2) The null-twin criterion that perturbing x0 changes qualitative outcome in the real case; for the logistic map the stable attractor is typically unique, so x0 perturbations mostly do not change attractor type, except near thresholds, where delay and phase effects matter.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: Vary growth_rate over orders of magnitude and add controlled noise. A true slow-passage bifurcation mechanism shows these signatures: transition times that lag the static thresholds r1, r2, r3 by a rate-dependent delay that shrinks as growth_rate goes to 0; noise that reduces this delay; and critical slowing down (rising autocorrelation and variance of x) just before each jump. A time-indexed lookup table shows none of these: no rate-dependent delay, no noise-sensitive timing, and no precursor slowing. Freezing r mid-run should also hold the current attractor indefinitely in the real mechanism, but not in a clock-driven table.

blind_text:
statement: A state vector updates by a contraction map (Lipschitz constant strictly less than 1 in some metric); repeated iteration drives every initial condition within a basin to the same fixed point, giving a computable content-addressable memory. The fixed point is not stored explicitly anywhere but is reconstructed by dynamics from partial or noisy cues.
what exists: state x in R^n; weight matrix W with spectral norm < 1; bias b; update map f(x)=tanh(Wx+b)
what changes: x_{t+1} = f(x_t); trajectories evolve deterministically each step
what persists: the fixed point x* = f(x*) within each basin, and the basin boundaries themselves
what is selected: parameter regimes (W,b) that keep the map contractive are retained; non-contractive regimes are discarded
what can reproduce: any initial condition inside a basin reproduces the same terminal state x*
what can learn: W,b can be updated by a local rule (e.g. gradient descent on distance to target patterns) to relocate fixed points to desired attractors
what can transfer: the same fixed-point structure completes partial or corrupted inputs that fall in an existing basin
distinguishing observable: exponential convergence rate to a single point independent of initial condition (within basin), versus a non-contractive baseline (spectral norm ≥1) showing divergence or sustained wandering with no convergence
minimal world: World: 8-dimensional binary-ish vectors evolving under x_{t+1}=tanh(Wx_t) with W built to have spectral norm 0.8. Intervention: corrupt a stored pattern in k bits and iterate the map, measuring recovery. Null twin: identical dimensionality and identical marginal [X] of W's entries, but W rescaled to spectral norm 1.5 (matching mean/variance of entries but not the contraction property); this twin shows no reliable convergence to the original pattern despite matching first- and second-order [X].

nearest_priors.explains: Content-addressable memory: stored patterns are attractors, recall from partial or noisy cues, patterns held in the weights rather than stored explicitly, a tanh recurrent update, and learning W and b to move fixed points onto target patterns.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Hopfield memories need multistability, which requires gain or spectral radius above 1. That conflicts with the described contraction property, so the spectral-norm-0.8 regime cannot store multiple patterns.

nearest_priors.name: Banach contraction mapping theorem applied to contractive RNNs / echo-state property
nearest_priors.explains: Exponential convergence at rate ≤0.8^t from any initial condition to a single fixed point x* = f(x*). Also explains divergence or wandering in non-contractive regimes, and why contractive parameter regimes would be retained.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Multiple basins, basin boundaries and pattern-specific recall. A global contraction (tanh is 1-Lipschitz and ||W|| < 1) has exactly one fixed point on all of R^n. With b = 0 that point is x = 0, so corrupted patterns decay to zero rather than being recovered. The echo-state property is precisely the forgetting of initial conditions.

nearest_priors.explains: A contractive fixed-point iteration used as computation, with W and b trained by gradient descent (implicit differentiation) so the input-conditioned fixed point hits targets, and contractivity enforced by constraining parameters.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Content-addressable memory from the initial state. In DEQs the input enters through the bias, and the initial condition is irrelevant by design.

A map with Lipschitz constant below 1 in a single metric has a unique global fixed point, so 'every initial condition within a basin', 'basin boundaries', and 'recover the stored corrupted pattern' cannot all hold. Pattern-specific recovery would require locally contractive attractors in a globally non-contractive map, which is a Hopfield regime. Repeating the test with the gain-1.5 twin built by Hebbian outer products would show that twin performing recall.

statement: A hierarchy of layers each maintains a state estimate and generates a top-down prediction of the layer below; only the residual prediction error is passed upward and used, locally, to update both the generating layer's weights and the lower layer's state estimate. what changes: Each timestep: higher layers predict lower layer states; error units compute residual; residuals drive local gradient updates to generative weights and to the state estimate at the layer below, iterated to convergence per input.
what persists: The learned generative weights, encoding regularities that make future prediction errors small for structurally similar inputs.
what is selected: Weight configurations that minimize accumulated residual error across the training distribution are retained.
what can reproduce: The full weight set can be copied to seed instances, propagating the learned generative model.
what can learn: The hierarchy learns a multi-level generative model online from a stream of inputs.
what can transfer: Learned high-level priors transfer to inputs sharing the same compositional structure (e.g., occluded or partially corrupted versions of trained patterns).
distinguishing observable: On partially occluded test inputs, the hierarchy fills in plausible completions with error concentrated at the occlusion boundary and decreasing over iterative settling; a null twin — a purely feedforward network trained with the same per-layer loss magnitudes but no top-down generative pathway or iterative settling — shows uniformly high error across the occluded region with no boundary-localized decay.
minimal world: World: sequences of small synthetic images with structured occlusions (e.g., a moving bar sometimes hidden behind a static mask). Intervention: train the layered [X] network on unoccluded sequences, then test completion accuracy and per-pixel residual error dynamics on occluded sequences with top-down connections optionally lesioned. Null twin: same layer sizes and total parameter count, trained purely feedforward to predict the next frame with matched loss, no recurrent top-down/error-driven settling loop; compare occlusion-completion accuracy and residual spatial profile between the two.

statement: Training is driven jointly by prediction accuracy and by an explicit description-length penalty on the model's parameters, computed via a code-length estimator (e.g., adaptive quantization bins). This pressure favors compact, rule-like parameter configurations over configurations that merely memorize the training set, even at equal training accuracy.

what changes: w is updated to jointly reduce error and code length; the effective bit-budget allocated to w shrinks over training as compressible structure is found.
what persists: compact, generalizable sub-structures in w that account for most of the accuracy at low code cost persist; idiosyncratic high-code-cost parameters get pruned or merged.
what is selected: parameter configurations achieving the best accuracy-per-bit are retained across training iterations.
what can reproduce: in a population-search variant, models can reproduce with mutation preferentially from lower-codelength, higher-fitness ancestors.
what can learn: an underlying short logical/algebraic rule generating the labels, rather than a lookup table, when the data supports a compressible rule.
what can transfer: the rule-like representation generalizes correctly to out-of-distribution inputs that a memorized lookup table cannot handle.
distinguishing observable: held-out generalization is substantially better under codelength-penalized training than under a matched-capacity model at equal training accuracy — the gap appears specifically off-distribution, not on-distribution.
minimal world: A symbolic task where labels follow a short logical rule plus label noise. Train (A) a network with the [X] penalty and (B) an identical architecture with a fixed uniform quantization/regularization tuned to match A's average weight-magnitude [X] but with no adaptive pressure to further compress (a fixed, non-adaptive bit-budget). Compare out-of-distribution generalization at matched training accuracy.

what changes: iterating K_{t+1} = [X](K_t) traces a flow in parameter space as the observation scale increases
what persists: fixed points K* of the [X] flow persist as attractors; systems flowing to the same K* share the same long-distance [X]
what is selected: initial parameter values are effectively sorted into basins of attraction ('phases') of the [X] flow
what can reproduce: different microscopic lattices with different initial K, if in the same basin, reproduce identical coarse-grained correlation [X]
what can learn: the effective coarse-scale rule can be learned/estimated by observing successive coarse-grainings of any single realization
what can transfer: a macroscopic description learned from one microscopic system transfers to any other system in the same universality class
distinguishing observable: correlation functions collapse onto a single curve under the scale-dependent rescaling predicted by the [X] fixed point, whereas a baseline system without the coarse-graining structure (same average correlation length, but no true self-similar generating rule) fails to collapse across scales
minimal world: World: 2D Ising-like lattice with coupling K, coarse-grained by 2x2 block-majority voting repeatedly. Intervention: measure spin-spin correlation function at several coarse-graining depths and check for scale collapse near the critical K*. Null twin: a lattice with spins drawn i.i.d. but reweighted to match the same single-scale correlation length as the critical system (matched two-point [X] at one scale only); its correlation function does not collapse under repeated coarse-graining.

nearest_priors.does_not_explain: Nothing central. The 'learned from a single realization' clause is not part of classical RG, but it is standard in Monte Carlo RG (Swendsen) and in inverse or ML-learned RG.

nearest_priors.explains: Estimating the effective coarse-scale couplings and RG map by measuring correlations on successively blocked configurations of sampled lattices, including a single large realization.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: The conceptual origin of universality and fixed-point theory. It is a numerical implementation of the first prior, not a separate mechanism.

nearest_priors.explains: Collapse of correlation functions onto a universal curve under scale-dependent rescaling; this is the distinguishing observable.
nearest_priors.does_not_explain: It supplies no explicit coarse-graining map, no parameter flow and no basins. It is phenomenological rather than generative.

This is imprecision, not new mechanism.
parsed.discriminating_intervention: No intervention separates the description from Wilson-Kadanoff RG, because they are the same mechanism. Within RG, a sharp test is to compute the linearised block-majority map at K* and compare its eigenvalue-derived exponents with the observed collapse exponents.
